333. The Committee is constrained to note that Government failed to protect the interests
of the Visakhapatnam Port, a PSU unit that could not control the situation which led to
setting up of Gangavaram Port. The Gangavaram Port was initially proposed by the
Visakhapatnam Port Trust to serve as a satellite port of the Visakhapatnam Port Trust to
meet the requirement of SAIL steel plant with a view to reduce the air pollution at the
Visakhapatnam area. However in the year 2000 the State Government had formulated a
steering committee for Gangavaram Port Development with State Government as the nodal
agency. The project was ultimately taken away from the Visakhapatnam Port Trust and
handed over to the private operator.
334. The Committee is of the view that Vishakhapa1nam Port has to face a stiff
competition from Gangavaram Port. The Visakhapatnam Port for years remained number
one among the Major Ports in cargo traffic. However, during the past two-three years it has
slipped to second position behind Kandla mainly due to the fact that a major portion of its
cargoes consisting of coking coal, thermal coal and others have been diverted to the
Gangavaram Port. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Visakhapatnam Port
should be given all financial assistance and autonomy to ensure that the upgradation
projects including deepening of draft, deepening of Ports, strengthening of berths in inner
harbour, development of truck parking terminal and mechanical handling facilities and
inner harbour are completed in a time-bound manner to compete with the Gangavaram
Port. The Committee has observed that the loss of Gangavaram Port from the hands of
Visakhapatnam Port is a classical example how dear the delay in timely decision making
could be.
335. The Committee also recommends that the Government should come out with
appropriate guidelines to ensure that no port is coming up in the vicinity of the Major
Ports. Even if some port has to be developed near to the Major Ports, the Major Ports
should be given the option to develop it rather than allowing other agencies encroaching
into those areas which may ultimately affect the functional viability of the Major Ports.
336. A blanket ban on privatization in the maritime sector is not possible. The
Committee, however, recommends that in the broad interest of the nation, the
Government’s endeavour should be to take steps for expansion and improvement of the
Public Sector and to ensure that tax payers money invested in the PSU do not go waste.
337. The Committee also recommends that the Government should ensure that the
management of private ports fulfills their obligations/promises towards the society. There
are reports that the people of Gangavaram and Dibbapalem villages were protesting for not
providing employment to the fisherman by the management of Gangavaram Port.
Cabotage Issue
338. India follows a Cabotage policy by exercising powers under Section 406 and 407 of the
MS Act, 1958 dealing with licensing of ships. Section 406 governs the provision of granting license
to two categories of ships
(i) Indian ships within the meaning of section 21 of the Act
(ii) Ships chartered by an Indian entity
339. Such licenses include the license for the whole or any part of the coasting trade or India.
Section 407 deals with licensing of foreign flag ships for the remaining category for coasting trade
which are essentially foreign flag ships not chartered by any Indian entity.

59
340. For the successful commencement of operation of India’s first Transshipment Terminal
there is need for immediate resolution of the Cabotage issue, which has serious implications. To
be developed and recognized as a transshipment hub port in the region, the ICTT need to mainly
attract the mainline vessels, which are at present transshipping the Indian bound/origin containers,
mainly at Colombo. The ICTT is thereby expected to facilitate price competitiveness of the Indian
produce and reduce the dependence on foreign ports for transshipment, in the strategic interest of
the Indian Exim trade.
341. The Committee was informed that the Cabotage Law (Section 406 and 407 of Merchant
Shipping Act, 1958) acts as a serious deterrent in the diversion of India bound transshipment traffic
from Colombo and in facilitating the development of ICTT as a transshipment hub port. The
existing Cabotage Law mandates that movement of containerized cargo between Indian Coastal
Ports is permissible only on Indian flag vessels. This effectively means that a foreign shipping line,
irrespective of whether it operates a ‘feeder’ , non-feeder or mainline vessel, would not be able
to carry a container either to or from ICTT to any other port in India.
342. M/s. India Gateway Terminal Private Limited (IGTPL), Cochin, the BOT operator of ICTT
had sought the intervention of Cochin Port Trust to request the Government for considering the
relaxation in Cabotage Law. They have inter alia stated that they have taken up the matter of
exemption for containerized trade at ICTT from the applicability of Cabotage with the Director
General of Shipping and also with the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, etc. They have further
requested for a waiver of the Cabotage Law and for the correct interpretation by the authorities
regarding its applicability to containerized EXIM cargo proposed to be transshipped from
Vallarpadam (ICTT).
343. M/s IGTPL have mentioned that the sizeable investments made by them as well as by the
Government of India in providing rail-road connectivity and for the deepening of navigational
channel, would be jeopardized in case no waiver is granted to ICTT. The Cochin Port Trust has
already made a representation to the Ministry of Commerce in June, 2009 seeking their intervention.
344. The Government is empowered to grant relaxation regarding Licensing of ships for coasting
trade in terms of Section 407, sub section (3) of the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958. The relevant
provision is quoted below:
“The Central Government may, by general or special order, direct that the provisions of sub-
section (1) shall not apply in respect of any part of the coasting trade of India or shall
apply subject to such conditions and restrictions as may be specified in the order.”
345. Some of the important aspects in this regard, to be taken cognizance of, are as given below:
• The present annual volume handled at Colombo port is around 3.80 million TEUs, of
which roughly 75% (2.85 million TEUs) is total transshipment. Of this, about 70%
(1.99 million TEUs) per annum is transshipment from Indian Ports, and out of which,
60% (1.19 million TEUs) is to and from South Indian Ports; which could be the
potential business for ICTT Vallarpadam.
• On commissioning of Vallarpadam, many advantages will accrue to Indian exporters, in
terms of reduction in feeder service costs and faster shipping service if the cargo is
routed through Cochin instead of Colombo.
• This advantage, however, can be optimized if the present system of transportation of
containers by the Main line operators through Colombo port where they are re-routing
their India bound transshipment containers through foreign flag vessels of their own
or of the lines in  their global consortia, is permitted at ICTT, Vallarpadam too.

60
• As per the existing regulations, the present capacity of the Indian flag Ships engaged
in coastal transportation is highly inadequate even to handle present total traffic of 1.19
million TEUs bound for South India. Moreover, some of these ships are also engaged
in transportation of India based coastal containers on fixed routes and would not be
available.
• In effect, the Cabotage regulations will act as the limiting factor for attracting the
traffic from the port of Colombo as most of the main line carriers would like to
continue there at, availing present advantage of sharing slots on heir ships amongst the
members of consortia operating worldwide.
• While it is essential to protect the interest of the Indian flag vessles in coastal trade,
protection of the interests of the Indian port at Vallarpadam being developed as major
transshipment hub, and also the Indian EXIM trade at large cannot be undermined.
346. In view of the critical implication of this regulation in the successful
implementation of the ICTT project and in the larger interest of economic self-reliance
of the Indian EXIM trade, it is imperative that the Cabotage Law is relaxed to enable
transshipment of containers through foreign flag vessels from ICTT, Cochin. The
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government should immediately undertake a
review of the Cabotage law and take appropriate decision in consultation with all the
stakeholders involved.
Tourism
347. Cruise facilities and passenger water transportation may be better explored especially in the
case of States which are having plenty of inter-land water connecting canals and/or rivers are
available. Tuticorin is an ideal place for  the development of water based sports activities like Ports
of Kerala, Andaman and Maldives to develop Tourism.
348. The Committee recommends Tuticorin Port authorities to earmark a few waters front
for this purpose. The Committee has observed that tourism can supplement to the revenue
earnings of the Ports. Separate cruise terminals at suitable places need to be maintained
for the benefit of the visitors. Care should be taken for the easy access of the terminals
to the main tourist places in the area. Also proper security clearance facilities should be
created at the respective places in consultation with security agencies.
Inland Water Transport
349. Inland Waterways Authority of India is undertaking projects for  making National Waterways
1, 2 and 3 (Ganga, Brhmaputra and West Coast Canal) fully functional by providing. navigational
channel of 3 m/2m/1.5m depth for  about 330 days in a year, in various stretches, fixed and
floating terminals at selected locations and aids for day and night navigation with DGPS
connectivity. Many of the projects made progress, during the year viz., construction of Cutter
Suction Dredging units and Hydraulic Surface Dredger for National Waterways 1, 2 & 3,
installation of DGPS stations at Bhagalpur and Jogighopa, capital dredging between Alapuzha and
Edapallikota in National Waterway-3, extension of night navigation facilities in some stretches,
construction work for high level jetty at Patna terminal, high level jetty at Pandu terminal, terminal
at Kolkata (G.R. Jetty) and Kollam, etc. Six Cutter Suction Dredgers (CSD) have been received.
Two RO-RO jetties at Bolgatty Island and Willingdon Island in Cochin Port Trust area have been
constructed to provide connectivity between National Waterway-3 and International Container
Transshipment Terminal (ICCTT), Vallarpadam.

61
350. W ith regard to cargo transportation on three National Waterways, regular transportation of
stone chips on National Waterway-l and transportation of ODCs on National Waterways 1 & 2,
introduction of cruise vessel operation between Kolkata and Varanasi, apart from  regular movement
of cruise vessels/house boats in National Waterways 1, 2 & 3, show revival of Inland Water
Transport (IWT). NTPC agreed for  long-term commitment of transportation of 3 million tonnes
imported coal through IWT mode to Farakka and Kahalgaon STPS for  a period of 7 years. Under
Indo-Bangladesh Protocol on IWT, Ashuganj in Bangladesh and Silghat in India has been added as
a Ports of Call in the Protocol route and also Ashuganj as a multi modal point  for transportation
of goods to North-East. MEA has appointed an Indian contractor for construction of port and IWT
components of Kaladan Multimodal transport project at a cost Rs.342 crores based on the DPR
developed by Inland Waterway Authority of India. Contract was signed In May, 2010 and the
completion period of the project is 3 years.
351. The Committee is of the view that linking of water ways as in the case of National
Waterways 1&2 with the Kolkata Port system, National Waterway-3 with the Cochin Port
and the proposed plan for linking of National Waterway-5 with Paradip Port all will
supplement to the inland movement of cargo in a more economical way. The Committee
therefore recommends that more such options may be worked out in other parts of the
country so that it may have a positive impact on the Port activities in tile adjoining areas.

62
OBSERV ATIONS/CONCLUSIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS — AT A GLANCE
The Committee notes that the traffic handled by the Major Ports has increased from
313.53 million tonnes in 2002-03 to 560.96 million tonnes during 2009-10. The aggregate
capacity of the Major Ports has also increased from 362.75 million tonnes per annum to
628.03 million tonnes during that period. The Committee is, however, constrained to note
that despite the increase in capacity and traffic handled by the Major Ports, there has been
negligible growth in efficiency parameters at Major Ports. For example, average turn around
time has gone up from 4.24 tonnes in 2001-02 to 4.5 tonnes in 2009-10 and also the average
pre-berthing detention time has increased from 11.04 hours in 2000-01 to 12.19 hours in
2010-11. Though the average output per ship per berth day has gone up substantially from
6961 tonnes in 2000-01 to 12133 tonnes in 2010-11 (up to December, 2010) which, however,
is not a matter of great solace as all our Major Ports are far behind as efficient as
compared to some of the Ports in nearby countries. Even today the majority of Indian
exports/imports are carried through transshipment centers at Ports in Colombo, Singapore
and Dubai. The average dwell time at Indian Major Ports is 1.88 days for import and 3.78
days for export of containers in comparison to the dwell time at Singapore Port is 0.6 days
for import or export of containers. (Para : 109)
While going into the reasons for low efficiency of the Major Ports, the Committee
finds that inadequate Port capacity, old and out-dated cargo handling equipments/
machineries, lower draft, non-availability of berth, poor road and rail connectivity with
Ports, inadequate navigation aids facilities, narrow entrance channels, low labour
productivity, shortage of storage spaces, regulatory restrictions, low IT applications and
delay in obtaining sanction/clearance from the Ministry are some of the major factors that
are affecting the efficiency of the Major Ports, adversely. (Para : 110)
The Committee found and the stakeholders also complained that cargo handling
equipment/machinery at the Ports were very old, installed decades ago and the right type
of equipment required by the trade were either not available or insufficient. The Committee
also found that modern container handling equipment like Quay Gantry Cranes (QGC) were
available in some Ports only Chennai, Cochin, Mumbai, Vishakhapatnam and JNPT like.
Similarly, Rubber Tyred Gantry Crane, Rail Mounted Gantry Crane and other similar
equipments are not in adequate numbers at most of the Major Ports. (Para : 111)
The Committee finds that proposals of Major Ports for replacement of old cargo
handling equipments/machineries with modern ones are in the process stuck at one level or
the other. The Committee came to know that Major Ports are authorized to undertake a
work worth only Rs.50 crore for new projects and Rs.100 crore for replacement of outdated
equipments. A general feeling amongst the port management, Port trustee and port users
was that lack of adequate financial powers with the Ports in undertaking developmental
projects was the major factor for delays. The Committee, therefore, recommends that all
the proposals for modernization/expansion submitted by the Major Ports may be processed
at the fast track and step be taken to ensure that the projects were cleared/completed in
time, particularly there for the replacement of old cargo handling equipment and other
machinery. The Committee further recommends that Government should enhance the
present limit (Rs.50 crore) for new projects and (Rs.100 crores) for replacement of
equipments available to the Major Ports so that Ports get more autonomy. (Para : 112)
62

63
The Committee observes that a large number of these projects are either under
implementation or are being planned for future requirement. The Committee also notes
that the pace of capacity addition has not been in keeping themselves with the growth in
cargo. The Ports, the Committee feels, will have to prepare to handle the increased volume
of traffic in view of the anticipated GDP growth in future. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that Government must take step for immediate enhancement of port capacity
and efficiency. (Para : l13)
The Committee is constrained to say that the Government has not been sensitive to
the genuine requirement of the Kolkata Port Trust. As a result a number of projects critical
for the survival of Kolkata Port are held up. The Kolkata Port has plan for construction
of 4 container-jetties which will handle a projected container traffic of 1.65 million TEUs.
The project is, however, held up because the Ministry of Defence has not made available the
river front land to the Kolkata Port. The Committee learnt that the Ministry of Defence
is considering transfer of land at Diamond Harbour in exchange of KoPT land and
Roychawk. The Committee recommends that the matter may be settled by both the
Ministries at the earliest so that the Kolkata Port Trust may take up its project of
development of berth facilities at Haldia Dock-II. (Para : 114)
The Committee also finds that KoPT requires 163 acres as backup land for
development of berths at Haldia Dock-II which is in possession of the Government of West
Bengal, which has transferred only 50 acre of land to the KoPT so far. The Committee
recommends that Ministry of Shipping should take up the matter with the Government of
West Bengal to ensure that remaining land is made available to the KoPT so that the
project of development of berths in Haldia Dock-II is not delayed. (Para : 115)
The Committee has been informed that transloading of capsize vessels carrying coal,
coke, limestone, etc. at deep drafted locations like sand-heads and Karina Sands and
transportation of cargo by barges/small ships to Haldia Dock Complex (HDC) will provide a
cost economic solution to the industries dependent on Haldia. In this context, SCI and SAIL
has formed a JV and approached KoPT for carrying out transloading operations along with
construction of a feed-in riverine jetty at Haldia in an integrated manner and a proposal
of signing of MOU between SAIL and KoPT is pending with the Ministry of Shipping. The
Committee recommends that the Ministry of Shipping should process the proposal
expeditiously and give its approval. The Committee also recommends that the Ministry
should expedite its approval for extension of jurisdiction of Kolkata Port Trust so that
transloading operations can be started in deep draft locations in sandheads and Karina
Sands. (Para : 116)
117. The Committee observes that due to the problem of shoaling and draft constraints
at Haldia dock, Haldia-bound vessels are availing of higher draft at Diamond Harbour and
Sagar Anchorage for lighterage/topping up of cargo in the barges. The KoPT has plans for
development of 5 barge jetties to meet the increased barge requirement at Haldia. The
Committee recommends the Ministry of Shipping to ensure that the project is not held up
for want of its approval and the work is completed within targeted time. (Para : 117)
118. The Committee also finds that Major Ports in the country are not working 24X7.
In some of the Ports like Mumbai substantial time is lost during shift changeover. The
personnel of Custom Departments work only 5 days in a week. Besides, manual work and
detailed scrutiny process by the custom department results in delay of evacuation of
cargoes. The Committee is of the view that in order to avoid delays and achieving the
highest level of efficiency, the port should work round the clock without any interruption.
The Ministry of Shipping should take up the matter with the Ministry of Finance to

64
ensure that the Customs personnel at the Ports work 24X7. The Committee also
recommends that steps be taken to ensure that minimum or no time is lost during shift
changeovers. (Para : 118)
119. The Committee also recommends that Government should take measures for four
lane roads without any crossings within the port areas added with efficient traffic
management. (Para : 119)
120. The Committee notes that inadequacy of navigational aids and facilities is also one
of the factors for inefficiency of the Major Ports in the country. The Committee finds that
certain Ports like Mumbai are equipped with Vessel Traffic Management System. However,
most of the other Major Ports yet to have this system. The Committee is of the view that
existing number of marine craft like tugs, launches and marine crew/pilots are not
sufficient to meet the increased vessel traffic in the coming years. The Committee,
therefore recommends that steps be taken for replacing the existing crafts with
sophisticated and modern marine crafts and augmenting the fleet strength to meet the
projected growth in traffic. (Para : 120)
121. The Committee was informed that about 350 barges are operating in Goa. The
Committee observes that the dry dock repair facilities for these barges are very insufficient
to the current requirement. The repair work shops currently are spread here and there and
the environmental pollution caused by their activities are a cause of great concern. The
Committee recommends that a maritime industrial estate may be identified for relocation
of all such work shops and docks to a single area with state of the art facilities like
syncrolift systems, trolleys, rails, jacks etc., which will cater to the requirement of the
barge repair demands as well as the polluting problems. Such large-scale facilities may also
attract foreign barges to come for repair. (Para : 121)
DREDGING
The dredging plays an important role in facing the challenges of increased vessel
sizes and handling operations of the port. With the development in the port sector the
requirement of dredging has also increased manifolds. Nowadays, modern vessels like
panamax and supermax cargo ships are used by the international carriers, these vessels
require draft of 14 meters or more. However, Committee is constrained to note that
execution of dredging projects has not been given due priority and as a result thereof the
capacity addition programme of the Major Ports have affected substantially. The Committee
notes that a number of projects have been taken up for capital dredging of berths. The
Ennore Port have plans to carry out capital dredging for berth area of iron ore to 18
meters, port basin to 18.5 meters, channel to 20 meters to handle cape size bulk carriers.
Under phase II of the capital dredging programme the Ennore port is likely to incur an
amount of Rs.440 crores from internal resources and commercial borrowings. They have
also planned to carry out phase III of dredging to provide a depth of 18 meters to TNEB’s
third and fourth coal berths, which are likely to cost an amount of Rs.200 crores. Kandla
Port is also facing problem of lack of adequate natural depth in approach channel from the
open sea. The dredging expenditure there has increased year after year and an amount of
Rs.120 crores was likely to be spent during the year 2010-11. Committee also notes that
Tuticorin Port is having draft of about 10.7 meters only which is highly inadequate when
compared to the neighboring Indian Major Ports and international port of Colombo. The
award of contract for deepening the approach channel and basin to cater to 12.8 meters
draught vessels is pending for final approval of the Government. (Para : 140)

65
In the case of Mangalore Port, the Committee has been informed that there is
annual requirement of dredging of around 5 million cubic meters and the dredger is
required for almost 100 days in a year. (Para : 141)
Both capital and maintenance is an important component for cargo handling capacity
and to increase the efficiency of the Indian Major Ports. The Committee recommends that
projects taken up/proposed to be taken up are executed in a time bound manner. The
Committee further recommend the projects of dredging of Tuticorin Port should be
processed seriously and promptly as project is critical for survival of a port. The Committee
also finds that cost estimates were prepared for 5 years back in the case of New Mangalore
Port need review in view of the increase in the cost as on date. The Committee also
recommends to explore the possibility of making available dredger exclusively for the use
in New Mangalore Port as its requirement of dredger is for almost 100 days in a year. The
Committee notes that there has been increase in expenditure on dredging by the Major
Ports. During 2000-01 around 17% of the total operating expenditure of Major Ports has
increased to around 20% in 2005-06. The Committee, therefore recommends that in view
of the increase in the expenditure on dredging, the Government of India should take the
responsibility and prepare a long term plan for financing the dredging operations in all the
Major Ports. (Para : 142)
The Committee also recommends that the approach channel of all Major Ports of the
country should be treated at par with national water ways and therefore funding for the
same should be taken up by the Government of India. (Para : 143)
The Committee is constrained to note that Government of India have not been able
to implement their decision of making 100% reimbursement of dredging subsidy to KoPT
which is already reeling under a severe financial crisis. The Committee notes that an
amount of Rs.873.12 crores is receivable by KoPT from the Government of India. The
Committee observes with vested interest the Government of India have imposed certain
decisions on the Ports/DCI and DCI was forced to shift its dredgers to SSCP ignoring the
critical operational requirement of dredging of KoPT. This led to dispute between KoPT and
DCI as the latter could not fulfill its commitment of dredging as per the agreement and
was imposed penalty of 20% by KoPT. This in turn affected the already deteriorating
financial health of DCI. The Committee recommends that the Government of India should
take steps to release an amount of Rs.873.12 crores to KoPT towards dredging subsidy. The
Committee also recommends that amount held by KoPT as penalty on DCI should be met
by the Government of India because it was their decision which forced DCI to remove
dredger from Haldia to SSCP. (Para : 144)
Dredging Corporation of India Ltd. (DCIL)
The Dredging Corporation of India is the only public sector dredging company in the
country and is a global player in the field of dredging. The Committee, however is
constrained to note that the company has been given shabby treatment and forced to carry
out certain commercial activities totally against the financial canons. It appears that there
is no autonomy available to the Company. The Committee finds that the order for third
dredger has been placed. The Committee fails to understand the hurry for placement of
order for purchasing of third dredger when DCI is not in a viable financial condition to
meet its cost. The Committee also finds that certain work performance certificates were
issued to private companies by DCI which resulted in loss of business to DCI later on.
Already poaching in DCI has left it dry. The Committee was informed that many shore-
based executives of DCI has resigned/left DCI and joined different private organisations in

66
2005-06. The Committee also finds that some higher officers after retirement joined the
Rival Dredging Companies. The Committee is afraid that some officials of DCI directly or
indirectly are maintaining some sort of relation with the private companies and might have
disclosed certain business secrets and key information to them leading to enormous losses
to DCI. (Para : 157)
The Committee also notes that huge funds are outstanding due to DCI from various
agencies and as a result of which the DCI has not been able to take up development
activities. It seems some sort of anarchic decisions are being taken with the vested
interests in the Government to make DCI a sick unit which resulted in taking over of the
dredging work by the private companies at exorbitant rates. (Para : 158)
The Committee is apprehensive of the fate of the DCI as it has been made a
scapegoat in the SSC Project and in placing purchase order for third dredger. The
Committee recommends that inquiry may be conducted to look into the affairs of the DCI,
particularly the handing over of work to private dredging company through DCI, issuing of
work performance certificate to private companies, making of payment to private companies
without being reimbursed by SSC, placement of purchase order for third dredger by DCI
and unsatisfactory repair of dredger by foreign companies. The Committee is of the view
that tax payers’ money has been invested in the DCI and Government should ensure that
no ulterior motive get succeeded which harm the interest of the company. Let there be level
playing field and no private company should be favoured at the cost of DCI. The Committee
is of the view that we cannot rely solely on the private dredging company. The Committee
in this context would like to invite the attention of the Government to the recent media
report wherein it has been stated that the private company engaged by the Cochin Port
Trust for dredging failed to fulfill its obligations and the matter finally was taken to the
court. The Government should ensure that while entering into the agreement with the
company, the interest of the Major Ports and DCI are protected by including safety clauses
in the agreement. The Committee also recommends that Government should take every
step to strengthen DCI to provide adequate autonomy to it so that it can function in fair
and unbiased manner. (Para : 159)
The Committee also came to know that the repair work of dredger owned by DCI
were awarded to some foreign companies irrespective of the fact that sufficient indigenous
facilities are available in the country. The Committee recommends that whatever be the
competitiveness of the tendering process, there should be an effort to create an
environment where native firms engaged in dredgers repair works can flourish and
contribute in nation’s development. (Para : 160)
Rail Connectivity
The Committee was informed that work in some Ports has been delayed due to land
acquisition problem. The Ministry of Railways has not provided the status of work as such
it seems most of the work have been delayed. The Committee notes that the lifeline of the
Ports i.e.  rail connectivity is being neglected by both the Ministries of Shipping and
Railways. If the connectivity remains a problem the Indian Ports will meet untimely death.
The Committee recommends that the Ministry should work on the projects in a time bound
manner and provide the action they have taken to set the rail on track to the Committee.
(Para : 182)
The Committee observes that all the Major Ports in the country are having rail
connectivity and the Ministry of Railways has taken up 8 projects to provide additional rail
connectivity to the Major Ports in the recent past. The Committee is constrained to note

67
that most of the projects are lagging behind the schedule. The better rail connectivity is
very crucial for improving the efficiency of the Major Ports. The Committee recommends
that the Ministry of Shipping should take up the matter with the Ministry of Railways to
ensure that projects are implemented in a time bound manner. (Para : 185)
The Committee was also informed that Konkan Railways impose 50% additional
charges on the freight rates due to non-utilisation of capacity thereby increasing the freight
charges to 150% of the prescribed tariff. This has put the additional burden on the
exporters of iron ore from Bellary-Hospet rendering the rail transportation uneconomical.
The Committee fails to understand the rationale behind imposing the additional charges on
certain trade. The Ministry of Shipping may take up the matter with the Ministry of
Railways to do away the practice of levying of additional charges by the Konkan Railways.
The Committee also finds that development of rail link from coastal to hinter-land is faced
with environmental hindrances as the rail link needs to be developed cutting across the
western ghat section. The Committee recommends that the matter may be taken up with
the Ministry of Environment and Forest to find out the viable solution for the issue. The
Committee finds that Paradip Port is facing the problem of cargo evacuation due to the
absence of adequate rail link to the hinterland. The Committee also recommends that
matter may be taken up with the Ministry of Railways to ensure that the Paradip-
Haridaspur rail link project is completed within the targeted period. The Committee also
recommends exploring the possibility of connecting the Paradip with the Kolkata and
Vishakhapatnam Ports by rail. The Committee is of the view that this will enhance the
business opportunities, traffic sharing and development of specific cargo facilities at these
three Major Ports. The Committee also notes that there is inadequate supply of rakes by
the Ministry of Railways which has affected the evacuation of containers/cargo from the
port premises. The Committee also finds that cargo carrying capacity by road and rail, is
below the requirement which has affected quick movement of cargo. (Para : 186)
The Committee recommends that high capacity rail loading equipment and efficient
traffic regulation may be arranged for better cargo movement from the Port. The
Committee also recommends that Railways should bring ‘dedicated trains’ rather than
‘mixed trains’ which only add to increase of work load due to inter-terminal trucking.
Environment friendly stack yards and warehouses for the projected future traffic movement
should be established. The efficiency of the present day rail service may be made in
accordance with the developing needs of the services and shortage of engines while loading,
may be met with in order to minimize the waiting periods of the wagons. (Para : 187)
Cochin Port situated in Willingdon Island is not well connected. However, even after
completion of the full electrification of rail lines in Kerala, the stretch of railway from
Ernakulam Junction to Willingdon Island has not been electrified due to objection from
Indian Navy. Railway is constructing a new bridge across Vembanad Lake connecting
Ernakulam to Willingdon Island. However, the effective utilization of this facility and the
rail connectivity to the Port can be made only though electrification of this stretch of
railway. The Committee would like to seek clarification as to why NoC was not obtained
from Ministry of Defence before taking up the work of electrification of rail line. The
Committee recommends that the matter should be sorted out with Naval authorities and
Ministry of Defence. (Para : 188)
Road Connectivity
The Committee recommends that in order to ease the road congestion, National
Waterway passing through hinterland of Cochin Port may be developed. (Para : 204)

68
The Committee also recommends that construction of Turicorin-Kollam Express way
may be materialized for the ease of road connectivity to the Port. (Para : 206)
The Committee observes that most of the projects of road connectivity have delayed
due to one or the other reasons and most of the roads maintained by Government
department are in bad shape and the maintenance more often are behind the schedule. This
shows the casual attitude of the Ministry towards the Major Ports. (Para : 210)
The Committee observes that road connectivity is not adequate to cater to the needs
of the existing traffic in the Ports. Road widening and upgrading process are not up to the
requirement of the current day development needs of the Port. The Committee recommends
that road widening and other interlinking plans as proposed by the Ports need to be taken
with the Ministry of RTH at the highest levels for its speedy completion. The Committee
also recommends that the addition of infrastructure in the recent time should be taken into
consideration while formulating the road connectivity upgradation projects to the Port.
(Para : 211)
The Committee observes that port connectivity to NMPT is insufficient as the
connectivity to National Highways is poor, heavily congested and not suitable for heavy
truck traffic. The Committee recommends that Government should accede to Port’s request
for the NHAI to take up improvement to the NH-48 and NH-13 under Port Connectivity
(PC) programme of the National Highway Development Programme (NHDP) so that the ban
on passage of heavy vehicles could be lifted on these stretches. The Committee recommends
for widening and strengthening of Chitradurga-Mangalore stretch of NH-13 so that the
distance between Hospet-Bellary region and the port will be reduced by 150 km.
(Para : 212)
The Committee is of the view that at least 4-lane road connectivity is required in all
the Ports. Uniform infrastructure facilities may be made in all the Major Ports so that the
goals and bench marking of port operations may be attained and performance monitoring
also may be possible. At present there is transportation problem inside the port for cargo
movement from eastern side gate to the western side gate of the Visakhapatnam port and
vice versa. Necessary flyovers and roads will be able to solve the problem. Evacuation of
cargo from the port and movement to the port areas need to be properly synchronized so
that inter-modal network functions smoothly. (Para : 213)
Poor maintenance of roads in India leads to accidents and also forces vehicles to
move at a slow pace, resulting in loss of time and energy. There has not been much
development of road and rail infrastructure which can meet the requirement of Major Ports.
One reason is multiple agencies at the centre such as Ministry of Road Transport and
Highways, Ministry of Railways and Ministry of Shipping and the lack of coordination among
them. The Committee recommends that there should be a coordinating agency to oversee
the rail and road connectivity at the Ports. The Committee recommends that the local self
governments such as municipal entities are also made the stakeholders in the development
process. (Para : 214)
The Committee is of the opinion that a good road and rail connectivity will enhance
any port’s business potential and in the case of Ennore Port, its development and rail and
road connectivity have not progressed in tandem. The Committee feels that Ennore Port has
abundant virgin land to create world class facility, however, the Port is not in a position to
reach its peak in the absence of proper planning at the early stage of conceptualization of
the Port for good connectivity using all modes of transport. The Committee feels that
critical rail connectivity from Athipattu to Ennore and the new line between Puttur and

69
Athipattu which will provide a shorter route for iron-ore traffic to Ennore Port should be
expedited at the earliest. The Committee also feels that the approach roads to the Port from
National Highways should be widened so that movement of heavy vehicles carrying cargo to
Port is not hindered. (Para : 215)
IT, Security and Traffic Monitoring
The Committee is of the view that in the present context and given the fact that
India has vast coast line extending to 7517 km., Port security is to be given utmost
importance for the security of the nation and smooth trade. The Committee notes that all
the Major Ports are ISPS compliant. But that fact should not bring complacency in the
efforts and, more, is need for constant vigil in port and sea area. The Committee observes
that there is lack of coordination in various agencies involved in security of Mumbai Port.
The Committee, recommend that the Ministry of Shipping should take up the matter with
the concerned of Centre and State Government agencies and evolve a permanent
Mechanism to address the problems. (Para : 226)
The computerization and web-based operations are the need of the hour. Due to lack
of sufficient IT implementation the Major Ports are still facing multiple problems in terms
of voluminous documentation, inconsistency in data, duplication of work, redundant book
keepings, these problems have led to lower productivity and non working time at berths.
The Vessel Traffic Management System (VTMS) facilities are used for regular berthing/
deberthing of ships. The Committee observes that only Mumbai Port is having VTMS
facilities and the VTMS projects are under implementation at Kandla, Kochi and
Vallarpadam Ports. The Committee is, however, constrained to note that majority of the
Major Ports are not equipped with VTMS facilities which has affected their efficiency. The
Committee recommends that IT infrastructure should be installed for exchange of
Electronic Data Interchange (EDI) messages between Major Ports and other stakeholders.
The Committee also recommends that all Major Ports should undertake an assessment of
utility of documents, involved in various operations and web enabled services should be
made available to port users. The Committee recommends that proper training facilities for
handling the modern monitoring systems need to be provided to the concerned personnel
operating such equipments. (Para : 227)
The Committee observes that Port Security is having utmost importance and all the
concerned departments may be kept on vigil in this matter. The Committee is of the view
that extended use of IT will supplement its effort of making in port and sea area safe and
secure by tracking movement of suspected dangerous vessels. The Committee came to know
about the threats of various kinds to the Port personnel and property as also interference
in their day-to-day functioning at port from local mafias/goons. The Committee takes
serious view of the development and recommends that adequate security may be provided
to port officials so that they can discharge their functions/duties without fear and
interference. (Para : 228)
Land Policy/Problems
The Committee observed that the land transferring issue is a hindrance to various
Port expansion projects of the Paradip Port. The Committee therefore recommends that all
the disputes may be settled amicably and the transfer of land may be done at the earliest
so that it may speed up the modernization projects at Paradip. (Para : 232)
The Mumbai Port’s 753 hectares land is contiguous with the land of the city of
Mumbai and has become an integral part of the city. Real Estate is one of the key assets

70
of Mumbai Port and care has to be taken to ensure that its land usage policy is carefully
monitored in the future. The Committee is aware that the demand for land is aggravating
in most of the cities and Mumbai is not the only one. The expansion of the city limits is
now a problem with the port and vested interests are making all out efforts for grabbing
the land of the port. The Committee therefore recommends that a clear-cut land policy may
be made for proper utilization of the land with the Port. The Committee also recommends
that every effort should be made to protect the land of the port from encroachment.
(Para : 233)
The Committee was informed by the stakeholder that the Mumbai port is earning
exorbitant rental on land leases to the operators. The recent tariff revisions were made on
retrospective effect which reportedly causing financial liability to the land users. The
Committee is of the view that the Port authorities may discuss the matter with port users
and review the order taking in view the commercial viability of activities. (Para : 234)
The Committee is of the view that land price issue as regards the Ennore Port may
be settled amicably with the State Government. (Para : 235)
Environment
The Committee is of the view that port operations can be made environment friendly
by developing reclamation wall around the sea shores and by imposing certain environment
management conditions like development of sewage treatment plant, day to day monitoring
of environment conditions and banning sewage or any other debris into the sea. Otherwise,
the Committee is afraid that if the Ports are not allowed to carry out its developmental
activities given the environmental regulations the Ports’ efficiency would be substantially
affected and may lead to under-utilisation of resources at the port. The Committee,
therefore, recommends that the matter may be taken up with the Ministry of Environment
and Forest to consider the proposal of Major Ports and may be allowed to execute their
developmental projects. (Para : 240)
The Committee notes that environmental pollution caused by trafficking of bulk
cargos like iron ore, coal, sulphur, rock phosphate, crude oil, gas, fertilizers, chemicals, etc.
are very frequent in the Port areas. The sprinkling of water is carried out on dusty cargo
but the problem of pollution has not been addressed satisfactorily. The Committee is of the
view that laxity in taking adequate steps to check the pollution cast by port operations can
prove to be expensive. The Committee would like to invite the attention of the Government
to the media reports stating that Madras High Court has ordered Chennai Port Trust to
move coal and iron ore out of Chennai Port to the Ennore Port. This move is likely to cause
a loss of revenue amounting to Rs.250 crores annually and render 5000 workers jobless. It
is also reported that stopping coal and iron ore handling by the Chennai Port may also
affect supply to electricity generating units and cement plans in Tamil Nadu. The Committee
is afraid that unilateral decision to shift these cargoes to Ennore may prove counter
productive and benefit the private Ports as the stakeholders have other options and may
move to private Ports. The Committee, therefore recommends that Government should
come forward to help the Chennai Port to sort out the problems. The Committee hopes that
the Government will take care of the interest of the 5000 employees likely to be affected
by shifting the cargoes to Ennore Port and ensure that there will be no retrenchment as
directed by the Hon’ble Court. (Para : 241)
The Committee also recommends that Government should direct the Major Ports to
explore modern ways of cargo handling and storage in order to reduce the environmental
pollutions. The Committee is of the view that keeping a pollution free environment is a

71
social obligation, therefore, Government may also consider funding the cost of pollution
checking operations by the Ports. (Para : 242)
At present, environment clearance is to be obtained separately for each individual
port project, which causes a lot of delay in the project implementation. The Committee is
of the view that the issues related with the Ministries of Commerce, Environment & Forest,
etc. need to be discussed at the Ministry level so that a common policy for all the Ports
could be formulated. Since the Environment and Forest Ministry is considering the
individual cases separately because of the complex nature of the geographical distribution
of the country, the cases could be taken up by the Ministry of Shipping for pursuing the
matter. The Committee, therefore, recommends that within the port limits, Ports may be
permitted to prepare Coastal Zone Management Plan (CZMP), taking into consideration the
future construction/expansion requirements and also commitments if any, based on earlier
environment clearances issued. The proposed new environment guidelines/norms, which are
not in line with the earlier commitments should not be made applicable in case of existing
Ports and the norms should be in such a way that they do not hamper the future
development. Only in cases where Ports can spare green area, shall such norms be insisted
upon; i.e, relaxations, exemptions of the guidelines/norms, on a case to case basis shall be
permissible. (Para : 243)
The Committee also recommends that efforts should be made to set up green Ports
by installing wind and solar power centres, with CNG fitted vehicles, water harvesting and
forestation. Enhancing the port capacity in a sustainable way, better water and waste
management, reduction of emissions from fuels, switching over to non-conventional energy
sources etc., should be taken up to save the environment. (Para : 244)
Storage Space for Cargo
The Committee notes that thousands of acres of land is in possession of Major Ports
and they are more known as ‘landlord Ports’. The Committee is however constrained to
note that Major Ports are facing acute shortage of storage space which has affected cargo
aggregation/evacuation. It also affects the discharge/loading of vessels. The Committee
recommends that proper storage facility may be planned in such a manner depending on the
type of cargo handled by the Port. Similarly such storage places could be equipped with
direct cargo transfer conveyor belts so that the double handling of the same cargo could be
avoided. The Committee recommends that additional space can also be created by
demolishing redundant structures and that the un-cleared goods, warehouse activities which
include unaccompanied baggage clearing etc. should be shifted to outer areas. (Para : 255)
The Committee had observed at Paradip Port that iron ore and coal are accumulated
open around the port premises. The Committee therefore recommends that the waste
disposal mechanism should be made operational in all the Ports in order to avoid
accumulation of huge dumping yards around the port premises. (Para : 256)
The Committee notes that environmental clearance norms are cumbersome and
causes undue delays due to which the projects get delayed. The Committee recommends that
separate lands may be earmarked for specific types of cargo so that basic facilities to handle
such specific cargo could be developed. The usage formula should be confined to the specific
purpose only so that wastage of resources could be checked. (Para : 257)
The Committee notes that inspection/testing facilities for imported food items/grains
are highly inadequate at the Major Ports and getting the reports/certificates from the
specialized laboratories located at a distant place takes more than two weeks time. The

72
Committee therefore recommends that adequate number of food testing laboratories may be
established in the premises of Major Ports for speedy disposal of perishable food articles.
The Committee also recommends that till the testing facilities are set up at the Ports,
Government may consider the possibility to allow test reports/certificates issued by the
accredited testing laboratories. Since the food import is an unavoidable phenomenon,
therefore even at a short notice matter is to be taken up with utmost care and seriousness.
The Committee further recommends that adequate number of Drug Controlling Officers
may be deputed near the port vicinity to avoid delay in cargo clearance. (Para : 258)
Wage Policy/Contractual Labour Issues
The Committee notes that there has been tendency now a day to engage workmen
on contract basis in Government owned PSUs. The Committee is dismay to note that
workmen even after service of 10-20 years are not regularized and they are denied of other
benefits also. The Committee also received complaints of under-payment to workers in
violation of Minimum Wages Act. The Committee recommends that PSU should not shy
away from meeting their social obligation. The Government should ensure that workers who
had served for many decades must be considered for regularization. The Committee
recommends that regular appointments may be made to fill the vacant posts so that the
hospital may become more service oriented. The Committee also recommends that the
compassionate appointment should be restored without any conditions. Since regular trained
workforce is required for the Port’s functioning, the in-house as well as outdoor training
facilities may be explored along with the modernization projects. (Para : 269)
The Committee has the view that different Ports may be handling different type of
equipments and machineries as per the type of cargo handled in each case. Therefore, the
training requirement also may be port specific especially at certain technical fields. It is
better to adopt a training strategy not for academic purposes but for the practical utility so
that a trained person would be able to handle all the operational know-how of a particular
area. Such a pool of trained manpower is required for each port immediately before modern
equipment is installed there. A long term training plan may be formulated with the sole aim
that the productivity per staff is maintained in the upward track. (Para : 270)
The Committee is of the view that certain issues as mentioned by the employees are
needed to be looked into an unbiased manner. The sectarian approach should not be
tolerated and immediate intervention should be required. In the case of posts require
specific training and qualifications, those employees who may be in the zone of
consideration of such posts may be provided with adequate trainings if necessary so that
such avenues could be made accessible to the persons from SC/ST categories. (Para : 272)
The Committee has the view that a remedy to the situation may be sorted out in
consultation with the local bodies. (Para : 274)
The Committee recommends that passenger jetty development is important for the
benefit the cruise vessels. The road development has importance in the tourism
development as well. (Para : 276)
The Committee notes that a large population directly and indirectly related to
Paradip Port are without benefits of Port activities. This situation has created discontent
among the local people and may cause serious problem for the Port. The Committee is of
the opinion that this is a serious issue which needs to be taken up with the State
Government so that all the people may get the proper living condition. (Para : 277)

73
The Committee recommends that the Port Trust may take necessary actions in the
matter of Sitaram Sarswat U  P School in consultation with the State authorities to solve the
problems. (Para : 278)
Issues Raised By Employees’ Unions
The Committee was also informed that most multi-national companies in port sector
undertake work which hardly benefits the workers and therefore it is important to ensure
that the Government should frame policies that the interests of the workers are taken care
of in accordance to the law of land. (Para : 280)
The Committee recommends that wages of the contract workers compared to regular
employees are very low and need an urgent re-think. The other grievances as regards the
service conditions and welfare measures need to be looked into on an urgent basis.
(Para : 281)
The Committee recommends that strict vigil may be made on such issues in
consultation with the State Governments so that the Contractors may adhere to the labour
laws. Violation of labour law need to be dealt with sternly and the multinational companies
operating in the port may be directed to act as per the law of land. (Para : 282)
Lack of trained and qualified manpower is a major challenge to all new port projects.
There are very few structured courses offered and hence poaching is a big risk.
(Para : 283)
The Committee also notes that shortage of pilots is a regular problem and Major
Ports have to engage pilot on contract basis frequently. The salary of regular pilots is
meager as compared to the remuneration paid by the shipping companies. The pilots have
to perform an important job of maneuvering of ships which needs expertise and knowledge
of the port area. These pilots take the ships to the designated berth after their anchoring.
The Committee, therefore, recommends that shortage of pilots may be met with a vision
so that future requirements may be fulfilled without any difficulties. A separate cadre of
pilots should be created for all the Ports. (Para : 284)
The Committee recommends that the staff shortage may be met at the earliest. In
case the port find any vacancy found unfilled, suitable candidates among the port employees
may be selected and provide them with adequate trainings for the purpose. Such a step will
enhance the enthusiasm of the staff members. In addition to this it is required that annual
assessment of the staff requirement may be done so that the future training programme
could be formulated accordingly. This will enable the Port to deploy the staff as per the
actual requirement. In all of the Ports it was a common complaint from the management
as well as the employee’s unions that fresh recruitment are banned and the manpower
shortage is very rampant in the Ports. However, the Ministry of Shipping has informed that
there is no ban on technical and statutory posts and the DoPT has lifted the restrictions
on annual recruitment. The Committee hopes that each Port may now plan their manpower
deployment properly so that additional man-power requirement may be estimated and the
recruitment may be done accordingly. (Para : 285)
The Committee observes that the R.K. Jain Committee report has made important
recommendations on the issue of manpower requirement in the Ports. In the case of VPT,
the manpower almost reduced by more than 60% over a period of time however the
handling capacity has increased from 31 MT to 65.5 MT during the period. The Committee
recommends that adequate measures may be taken for the recruitment of staff since there
is no ban as on date on recruitment of personnel. (Para : 286)

74
The Committee also recommends that better HR management practices may be
adopted. The Committee also recommends that training of the staff to modern equipments
and machineries may be done instead outsourcing the work to private agencies for all these
works. Focus is needed for building transparent and actionable-internal communication
system on the part of the port management. (Para : 287)
The Committee feels that the Government should revisit its recruitment policy in
respect of the Tuticorin Port as shortage of manpower in essential operational areas has
already hampered the day-to-day functioning of the port. The Committee hopes that the
ferry service between Tuticorin and Colombo will definitely give a fillip to trade
development, tourism development and employment opportunities at the port. (Para : 288)
Autonomy in Major Ports
The Committee is of the view that there is an urgent need to revamp on the decision
making mechanism in the government as regards the developmental works of the Ports so
that every project may be implemented as per the requirement of the individual Ports
separately and there should be flexibility to them for competing with the private Ports at
their close vicinity. The promptness in decision making is a very requirement for the
sustaining of the Major Ports. (Para : 297)
The Committee notes that the Ministry is in the process of corporatization of the
Ports. After corporatization the Major Ports would be in a position to have more financial
powers as per the delegation of powers applicable to the PSUs. (Para : 298)
The Committee is of the opinion that the Major Ports require a more refined
expertise in order to compete with their counterparts in the private sector. The Committee,
however, desires that Government should handle the matter of corporatization of Ports
carefully as many of the port employees’ unions are very much concerned about job security
of the employees after corporatization. They have the fear that corporatization is an initial
step for privatization. It is learnt that in the month of March, 2011, there were
demonstrations by the workers of the Visakhapatnam Port and Dock against the
corporatization of Ports. JNPT workers were also on strike expressing their solidarity with
the workers of Visakhapatnam Port. The Committee, therefore, recommends that
Government should take employees’ union into confidence and take every step to instill
confidence amongst the employees about their job security so that there is no resentment
amongst the employees against the corporatization of Ports. (Para : 299)
The Committee further recommends that Government should take up the review of
administrative structure of the Major Ports with a view to ensure the improvement in
efficiencies, services and working atmosphere in the Major Ports which would lead the Ports
to more heights in the coming days. (Para : 300)
The Committee has the view that the surplus funds which are mostly lying idle with
ports could be utilized in a more practical manner for developing infrastructure in other
Ports by way of Inter-Port lending or making a common pool of funds. (Para : 302)
Tariff Authority for Major Por ts (TAMP)
The Committee observes that TAMP has also not been specifically mandated to
improve ef ficiencies or lay down quality of services standards in port operations. However,
the Major Port Trust Act provides that while fixing tariffs the conditions under which the
service is to be rendered can be prescribed. Using this as a mechanism, TAMP is now

75
seeking to relate tariff to efficiencies. But each port has its own tariff schedule and scales;
the accounting procedures are also different. The Committee, therefore, feels that it would
be necessary for TAMP in the first instance to establish some common accounting
procedures amongst Ports and move towards fixing uniform principles for fixation of tariffs;
this would go a long way towards promoting inter-port competition. (Para : 304)
However, the Committee is also of the view that with private investment coming in
shipping industry, in view of competition in the port sector Government should consider
setting up a tribunal to hear complaints against port tariffs. (Para : 305)
The Committee is of the view that to strengthen Major Ports, a policy whereby the
two Acts, namely Indian Ports Act, 1908 and Major Ports Act, 1963, can be amalgamated
into a single Act should be conceived. The consolidated Act should oversee operations of
both major and minor ports in India as both the Acts have become old and outdated. Since
the inception of these two Acts, the Indian shipping sector has undergone tremendous
transformation in its working structure, with significant private participation now being
witnessed in the sector. (Para : 306)
With the coming of minor ports in the country, the pace of development has
slackened for the Major Ports. Since minor ports are governed by the Indian Ports Act 1908
and are outside the purview of the Tariff Authority of Major Ports (TAMP), a single
comprehensive Act will provide a level playing field to the Major Ports in terms of
infrastructure development, better railway networking etc. Currently, the tariff structure
also differs to a great extent for major and minor ports of the country, which needs to be
bridged. (Para : 307)
To develop Indian ports to global norms there is an urgent need for the government
to change its role from a regulator to being a facilitator. There is an urgent requirement
for aggressive second generation regulatory reforms, backed by the requisite legal and fiscal
changes to give Indian Ports a competitive edge in the global market. (Para : 308)
A port promotion council could be formulated to take initiative on the developmental
activities as well as the proper marketing of the services available with the Port. Since the
performances of the Ports are little bit negative during the last years, it would be more
desirable if proper monitoring on the performance be made regularly with immediate
measures to rectify the faults and drawbacks. (Para : 309)
Income Tax
The Committee is of the view that Public Sector entities which are not purely
commercial units have to meet social obligations. To help in further welfare objective of the
government must be viewed differently and be kept out of the purview of the income tax.
The Committee therefore recommends that the Ministry of Shipping may take necessary
action to include the sub-clause (v) in the explanation to Section 10(20) of the Income Tax
Act in order to restore the income tax exemption to the Major Ports as requested by the
Ministry. (Para : 313)
Public Private Partnership
The Committee observed that Joint Venture projects get delayed because of lack of
proper guidelines and standard documents. The Committee recommends that the
Government may make proper guidelines in this regard for a speedy disposal of such
projects. (Para : 317)

76
The Committee also notes that Concession Agreements have not been kept at pace
with the development and the growth of containerization in India. The Committee
recommends that the Concession Agreements should be reformulated keeping in mind the
national interest and to avoid any monopoly or unilateral actions by the private participants.
(Para : 318)
The Committee notes that the private partners eventually use the operating right as
captive facility. They levy certain extraneous charges and claim that such charges do not
form part of revenue eligible to be shared with the Port Trust. (Para : 321)
Under the name of privatization, foreign shipping cartels are getting a foot hold in
the centre of economic activities of our country. It has been propagated that privatization
will introduce competition and will reduce the Port charges but in reality, Multinational
Companies are charging more terminal handling charges than the Major Ports. (Para : 322)
Profit making services are taken over by the multi national companies leaving
behind unremunerated services with the Port Trust which may convert the Ports as loss
making units. This has taken away the job of thousands of workers working in the Ports.
(Para : 323)
The Committee recommends that government should examine the experience and
performance of PPP abroad particularly in countries which have been the mother of the PPP
contracts. It would not be in the interest of the nation to allow foreign MNCs to take over
the port related activities. Moreover, the Ports have strategic Naval defence systems within
its periphery, which will be open to monopoly of Multi National Companies who may control
Ports and Indian defence secret will be exposed to Foreign Countries. (Para : 324)
Major and Minor Ports
The Committee observes that Major Ports are facing a stiff competition from the minor
ports. The Committee does not agree to the view of the Ministry that the presence of private
ports creates a healthy competition amongst the ports. The Committee is of the view that the
competitiveness of the Major Ports is missing. The Board and Managements of these ports
including operations are regulated by the Government as a result thereof the Major Ports
largely remain confined to their respective hinterland. Major Ports are also serving the cause
of welfare of the society. On the other hand the private ports are enjoying full autonomy in
their functioning and are working purely with the commercial motives. (Para : 332)
The Committee is constrained to note that Government failed to protect the interests
of the Visakhapatnam Port, a PSU unit that could not control the situation which led to
setting up of Gangavaram Port. The Gangavaram Port was initially proposed by the
Visakhapatnam Port Trust to serve as a satellite port of the Visakhapatnam Port Trust to
meet the requirement of SAIL steel plant with a view to reduce the air pollution at the
Visakhapatnam area. However in the year 2000 the State Government had formulated a
steering committee for Gangavaram Port Development with State Government as the nodal
agency. The project was ultimately taken away from the Visakhapatnam Port Trust and
handed over to the private operator. (Para : 333)
The Committee is of the view that Vishakhapatnam Port has to face a stiff competition
from Gangavaram Port. The Visakhapatnam Port for years remained number one among the
Major Ports in cargo traffic. However, during the past two-three years it has slipped to second
position behind Kandla mainly due to the fact that a major portion of its cargoes consisting
of coking coal, thermal coal and others have been diverted to the Gangavaram Port. The

77
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Vishakhapatnam Port should be given all
financial assistance and autonomy to ensure that the upgradation projects including deepening
of draft, deepening of Ports, strengthening of berths in inner harbour, development of truck
parking terminal and mechanical handling facilities and inner harbour are completed in a
time-bound manner to compete with the Gangavaram Port. The Committee has observed that
the loss of Gangavaram Port from the hands of Visakhapatnam Port is a classical example
how dear the delay in timely decision making could be. (Para : 334)
The Committee also recommends that the Government should come out with
appropriate guidelines to ensure that no port is coming up in the vicinity of the Major
Ports. Even if some port has to be developed near to the Major Ports, the Major Ports
should be given the option to develop it rather than allowing other agencies encroaching
into those areas which may ultimately affect the functional viability of the Major Ports.
(Para : 335)
A blanket ban on privatization in the maritime sector is not possible. The
Committee, however, recommends that in the broad interest of the nation, the
Government’s endeavor should be to take steps for expansion and improvement of the
Public Sector and to ensure that tax payers money invested in the PSU do not go waste.
(Para : 336)
The Committee also recommends that the Government should ensure that the
management of private ports fulfills their obligations/promises towards the society. There
are reports that the people of Gangavaram and Dibbapalem villages were protesting for not
providing employment to the fisherman by the management of Gangavaram Port.
(Para : 337)
Cabotage Issue
In view of the critical implication of this regulation in the successful implementation
of the ICTT project and in the larger interest of economic self-reliance of the Indian EXIM
trade, it is imperative that the Cabotage Law is relaxed to enable transshipment of containers
through foreign flag vessels from ICTT, Cochin. The Committee, therefore, recommends that
the Government should immediately undertake a review of the Cabotage law and take
appropriate decision in consultation with all the stakeholders involved. (Para : 346)
Tourism
The Committee recommends Tuticorin Port authorities to earmark a few waters front
for this purpose. The Committee has observed that tourism can supplement to the revenue
earnings of the Ports. Separate cruise terminals at suitable places need to be maintained
for the benefit of the visitors. Care should be taken for the easy access of the terminals
to the main tourist places in the area. Also proper security clearance facilities should be
created at the respective places in consultation with security agencies. (Para : 348)
Inland Water Transport
The Committee is of the view that linking of water ways as in the case of National
Waterways 1&2 with the Kolkata Port system, National Waterway-3 with the Cochin Port and
the proposed plan for linking of National Waterway-5 with Paradip Port all will supplement to
the inland movement of cargo in a more economical way. The Committee therefore
recommends that more such options may be worked out in other parts of the country so that
it may have a positive impact on the Port activities in the adjoining areas. (Para : 351)
