REPORT
The Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Government on
observations/recommendation as contained in its One Hundred and Seventy Seventh Report on
Demands for Grants (2012-13) of the Ministry of Shipping, which was presented to the Parliament
on 7
th May, 2012.
2. Action Taken replies were received from the Government on 24 th September, 2012, in
respect of all the observations/recommendations contained in the Report. The Replies have been
categorized as follows:–
(i) Recommendations/observations that have been accepted by the Government: Para Nos.
6, 7, 12, 13, 14, 15, 21, 32, 33, 34, 35, 36, 37, 38, 47, 48, 49, 55, 56, 62, 64, 73,
75, 83, 84, 93, 94, 95, 97, 103, 105, 110, 114, 115, 116, 117, 118, 119, 120 and 121.
(ii) Recommendations/observations which the Committee does not desire to pursue in
view of the Government replies:
Para Nos. 7, 14, 15, 21, 36, 62, 73, 84, 103, 105, 110, 114, 115, 116, 119, 120 and
121.
(iii) Recommendations/observations in respect of which replies of the Government have
not been accepted by the Committee:
Para Nos. 39.
(iv) Recommendations/observations in respect of which final replies of the Government are
still awaited:
Para Nos. Nil
The Recommendations of the Committee contained in the one hundred and Seventy Seventh
Report, Action Taken thereon by the Ministry and recommendations/Observations of the Committee
on each item of action taken has been given in the succeeding paragraphs.
PERFORMANCE DURING XI PLAN
Recommendation/Observation of the Committee
3. The Committee notes that in the absence of consolidated data for the Eleventh Plan period
with outlay, actual allocation and expenditure for both the Port and Shipping sector, and there being
no physical targets shown, comment on the performance cannot be made. However, as admitted
by Secretary, Ministry of Shipping, underutilizing the Budgetary support, due to any reason, in
Committee’s view, is acceptable only to a limited extent.
(Para No. 6 of 177
th Report)
Reply of the Government
4. In the Eleventh Plan, an outlay of Rs. 1301.00 crores and Rs. 13,725.00 crores as Gross
Budgetary Support (GBS) and IEBR were provided for shipping sector out of which Rs. 923.63
crores and Rs. 8864.76 crores have been utilized which works out to 71% of GBS and 64.58%
of IEBR respectively. Primarily, the shortfall of expenditure has been in two cases namely (i) Indian
Maritime University and (ii) Ship building and Ship repair Sector.

2
5. Insofar as Indian Maritime University (IMU) is concerned, it may be stated that for
implementation of OBC reservations, additional classrooms and hostel facilities were needed but
tender for construction of building in Mumbai campus could not be issued as necessary approval
of plan/design were not forthcoming from local bodies and as a result entire outlay could not be
utilized. Similarly, an outlay of Rs.224.56 crores were provided for carrying out new development
works but the Patta and land of Vizag campus has not been transferred and as a result construction
work could not started.
6. Shipbuilding and Ship Repair sector consist of (i) Hindustan Shipyard Limited (HSL)
(ii) Hooghly Dock and Port Engineers Limited (HDPE) and (iii) Ship Building and Repair (SBR).
The Government has transferred Hindustan Shipyard to Ministry of Defence in December, 2009
resulting the fund left unutilized. Owing to lack of Ship building orders, the activity of HDPEL was
restricted to Ship repair work resulting considerable erosion of working capital of the Company.
The Ministry started providing assistance to pay salary, wages and statutory benefit to its
employees. The Cabinet in its meeting held on 13.10.2011 has approved the Rehabilitation-cum-
Restructuring of HDPEL. In the case of SBR, the budgetary projections were made on the basis
of projections provided by IMU, Vizag which is executing a number of R&D projects in
shipbuilding. IMU had projected on the basis of ongoing projects as well as the new R&D Projects.
In the IMU there was shortage of technical staff hence, efforts were made for recruitment of
experienced staff but considerable time was lost in this process resulting R&D scheme could not
be taken up and fund left unutilized.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
7. The Committee is not satisfied with the reasons given for under-utilisation of funds
of IMU as that is due to non clearance of plan/design from local bodies and the Patta and
land of Vizag campus has not been transferred. The Committee observes that this delay in
construction work have deprived a number of eligible students from getting admission to
IMU.
8. The Committee notes with concern the delay in the recruitment of technical staff,
research and development activities in IMU could not be carried out and finally the funds
left unutilized.
9. The Committee recommends the Ministry of Shipping to expedite Rehabilitation-cum-
Restructuring of HDPEL which has already been delayed. This is a need to sensitize the
concerned agencies to ensure that necessary approved plan for execution of schemes is
obtained in time so that funds allotted for those schemes do not remain un-utilized.
Recommendation of the Committee
10. The Committee was also informed (in the working) group report) that only 1/3
rd of the Total
outlay of Rs.30305.16 crores during the Eleventh plans outlay, i.e. Rs. 10388.87 crores was
allocated to the Ministry of Shipping under the port sector. However, it is equally surprising that
the utilization stands at 59.62% (or Rs.7684.61 crores) only. The Committee finds that this under-
utilization was mainly due to reasons such as delay in clearances, approvals etc. These are, no
doubt, time-taking exercises but if taken up with proper procedure and formalities as prescribed,
it could be expedited easily and quickly. In view of urgent need to modernize and expand our port
facilities and stiff competition with Private Ports staring at them, we cannot afford to delay
projects at our Ports. The Committee recommends that thorough home work needs to be done
before approaching each plan year projects for optimum utilization of scarce fund allocation.
(Para No. 7 of 177
th Report)

3
Reply of the Government
11. The recommendation has been noted for compliance in future.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
12. The Committee notes the reply.
ANNUAL PLAN 2011-2012
Recommendation/Observation of the Committee
13. The Committee notes that the funds at BE 2011-12 was reduced to almost half at RE 2011-12
and the utilization was only 50% of BE. The reason submitted by Ministry of Shipping such as
delay in approval, non-submission of extension of dredging subsidy, non-receipt of proposal/
incomplete proposals from shipyards are of routine nature and not convincing.
(Para No. 12 of 177
th Report)
Reply of the Government
14. In the Annual Plan 2011-12 an outlay of Rs. 273.60 crores and Rs.812.92 crores under Plan
and Non-Plan head were provided at BE stage for the Shipping Sector which was reduced to
Rs.207.61 crores and Rs.414.86 crores respectively at RE stage. Against these allocations, the
expenditure were Rs.187.51 crores (68.53% of BE) and Rs.386.12 crores (47.50% of BE)
15. In the plan side, the major shortfall of expenditure has been under the following heads:
(a) Inland Water Transport (IWT)- North Eastern Area: In the North East Region, there
is only one National Waterways i.e. NW-2 hence, there was not much scope for
utilization of fund in the North East Region.
(b) R&D Grant: The budgetary projections were made on the basis of projections provided
by IMU, Vizag which is executing a number of R&D projects in shipbuilding. IMU had
projected on the basis of ongoing projects as well as the new R&D projects. In the
IMU there was shortage of technical staff hence, efforts were made for recruitment
of experienced staff but considerable time was lost in this process resulting R&D
scheme could not be taken up.
(c) Indian Maritime University: An outlay of Rs. 40.00 crores was provided in the BE but
seeing to the pace of expenditure, the requirement of fund were reduced to Rs.30.00
crores at RE stage which was fully utilized.
(d) Directorate General of Lighthouse and Lightships (DGLL): An outlay of Rs.78.60
crores for construction and development of Lighthouses was kept which was reduced
to Rs.45.00 crores at RE stage. But DGLL could utilize Rs. 31.86 crores only because
a few prime projects such as (i) Establishment of VTS-GoK (ii) Estt. of National AIS
net work (iii) Automation of Port Blair LH Distt and (iv) Automation of remaining
Lighthouses could not commissioned resulting there is saving in the outlay provided for
these schemes.
16. In the Non-Plan side, an outlay of Rs.542.11 crores as subsidy for private shipyard was
provided which was reduced to Rs.129.78 crores at RE stage out of which the utilization was
Rs.122.42 crores only. The entire amount could not be utilized because the shipyards had not
submitted complete documents as required by DG (Shipping) for issuing PRCs and Technical
Certificate. Further, the Shipyards could not deliver vessels as per contractual delivery schedule.

4
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
17. The Committee notes the reply and observes that the reasons for under utilization
of funds given are same as those given during submission of Demands for Grants’ detailed
note. The Committee notes with concern that provision for subsidy to private ship-yard was
being made continuously for many years but the same remains under utilized every year.
The Committee may be informed of the steps taken for utilization of non-plan outlay for
the subsidy for private shipyards.
Recommendation/Observation of the Committee
18. The Port Sector present really a gloomy picture in case of utilization of outlay for the year
2011-12 where only 55.16% of total allocation could be utilized upto December, 2011. It is just
0.58% in the case of R&D, 47.40% in IT. The post Tsunami works are still going and only
35.31% could be utilized during 2011-12 (upto December 2011). ALHW could utilize only Rs.9.87
crores out of Rs. 17.77 (upto December, 2011) which is just 55.54% of total allocation. A perusal
of the statement of expenditure incurred by ports reveals that there had been shortfall in utilization
of funds against the BE/RE during the plan.
(Para No. 13 of 177
th Report)
Reply of the Government
19. During 2011-12, a BE provision of Rs.96.00 crores was made for post Tsunami restoration
projects. At the RE stage, the allocation was reduced to Rs.43.75 crores. The entire 2011-12 RE
allocation for post Tsunami restoration projects was utilized.
20. It can therefore be seen that shortfall in expenditure for the post Tsunami restoration
projects has been with respect to BE allocation and not the RE allocation for the year 2011-12.
The reasons for shortfall in expenditure with respect to BE provision has been on account of
stoppage of all quarries in A&N Islands, re-tendering due to poor response of agencies in marine
works, downsizing of projects, non sanction of schemes due to non clearance from tribal council
etc.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/BSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
21. The Committee notes the reply with concern that all expects the Ministry to try to
obtain required sanctions/clearance in time for post Tsunami restoration projects.
Recommendation/Observation of the Committee
22. The Committee is perturbed to note that the spending pattern of the Ministry of shipping
is resulting is cuts in allocations by the Finance Ministry. The Committee recommends that the
Ministry should look into the reasons for low utilization and take remedial measure by way of
proper planning and implementation.
(Para No. 14 of 177
th Report)
Reply of the Government
23. In order to ensure optimum utilization of fund, a periodical monitoring and review of plan
and non plan expenditure is conducted at the highest level and hurdles, if any, are found in smooth
execution of any scheme/project, remedial measures are taken in consultation with the concerned
agencies so that pace of the expenditure is accelerated.

5
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
24. The Committee notes the reply.
Recommendation/Observation of the Committee
25. The Committee in its earlier reports had also recommended that there is need to formulate
plan and policies in a realistic manner. Besides, all the schemes/plans should be reviewed to see
as to why these are not picking up, particularly subsidy to Ship Yards for which no proposal
completed in all respects with proper documentation were received. The growth of shipping sector
is closely linked with the overall development of the country and therefore, deserves top priority
in implementation of plan/schemes by the Ministry of Shipping.
(Para No. 15 of 177
th Report)
Reply of the Government
26. The observation of the committee has been noted. This Ministry is impressing upon the
shipyards applying for subsidy to submit proposals with complete documentation so as to facilitate
expeditious processing of the proposals for release of shipbuilding subsidy. During the current
financial year i.e.  2012-13, there is a budget provision of Rs.400.00 crores for grant of
shipbuilding subsidy to shipyards. This Ministry has received 13 proposals from shipyards for
Rs. 160 cr approx as yet for release. We have already released Rs.28.90 crores and it is expected
that by the second quarter, all the proposals received so far, shall be finalised for release.  Complete
proposals as and when received from shipyards shall be dealt with urgently so that funds could
be released as per the parameters of the scheme during the current financial year.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
27. The Committee notes the reply.
ANNUAL PLAN 2012-13
Recommendation of the Committee
28. Committee notes that the Ministry of Shipping has got without any cut from the Finance
Ministry their projected demand for Rs.812 crores has been made. The Committee recommends
that the allocated funds should be utilized fully as many important projects, especially in the port
sector are to be completed within the scheduled time in order to cope up with the growing demand
and the competition posed by the private players of the country . The Committee also recommends
that periodic monitoring and review should be made for better utilization of funds as in the year
2011-12 the expenditure was only 50% of the BE allocation”.
(Para No. 21 of 177
th Report)
Reply of the Government
29. Mechanism for monthly review and monitoring of expenditure of all entities on both port
and shipping sectors has been set up in the Ministry and is being monitored regularly.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
30. The Committee notes the reply.

6
PORTS
Recommendation of the Committee
31. The Committee considers the ports as the back-bone of the trade and commerce thereby
is strongly linked to the economic growth of a country. The Committee observed the enhancement
of provisions to the port sector under Plan Head to Rs.380.98 crores in the 2012-13 compared to
Rs.246.59 crores in 2011-12. The expenditure during 2011-12 (upto December, 2011) is Rs.75.08
crores only. The Committee, however is of the opinion that already the port sector was far behind
from the projected targets of its capacity additions, modernization of equipments, deepening of
drafts and ship channels etc. And even then they were not able to utilize the allocation. The
Committee is not satisfied with the reasons for low utilization and expresses its concerns that on
the delayed projects, resulting in tow-fold loss-more spending due to cost overruns and loss of
revenue which otherwise would have been generated after completion of the extra capacity. The
Committee strongly recommends for prioritized action on the above.
(Para No. 32 of 177
th Report)
Reply of the Government
32. Regular Review mechanism has been put in place to ensure maximum utilization of allotted
funds.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
33. The Committee notes the reply. It however, emphasizes that the Government should
strictly monitor the efficacy of regular review mechanism.
Recommendation of the Committee
34. The Committee notes the targets of 675.25 MCM in the capital dredging and 429.99 MCM
in maintenance dredging activities during the XI Plan period wherein only 278.93 MCM and 291.63
MCM respectively could be achieved which constituted 41.31% and 67.82% of the targets. The
Committee would like to reiterate its recommendations contained in the para 142 of its 170
th Report
on the “Modernization of Major Ports”. The Committee recommended:–
“Both capital and maintenance is an important component for cargo handling capacity and
to increase the efficiency of the Indian Major Ports. The Committee recommends that
projects taken up/proposed to be taken up are executed in a time bound manner. ...The
Committee, therefore recommend that in view of the increase in the expenditure on
dredging, the Government of India should take their responsibility and prepare a long-term
plan for financing the dredging operations in all the Major Ports.”
(Para No. 34 of 177
th Report)
Reply of the Government
35. The observations of the Committee are noted. The Planning Commission has constituted an
Inter-Ministerial Committee on Capital dredging for Major Ports to suggest measure to improve
capital dredging in all Ports. Based on the recommendations of the Committee a long-term Plan to
undertake capital dredging and financing will be formulated for Major Ports. The Ministry of
Finance and Planning Commission have agreed in-principle that capital dredging projects are eligible
for Viability Gap Funding (VGF) support. Accordingly, Ministry of Finance has conveyed that as
a concept, PPP projects for Capital dredging in Ports is admissible for VGF support, subject to
the other conditions of the Scheme and guidelines being satisfied.

7
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE

104. The international shipping market is facing problem of oversupply of tonnage and Indian

operates between Mundra and Pipavav to Cochin and Tuticorin.

referred to them by the PSU’s through Transchart. Then SCI carries this cargo by quoting
competitive rates and in some cases where the PSU’s have a rate limit, then by matching the rates
that the PSU has received. In case, SCI do not have a service to a particular location then it tries
to arrange the shipment by purchasing slots with other liners. SCI have also entered into Annual
Rate Agreements with some of the major PSU’s like IOC, BRBNML, BPCL/KRL etc. These
agreements are entered into between the SCI, the PSU and the Transchart.
117. Further, SCI is trying to garner more PSU’s to enter into Annual Rate Agreement so that
there is seamless movement of cargoes.
Joint Ventures
118. In addition to the above efforts taken by the respective Operating Divisions, efforts have
been taken by SCI by way of entering into JVs with PSUs to capitalize on opportunities emerging
from them. Some of the steps taken by SCI include formation of Joint Venture with SAIL and that
proposed with Coal India Ltd. These JV companies would cater to the cargo transportation
requirements of SAIL and Coal India Ltd. by building on SCI’s expertise in this field and in-turn
ensure that emerging opportunities from these PSUs are covered by us and not by Foreign players.

119. The Committee notes that the reply itself is a pointer to the lack of business

be utilized out of the allocation of Rs.1.58 crores during the 2011-12. The Committee feels that
delay in R&D activities might be affected in the long run as one of the reasons for non utilization
of the funds is lack of technical personnel in the R&D projects. The Committee recommends that
fast track search process need to be initiated for deputing qualified persons.

a continuous process and Secretary (Shipping) in his letter dated 28.12.2011 to Ministry of Finance
has highlighted some important tax related issues which were required to be addressed in the Union
Budget 2012-2013 to give the required Momentum for development of the Port Sector, Inland
Waterways, Shipping and Shipbuilding Industry. In the said letter, it was also suggested to arrange
a meeting where Maritime Industry could make a brief presentation on each of the tax related
issues. A pre-budget meeting was held on 10.1.2012 at the official level where an opportunity was

private sector can lead to a sustainable development of Inland Water Transport (IWT) related

138. The Committee is of the view that even though the Indian tonnage is growing as per the
projections, the India fleet are not gaining the momentum. Even the fleet acquisition plans of SCI
has been passing through a very difficult phase. At the same time Indian ship building industry and
ship repair sector are equally struggling to get enough business. This is happening at a time when
Ship Building Orders are given to foreign shipyard and Indian Ships and dredgers are looking

overseas destinations for the repair works. The Committee recommends that, the Ministry of
Shipping should make an assessment of the reasons for this contradictory situation and should
make remedies for the same.
(Para No. 117 of 177 th Report)
Reply of the Government
139. Absence of the significant domestic market and intense competition from foreign shipyards
have adversely affected the Indian shipbuilding industry. The Indian shipbuilding market is exposed
to threat of imports due to no protection of tariff barriers. In contrast, foreign markets are
projected by policy measures of their respective countries.
140. Governement of India introduced a shipbuilding subsidy scheme during 2002-07 which led
to unprecedented growth in Indian shipbuilding activity. Withdrawal of the scheme in August, 2007,
let to an immediate downturn in the shipbuilding industry.
141. A proposal was placed before the COS (Committee of Secretaries) in February, 2012 for
the following Policy measures for Indian shipbuilding industry:
(i) Provision of subsidy to Indian shipyards for construction of five years from 2012-13
to 2017-18.
(ii) Gr ant infrastructure status to shipbuilding industry.
(iii) Indian built-Indian flag vessels to be accorded first preference for movement of all
types of Government cargo, coastal cargo and cargo playing on Inland Waterways
Network.
(iv) Import duty exemption on import of capital equipment for ship building
(v) Service tax exemption to ship building and ship repair industry
(vi) Steel supplied by domestic steel companies to Indian shipyards to be treated as deemed
export for the purpose of duty concessions.
142. COS considered the above proposals on 17.2.2012 and inter alia directed that Ministry of
Shipping may take up the proposal for grant of infrastructure status for shipbuilding with Ministry
of Finance. A revised proposal may be submitted before the COS after carrying out a detailed study
on the policy support measures provided by the other countries like China, Japan and Korea, and
also data on investment likely to be generated by the shipbuilding industry. The Ministry is taking
necessary action as recommended by the COS and shortly shall again approach COS for policy
support measures to boost Indian shipbuilding industry.

REPORT
1. The Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Government on the
observations/recommendations as contained in its One Hundred Seventy Sixth Report on Demands
for Grants 2012-13 of the Ministry of Tourism which was presented to both the Houses of
Parliament on 7
th May, 2012.
2. Action Taken Replies have been received from the Government on the 6 th August, 2012 in
respect of all the observations/recommendations contained in the Report.
3. The Committee desires that final replies in respect of those recommendations/observations
which have been categorized as interim replies by the Committee should be furnished to it at the
earliest.
4. On scrutiny of the Action Taken Replies, the Committee has made observations on each
item of Action taken/proposed to be taken by the concerned ministries. The recommendations of
the Committee contained in the One Hundred and Seventy Sixth Report, action taken thereon by
the Ministry and recommendations/observations of the Committee on each item of action taken has
been given in the succeeding paragraphs.

expenditure under the scheme, it is equally important is to know reasons for excess expenditure
as the desired targets have not been achieved in terms of creation of infrastructural facilities and
the resultant tourist arrivals. The Committee also emphasizes the need for a thorough review of the
physical achievements made on the infrastructure projects of the Ministry during the Eleventh Plan
period.

th Report)
Reply of the Government
6. Product/Infrastructure Development for Destinations and Circuits (PIDDC) is the only
Centrally Sponsored Scheme (CSS) of Ministry of Tourism (MOT). MOT received more project
proposals for prioritization from various States and UTs, compared to the Budget allocation under
this scheme. Hence, the savings from the other schemes were utilized.
7. Ministry of Tourism monitors the implementation of projects through Regional Conferences,
field inspections by the officers of the Ministry and periodical review meetings taken by senior
officers of MOT with the State/UT officers.
8. During 2011, 6.29 million foreign tourists visited the country with an increase of 8.9% over
2010. During 2011 an amount of `16.56 billion US$ was the Foreign Exchange Earnings (FEE),
with an increase of 16.7% over 2010.

25. The Committee notes the cuts made in the outlay for Capacity Building for Service
Providers Scheme where in the outlay stands at `95.00 crores and the allocations are `89.00
crores. The actual expenditure of `67.79 crores shows that total allocations could not be utilized
by the end of the Plan period. This is disappointing mainly because Ministry of Tourism is
underutilizing the fund meant for skill development at a time when India is faced with huge
shortage of trained and skilled people in the tourism and hospitality industry. We must have
functional linkages with need of the industry and academic institutions specially IHMs, IITTM,
CCI, NIWS, etc.
(Recommendation at Para 20 of 176
th Report)
Reply of the Government
26. The underutilization of funds under the CBSP Scheme has been only during the year 2007-08
and 2008-09. The low expenditure under the scheme during this period is attributable to the fact
that scheme was relatively new in its operation and was still not known universally. Further, the
scheme as it existed in 2007-08 and 2008-09 generally targeted service providers at lower strata.
Often their day to day compulsions overwhelmed their need for skill upgradation. Even an
allowance of `100/- per day per trainee specific to short duration courses, to partly offset the wage
loss was not very attractive. The CBSP Scheme was therefore reviewed and revised so as to
enlarge its scope and provide for a much larger governmental intervention and pro activism. During
2008-09, a new programme titled Hunar Se Rozgar to create employable skills amongst minimum
8th pass youth in the age group of 18 to 25 years was launched. This scheme has been successful
and is now being implemented through MoT sponsored Institutes, State Governments and
Hotels. As a result the allocated funds have been fully utilized during the year 2009-10, 2010-11
and 2011-12.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
27. The Committee hopes that the entire allocation made for the scheme Capacity
Building for Service Providers would be utilized by the Ministry.

Reply of the Government
44. The collection of State level domestic tourism statistics is the responsibility of the
concerned State Governments/Union Territory (UT) Administrations. However, some States like
Delhi, Maharashtra, etc. do not have a mechanism of data collection due to lack of manpower and
required infrastructure.
45. In order to improve the quality of tourism statistics the Ministry of Tourism (MoT) has
taken the initiative of conducting State Tourism Surveys in some States.
46. In the Eleventh Plan, the first phase of State Tourism Surveys covering 5 States of Andhra
Pradesh, Delhi, Jharkhand, Maharashtra and Punjab was conducted from July, 2009 – June, 2010.
The second phase covering another five States of Haryana, Himachal Pradesh Chhattisgarh, Madhya
Pradesh and Sikkim started from April/June, 2011.
47. The States which were covered during the Tenth Plan included Assam, Bihar, Goa,
Karnataka, Odisha, Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh and Uttarakhand.
48. Apart from conducting such surveys, through its own panel of consultants, MoT also
provides Central Financial Assistance to the States to conduct surveys on their own. MoT is
supporting a three year Continuous Tourism Survey in the State of Kerala. The first phase of this
survey was conducted from 2008 to 2010; the second phase from 2011 to 2013 is currently
ongoing.
49. The State of Gujarat has a systematic data collection mechanism of “Tourist Flow
Information System” (TFIS) wherein field survey is conducted at 38 destinations, every month;
hence a separate survey for Gujarat is not required.
50. MOT is exploring the possibility of covering the following (remaining) 15 States and UTs
in the next phase of the Survey, subject to the approval of competent authority and willingness of
the State Government/Union Territory Administration:
51. Andaman and Nicobar (A & N) Islands, Arunachal Pradesh, Chandigarh, Daman and Diu,
Dadra and Nagar Haveli, Lakshadweep Islands, Jammu and Kashmir (J&K), Manipur Meghalaya,
Mizoram, Nagaland, Puducherry, Tamil Nadu, Tripura and West Bengal.

53. The Committee noted that Assistance to Large Revenue Generating Projects received a
lukewarm response from private investors. The Ministry has submitted that now it has proposed
to include projects such as hotels, amusement parks, theme parks etc. within the ambit of the
scheme. In view of poor response received for the Assistance to Large Revenue generating Projects
as accepted by the Ministry itself, the Committee recommends that the scheme be reviewed and
redesign and the new guidelines may be framed to attract more entrepreneurs to utilize the scheme.
(Recommendation at Para 27 of 176
th Report)
Reply of the Government
54. This scheme was formulated with an objective to attract private investments in large

8
revenue generating tourism projects such as tourist trains, cruise vessels, convention centres, golf
courses, etc. These projects are envisaged to be implemented with public private partnership (PPP)
and viability gap funding (VGF) provided by the MoT. Since the scheme did not get a good

enhanced.

Eleventh Plan period as the amount of `12.02 crores actually allocated for the purpose remained

Land Owning Agencies for creation of land banks. In order to make domestic tourism more

promotion of tourism during Twelfth Five Year Plan as envisaged in the approach paper of Planning

10
Commission. MOT’s Flagship scheme ‘Hunar-se-Rozgar’ is aimed at skill development in hospitality

229. The recommendations of the working group for improving regional air connectivity in India
to promote tourism in lesser known destinations are as under:-
CENTRAL GOVERNMENT
OPERATIONAL REFORMS
(i) Currently agencies like Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) and Bureau of
Civil Aviation Security (BCAS) do not distinguish between large scheduled Airlines and
small operators. Regulatory and compliance requirements for Small/Non Scheduled
operators have to be modified keeping in view the size of Aircraft, fleet and workload
of small operators.
(ii) Create a separate Feeder Scheduled Airlines Category to meet the requirements of
feeder sector. This category should be exclusively reserved for Aircraft/Helicopters

34
below 50 seats with sector length not exceeding beyond 500 kilometres. The Aircraft/
Helicopters below 5700 kilogram with minimum 6 seat capacity irrespective of number
of engines should be permitted to operate in this category. Non scheduled operators
desirous of operating at least one regular commercial flight with thrice weekly
frequency on new sectors (virgin or non operational since preceding 2 years) for
partial aircraft utilisation should be treated as ‘Deemed Operator’ in this category.
(iii) The existing guidelines for code share operations may be amended to promote regional
connectivity as a part of a long – haul itinerary by way of code share between the
long haul operator and the regional operator.
(iv) Non scheduled operators desirous of regular passenger flights with minimum thrice
weekly frequency should be allowed to file their flight schedule for approval of regular
operations for sectors which are not serviced at present. For such regular operations,
the operator should be permitted to advertise their schedules and undertake advance
booking through reservation network and search engines.
(v) Additional administrative/technical posts even in categories which are out sourced to
third party substantially adds to overhead of the operator and makes the small
aircraft operations unviable. In case of small operators flexibility of deployment and
multitasking by staff and crew should be permitted. DGCA should not insist on
minimum sets of flight crew etc. which should be based on level of operations and
flying hours while meeting Flight and Duty Time Limitations. Duality of functions
like quality control by operator and contracted Maintenance, Repair and Operations
(MRO) results in duplication of manpower and conflict in accountability. In technical
departments like engineering and operations one coordinator should be able to
perform all the departmental work and deal with multiple departments in DGCA and
BCAS etc.
(vi) In case of Non scheduled operators, DGCA headquarters should delegate more powers
to Regional Controllers so that they are not required to approach Headquarters for
every small approval.
(vii) In terms of regulatory approvals starting with NOC issuance, import permission,
Aircraft Type Rating and Endorsement, Air Operator’s Certificate (AOC) issuance etc.,
strict time limits should be specified for approval mechanism. Similar committee
mechanism to the present system of Empowered Committee in Ministry of Civil
Aviation should be established in DGCA with monthly frequency wherein all pending
matters requiring approval by Non Scheduled operators can be decided in timely
manner.
(viii) The current policy of Scheduled Airlines (Regional) restricts the operator to operate
from only one Metro Airport whereas the traffic affinity from many important cities
requires connectivity to at least two Metro Cities i.e. Jodhpur needs connectivity to
both Delhi and Mumbai, similarly Ranchi requires connectivity to Delhi and Kolkata.
Permission to connect two metros from any intermediate point will result in better
point to point servicing and provide higher Aircraft utilization of small operators .In
order to safeguard the interest of Scheduled Airlines, policy may forbid Scheduled
Airlines(Regional) to operate point to point nonstop services between two Metro
Airports.
(ix) The current policy of Scheduled Airlines (Regional) permits the operation of flights to
Metro Airport of the Region based on geographical base of operator i.e. Kanpur or
Jaipur based operator can operate to Delhi but not Mumbai. In many cases the traffic

35
requirement of some important cities may require flight operations to Metro Stations
of other Regions i.e., Surat or Pune based operator would find greater traffic flow
towards Delhi or Bangalore compared to Mumbai. Scheduled Airlines policy should
permit the Operator to connect any one Metro Airport instead of such geographical
stratification.
(x) Metro Airports like Delhi and Mumbai have classified the flight operations of Aircraft
less than 40000 kg as non revenue flights and discourage such operations. Small
operators are not given time slots and parking permissions. Ministry may issue strict
guidelines to Airport operators to facilitate Regional Operations.
(xi) Foreign Pilots of Non Scheduled Operators’ Permit (NSOP) Operators face serious
problems in operating flights to Defence Airfields since they have to obtain security
clearance from Ministry of Defence before operating every single flight. Such
clearance has to be filed at least 2 days in advance and during weekends such time
limit becomes even longer. Many times such stipulation results in cancellation of
flights and prohibits last minute substitution of operating crew in case of non
availability of rostered pilot due to any exigency. DGCA should obtain security
clearance of all Foreign Pilots from Ministry of Home Affairs before permitting
Foreign Pilots to fly in India and once they are endorsed, such requirement should
be dispensed with.
(xii) Extension of watch hours becomes a major constraint at airports having single shift
operations. In case the operators wish to operate minimum thrice weekly frequencies
on regular basis, Airports Authority of India (AAI) should provide an extension of
watch hours at such airports without additional overtime charges. This facility should
be extended only in case of regular passenger operations.
(xiii) DGCA should permit bush operations at unmanned Airports with limited Non-
Directional (Radio) Beacon (NDB) and Very High Frequency (VHF) facilities.
INCENTIVES
(i) In order to encourage investment in regional aviation category, Banks and Financial
institution like Small Industries Development Bank of India (SIDBI) should create a
special fund in the form of equity and loans including working capital loans against the
securitization of Aircraft Assets. Debt funding up to 50% of Aircraft value subject to
valuation of Aircraft should be provided by banks without seeking additional security
from promoters. Small operators should be entitled to benefits applicable to other Small
and Medium Enterprises (SMEs).
(ii) New sites should be given incentives. Special incentives should be provided for
regional connectivity at airports which are non operational. Allocation of cost of
operation should be done in a manner which makes regional connectivity viable. Start
– up aid or subsidies in the form of waiver of landing/navigational charges, wherever
applicable, should be considered in the initial few years or till such time the economies
of scale are achieved, whichever is earlier.
(iii) S ervice Tax should be rationalized from 10.3% and non scheduled operators should be
charged on per seat basis as the scheduled airlines are charged. Service tax on
Medivac (Medical Evacuation) flights should be abolished.
(iv) Fixed Base Operator (FBO) charges which account for more than half of the flying
charges at airports should be rationalized and make operations viable.

36
STATE GOVERNMENT
OPERATIONAL REFORMS
(i) State Governments should devise long term Aviation policy of the State enlisting the
priority routes for Intra-State connectivity.
(ii) State Governments can provide security and fire tenders during the time of flight if
operators undertake minimum thrice weekly frequency.
INCENTIVES
(i) State Governments may consider introducing scheme of providing limited seed capital
in the form of Equity and nominate one or two officers on the Board of the proposed
airlines. This would help small operators in professionalising their management and
Nominee Directors can assist the company in obtaining timely approval from various
banks and government agencies. This would ensure better market confidence amongst
Aircraft sellers, leasing companies and travelling public. Nominee directors will also
ensure judicious utilisation of funds and focus on well defined business plan including
State priorities. Nominee directors would be also be able to ensure fair cost and
subsidy assessment in cases where State Governments/Government of India are keen
to operate few sectors due to strategic reasons and are willing to subsidize such
flights.
(ii) Subsidies should be available to any operator on ‘first come first serve’ basis to attract
multiple operators within the State, who could become multi aircraft operator in due
course. Duration of subsidy can be limited to 18 to 36 months. Quantum of subsidy
may be up to 25% of seat revenue in case of aircraft below 20 seats and 15% of seat
revenue for aircraft between 20 to 50 seats in the form of seats guarantee or
operational subsidy. Such subsidy should be reimbursed to operator on monthly basis
since delay in providing payment to operator results in cash crunch defeating the very
purpose of such subsidy.
(iii) Reduction in sales tax on Air Turbine Fuel (ATF) should be offered based on the
Maharashtra Model, under which there is no taxation on fuel for flights operated out
of non metro cities for destinations within Maharashtra.

REPORT
1. The Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Government on the
observations/recommendations as contained in its One-Hundred and Seventy fourth Report on
Demands for Grants 2012-13 of the Ministry of Civil Aviation which was presented to both the
Houses of Parliament on 27
th April, 2012.
2. Action Taken Replies have been received from the Government on the 1 st October, 2012 in
respect of all the observations/recommendations contained in the Report.
3. The Committee desires that final replies in respect of those recommendations/observations
which have been categorized as interim replies by the Committee should be furnished to it at the
earliest.
4. On scrutiny of the Action Taken Replies, the Committee has made observations on each
item of Action taken/proposed to be taken by the concerned Ministries. The recommendations of
the Committee contained in the One Hundred and Seventy fourth Report, action taken thereon by
the Ministry and recommendations/observations of the Committee on each item of action taken has
been given in the succeeding paragraphs.
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
5.  The Committee notes that the Ministry of Civil Aviation was able to spend Rs.40.673.04
crores (anticipated) as against the allocation of Rs.49,267 crores for the Eleventh Plan period
resulting in a huge saving. The Committee finds that except Indira Gandhi Rashtriya Uran Akademi
which spent Rs.41.00 crore against the budgetary allocation of Rs.42.00 crore for the plan period,
all other organizations under the Ministry could not spend the allocated money fully. This is a
disturbing scenario. The Committee notes that Air India was able to spend Rs.25,603 crores only
against the allocation of Rs.32,730.71 for the Eleventh plan period, again saving a sum of Rs.7,127
crores. The Committee is surprised to note that when the national carrier was knocking the doors
of financial institutions to bail it out, it was unable to spend money it had been allocated during
the Eleventh Plan period.
(Recommendation at para 6 of 174
th Report)
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
6. The Eleventh Plan approved outlay of Rs.32730.71 crores of Air India Limited did not
include any budgetary support from the Government. The entire outlay was proposed to be met
from the internal and extra budgetary resources of the company. The actual outlay during this
period 2007-08 to 2011-12 was Rs.24,763.36 crores including equity infusion of Rs.3200.00 crores
by the Government of India. The reduction in the actual expenditure as compared to the Eleventh
Plan Outlay is primarily due to delay in delivery of B787 aircraft due to production related issues.
Further there was a reduction in the other capital projects due to the liquidity crisis faced by the
company during this period as only operationally essential projects were undertaken.
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
7. Another case of under-spending is that of Airports Authority of India, the leading
infrastructure provider for aviation industry in the country. AAI could spend Rs.11,873.41 crores
against the allocation of Rs.12,964.21 crores for the plan period. The Committee is not able to

2
understand the logic behind Airports Authority of India’s inability to spend even the budgetary
support of the Government; they could spend roughly 50% only. The Committee feels that such
under utilization of funds by AAI could have definitely slowed the pace and process of developing
airport infrastructure at various places including Chennai and Kolkata. A curious case in this respect
is that of the Hotel Corporation of India which was able to spend Rs.43.75 crores against Rs.75.00
crores. The Committee feels that time has come to assess the performance of this PSU in a
broader perspective and it should not be allowed to become a liability to pave the way for its
privatization. Air India Charters Limited is another example in this respect. They could spend only
Rs.2088.16 crores against the plan outlay of Rs.2475.26. Neither the Low Cost Carrier of the
Government is expanding its services nor able to spend the allocated plan outlay. The Committee
would like to be informed about the reasons for such under-utilization of funds by various
organizations of the Ministry of Civil Aviation and the remedial measures taken to prevent such
happenings in future. The Committee hopes that the Ministry will ensure that the organizations
under its control were able to spend their allocations to the maximum possible extent in the Twelfth
Plan. The Committee feels that any laxity on spending of allocation will have the direct impact on
aviation sector of the country.
 (Para 7 ibid)
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
8. AAI incurred an amount of Rs. 11868.41 crores as capital expenditure for development of
airport Infrastructure in the country during Eleventh Plan as against plan outlay of Rs.12964.21
crores which is 92% of plan outlay. The shortfall of 8% has been mainly on account of non-
availability of site, delays in obtaining necessary regulatory and statutory approval, environmental
clearance, and approval from Planning Commission etc. During the period 2007-08 to 2009-10, AAI
spent the entire amount approved in BE by MoCA in respect of schemes for which Government
Budgetary Support (GBS) was provided. However during the year 2010-11 and 2011-12, AAI was
able to spend only 50% of the funds allotted for GBS Schemes mainly on account of delay in
approval from the Planning Commission for various new projects i.e. Jalgaon, Gondia, Puducherry,
Itanagar, Cheitu (Kohima), Jammu airport schemes. The pace of work at mega projects namely
Kolkata and Chennai did not slow down due to non-availability of funds as the funding of these
projects was met out of the internal resources of AAI and borrowings. The delays occurred due
to other reasons.
9. The total outlay in the eleventh plan for Hotel Corporation of India (HCI) was Rs.75 crores
to be spent out of the Company’s own internal resources. However, due to the lower internal
generation during the Eleventh Plan period, HCI was able to spend only Rs 43.75 crores. At no
stage has the Company received any grants from the Government in the Eleventh Plan. The
approved outlay for Eleventh Plan for AICL was Rs. 2475.25 crores. The actual outlay for the plan
period was Rs. 2070.27 crores. The main reasons for reduction in actual expenditure as compared
to the Plan outlay were as follows:
(a) The plan outlay for aircraft induction was estimated based on certain aircraft prices
at certain exchange rate. The actual delivery price was slightly lower on account of
concessions/discounts obtained from Boeing on Aircraft list price compared to our
estimates and exchange fluctuation.
(b) It was assumed that five spare engines would be acquired in the plan period. As
against this, only four spare engines were acquired.
(c) The budgetary outlay was proposed based on estimates of internal revenue generation
which did not materialize. No Government budgetary support was given to AICL
separately.

3
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
10. The Committee notes the reasons furnished by the Ministry of Civil Aviation for
under-utilization of funds by Air India and Airports Authority of India during the Eleventh
Plan period. The Committee notes that most of the outlays that Airports Authority of India
and Hotel Corporation of India could not spent were to be arranged out of internal
resources. However, Public Sector Undertaking which set up out of tax payers’ money can
not be absolved over the lack of commitment merely because no Government budgetary
support was given to them. The Committee hopes that the Ministry will impress all the
organizations under its purview to spend the allocated funds during the Twelfth Plan to the
maximum extent.
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
11. The Committee notes that the Ministry of Civil Aviation was not able to spend fund allocated
in respect of DGCA, BCAS and AAI – three main organizations. It is not a welcome sign since
allocation under these heads constituted major share of the allocation under Plan, excluding Air
India. The reasons submitted by the Ministry for under-utilization of funds such as delay in
clearances to various projects, delay in acquisition of land for airport projects and delays in getting
necessary regulatory and statutory approvals may be understandable but not acceptable, if repeated
every year, For example, the project of construction of office buildings for DGCA and BCAS could
not be taken up for last two to three years. The Committee feels that failure to spend the allocated
moneys by these organizations shows a lack of proper planning for timely execution of major
programmes/projects. Delay on account of various administrative problems and procedural
difficulties cannot be acceptable as excuse as these could be visualized at initial stages and
precautions taken well in time. The Committee recommends that the long pending construction of
headquarters for DGCA and BCAS be started at the earliest in coordination with agencies concerned
and be completed in a fixed schedule. The Committee further recommends that the Ministry should
impress upon all the organizations under its purview to spend the allocations cent percent in a
planned manner.
(Para 9 ibid)
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
12. Construction of DGCA and BCAS Headquarters building is held up because the land at
Safdarjung Airport has been declared as “recreational green” by Ministry of Urban Development.
Secretary, MoCA, Chairman, AAI and DGCA, all have made collective efforts to get the title of
Safdarjung Airport changed in Delhi Master Plan but have not succeeded. Hence the construction
of above offices could not commence for the proposed buildings, though environmental clearance
has been obtained, drawings finalized and approved. AAI is ready to take up the construction and
the day the title for Safdarjung Airport is restored as Airport, the actual construction work will
commence.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
13. The Committee notes the reply of the Ministry.
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
14. The Committee after scrutinizing the allocations for 2012-13 finds that apart from equity
infusion to the tune of Rs.4000 crore for Air India under the budgetary support, the allocation for
the Ministry is inadequate. The allocation of Rs.738.80 crores under the Non-plan for the year

4
2012-13 is lesser than the allocation at Revised Estimates of Rs.764.86 crores for the year 2011-12.
The Committee expresses its concern over the static allocation to the Ministry which concerns with
one of the fastest growing sectors having lot of potential for further growth. The Committee hopes
that the Ministry will take up its case with Planning Commission for allocations of adequate funds
at RE stage so that ongoing aviation projects are not hampered and new ones are taken up.
(Para 14 i bid)
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
15. The observation of the Committee has been noted for compliance and its recommendation
will be conveyed to the Department of Expenditure/Planning Commission for seeking enhanced
budgetary allocations at RE stage. Secretary, Ministry of Civil Aviation has already written to the
Planning Commission seeking higher allocation in the Twelvth Five Year Plan.
Air India
16. The approved outlay Annual Plan 2012-13 for Air India is Rs. 4928 crores, of which
Rs.4000 crores is the budgetary support in the form of equity infusion. Financial Restructuring Plan
and Turnaround Plan of Air India has been approved by the GOI in April, 2012. As per the Plan,
the total amount receivable as equity from GOI in 2012-13 would be as under:
1. Upfront Equity Rs. 5,550 crores
(Rs. 6,750 crores – Rs. 1,200 crores)
provided in the Budget 2011-12 and already received
2. Equity for guaranteed loans
FY 2011-12 Rs. 1,786 crores
FY 2012-13 Rs. 1,787 crores
3. Equity for cash deficit (FT 2012-13) Rs. 1,539 crores
4. Equity for NCD’s Rs. 352 crores
T
OTAL Rs. 11,014 crores
17. Of the above, Rs. 4000 crores has already been provided in the Plan budget of 2012-13.
Ministry of Finance shall be approached to provide for remaining amount of Rs.7,014 crores as
Supplementary Grant in 2012-13.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
18. The Committee feels that Air India is still in critical phase. Any laxity in any matter
relating to Air India can play havoc to the public sector carrier. The Committee notes the
reply of the Ministry. The Ministry, therefore, should pursue with Planning Commission
vigorously for allocation of requisite funds at RE stage so that the ongoing Air India
projects are not delayed.
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
19. The Committee notes that the national carrier had to undergo a tough period during the last
year mainly on account of merger related issues, ever increasing ATF prices, employees’ resentment
over non-payment of dues, allotment of profitable routes to private carriers, its over-ambitious
aircraft acquisition plan, inability to raise funds from the open market and the reluctance of
financial institutions’ and Oil Marketing Companies to help the ailing Air India. The Committee finds

5
that though the company was able to increase its passenger load factor it witnessed a dip in share
in domestic and international aviation markets.
(Para 30 ibid)
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
20. Air India, the national carrier of India, has proposed to induct capacity in an effort to re-
capture the market share in the domestic and international market. To achieve this, various
measures are being taken as per the Turnaround Plan approved by the Government.
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
21. The Committee notes that a large number of amendments to Air Service Agreements with
foreign countries were signed for expansion of international air services by the national carrier
during the last year. The Committee finds that Air India operates almost 500 departures daily
offering more than 78000 seats per day connecting about 150 domestic city-pairs and 125
international city pairs with a 143 strong fleet but still not in a position to attain a visible
competitive edge vis-àvis other airlines. The Committee notes some serious efforts being made both
by Air India management and the Government for taking the national carrier out of the current
mess. There are improvements on some parameters indicating that things have started moving into
required direction, which is why the Government has decided to support the airlines’ recovery
process. But in view of the several challenges and over all slow down in the Sector, Committee
would like to caution the Air India management and the Government to be very careful while
implementing its restructuring/revival plans. The greatest challenge it must overcome on priority is
that relating to HR issues created due to ill-conceived merger plan. The Committee hopes that
allocation of unutilized bilateral /traffic rights to Air India will benefit it in regaining its lost market
share in international market.
(Para 31 ibid)
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
22. Air India is given first preference while allocating the traffic rights for international sector.
Air India has submitted their proposed operation plan upto winter 2013. Grant of traffic rights for
other airlines is considered only after taking into consideration the operational requirements of Air
India. Most of the amendments to ASAs done in recent years has not been done for the expansion
of Air India’s services. In view of its losses, Air India has been conservative and has 
not asked
for more traffic rights. It may be mentioned that rapidly increasing capacity, as recommended,
could escalate the losses. The aim should be to increase profitability and competitiveness by service
quality, reliability and revenue generation. Once a profitable model is established, the capacity could
be scaled up rapidly to increase profits further.
23. As regards attaining visible competitive edge vis-à-vis other airlines, following actions have
been taken by AI with respect to network and schedules:
(a) The aircraft on AI’s fleet are mostly new and standardized in term of in-flight comforts
and facilities.
(b) All the major domestic and international routes are operated with the newly acquired
aircraft.
(c) The timings of international services have been rationalized. AI now offers convenient
late evening/midnight hour departures with arrival in morning hours at destinations on
most of the international routes. Further uniform timings are also offered on all days
on almost all international routes.

6
(d) Multiple daily services with uniform timings are offered on all major domestic routes
providing convenient same day return facility.
(e) Conveniently scheduled non-stop services have been introduced on India-N America
routes which is perceived as a Unique Selling Proposition (USP).
(f) The network of AI and its subsidiaries now spreads over to 64 domestic (covering all
remote areas of country) and 33 international destinations (covering North America,
Europe, Far east, South-East Asia, South Asia and Middle East) connecting 159
domestic city-pairs and 127 international city pairs on 305 domestic departures and 175
international departures daily.
(g) Delhi hub operationalized with 2 arrival/departure banks for long haul services. AI now
connects Delhi with 23 international and 48 domestic destinations. AI handles 2800
transfer passengers every day at the Delhi hub comprised by feeder traffic from/to
interior points in India and destinations in neighboring countries mainly Bangkok and
Kathmandu at this stage.
(h) With the merger and integration of the networks of erstwhile AI and IC, operation of
Hub and Spoke services have been increased to provide for convenient connections at
DEL/BOM for passengers originating at other metro cities including Ahmedabad, Goa
and Amritsar. The passengers traveling by the Hub and spoke services avail of
customs/immigration facilities at their point of origin/destination.
(i) Further, services carrying through flights numbers to onward international destinations
are operated from select interior points in India so as to improve AI’s ability to more
effectively market these destinations at the interior points.
Improved website
24. For enhancing customer satisfaction and for improving sales through website, effective
September, 2011, new webmaster and core team was designated with the objective of making the
website as customer friendly and making it as a marketing tool to enhance direct sales thereby
reducing distribution costs and other costs related to bookings through other channels i.e. agents,
portals, booking offices etc.
Initiatives taken so far
• The travel/ticketing rules and regulations related to customers are being updated on real
time basis (which has become an ongoing process now) to enhance customer
satisfaction.
• Constant development and modification of Website and Web page contents as per
market and commercial requirement (which has become an ongoing process) which in
turn enhances customer satisfaction.
• To make it comprehensive platform and single window for all e-business activities and
major source of revenue for AI.
• To enhance the speed and processing time the website has been migrated to NIC
platform (Government of India) effective January, 2012 which in turn enhances
customer satisfaction.
• The refund processing time has been reduced to couple of days to restore customer
confidence.

7
• The helpdesk response time (to respond to customer queries) has been reduced to
24 hours by augmenting the entire set-up to tune it to market requirement.
• A short term web based scheme has been launched effective January, 2012 to
encourage customers for web based bookings/ticketing.
• Aggressively using website as e-marketing tool for advertising promotional schemes,
destinations, new flights, schedule, fares etc.
25. These initiatives have helped Air India to restore confidence of e-customers, change the
focus of website i.e. customer related and above all increase direct sales i.e. web sales. At present
the percentage of web sales is approximately 10% of the total passenger sales on network basis
now. In order to enhance the direct sales (web sales) further, some of the major initiatives under
process or in the near future are:
• To make our site truly global and globally accessible site with regional foreign
languages option.
• To make it interactive and user friendly.
• To make it as major channel of revenue generation, competitive and at par with other
booking portals.
• Use as an effective platform to reduce unsold inventory levels.
• In the long run to develop website as interactive tool for
o Customers
o Prospective business clients
o global networking
o Press releases/information tool about our products, features etc.
o Blog writing, linking and development
o Platform to patronise and bring people closer, who matter for our business on
global basis
o As international tool for marketing, sales, publicity and promotion etc.
o Platform for developing business, partnerships and associations
o Platform for co-promotional, co-branding activities, launches etc.
o Developing data base for promotional activities.
• To link website to other social media networking sites for getting increased traffic with
objective of enhancing sales, constructive publicity and brand building.
• To develop website as tool for electronic media publicity for AI to reduce costs.
• To develop ancillary revenues for Air India by extending options like travel insurance,
visa processing, in-bound tourism etc for its customers.
26. The constant improvisation and modification of website enhances customer satisfaction and
enables the airline to increase its revenues i.e. direct web sales and at the same time reduces
distribution and ticket/booking related costs.

8
Advertising
27. In 2009-10 it was felt that due to the severe cash crunch being faced by the company,
expenditure towards publicity and sales promotion should be kept to the bare minimum. However,
in the current year 2011-12, the company has embarked upon major advertising campaigns in the
various media channels like Television, Print, Radio and Hoardings. Air India has also been
advertising in its website and online channels and just completed an Advertisement campaign on the
recent schemes and product upgrades in all the media channels. Another campaign in the beginning
of February 2012. Air India has also tied up with major events as part of sales promotion. It may
be noted that in contrast to Rs.460.80 lacs spent on Advertising and Sales Promotion during period
April – December, 2010, a sum of Rs.860.70 lacs has been spent on Advertising and Sales
Promotion, during April – December, 2011.
Schemes to promote executive class...
28. AI offers a number of schemes for promotion of Executive Class product on the domestic
network. These include:
– ‘Get Up Front’ Offer:  Air India has launched  an airport upgrade scheme, where
passengers at select domestic airports can pay a prefixed amount of Rs.4000 (distance
up to 750 km.)/Rs.6000 (distance above 750 km.) and upgrade their domestic travel
to Business class, subject to availability of seats and on First Come First Served Basis
at the airport. This scheme is available from 16 Airports in India.
– Upgrade through Option Town: In partnership with Option Town, this is a scheme
to solicit Business class upgrade through Email/SMS. A passenger registers at the

REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
78. In the past year, Air India Express has had to curtail operations due to an acute shortage
of cockpit crew. The problem was aggravated with the implementation of new Civil Aviation
Requirement (CAR) guidelines by the DGCA in February 2012. The new CAR stipulates that rest
hours for the pilots be increased. Further, the number of landings permitted for a pilot at night time
have been restricted from 3 to 2. Pilots are also restricted from operating on two consecutive night
flights. Most importantly, their duty hours have been severely curtailed when they fly in the
“Window of Circadian Low” which has been determined to be between 0200 hours to 0600 hours.
There are further restrictions on their travel as passengers, weekly and daily rest hours etc. These
restrictions have further dwindled the availability of cockpit crew for flying duty. The restricted
capacity is the primary reason for the drop in market share. As the crew situation improves, more
and more flights will be reinstated and new flights introduced. This will definitely provide a boost
to the revenues and market share of the airline. Increased domestic operations are also under active
consideration. Despite the crew constraints, effective April 2012, Air India Express has increased
the Mumbai-Mangalore-Mumbai service from twice weekly to daily. Similar expansion is being
considered for other domestic sectors depending on cockpit crew availability.

105. The Committee no tes that various recommendations and provisions made in the Budget has

positive signals to the aviation industry. The Committee also notes that provision has also been

REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
106. Recommendation of the Committee has been noted.
107. Regarding increase of service tax, the Minister of Civil Aviation had written to Finance
Minister to roll back the service tax on air travel. However, the Finance Ministry has not acceded
to the request of this Ministry. As regards the permission for import of ATF, the Aviation industry
would be benefited by the provisions in the Finance Bill. The direct Import of ATF would need
a lot of logistics to be put in place like arranging for storage at port, transportation on high seas
and then from Port to Airport. There are benefits arising out of the same but it may take almost
6 months for tying up all the logistics and only then the benefits can be seen. It is estimated that
the imported ATF may be cheaper by 8-10%.
108. Ministry also agree that hike in service tax rates will increase the expenses of the airlines
by 2%. It may, however, be noted that fares are determined by the competition in the market
and are not cost driven and as such all the increase on account of Service tax in the expenses
would not be passed on to the passengers. This would adversely affect the profitability of the
airline.
109. The budget provides a service tax for Economy class passengers at a rate of 4.94%
compared to the current levels of a fixed amount of Service tax pegged at Rs 150 per pax for
domestic and Rs 750 per pax for International flights. Therefore the service tax element in the
tickets for Economy class passengers has gone up. However, for First and Executive class
passengers, the service tax element in the ticket has come down from 10.3% to 4.94%.

INTRODUCTION 
  
 I, the Chairman, Department- related Parliamentary  Standing Committee on Transport, 
Tourism and Culture, having authorized by the Commi ttee to present on its behalf, do hereby 
present this One Hundred Eighty Sixth Report on Act ion Taken by the Government on the 
recommendations/observations of the Committee conta ined in its One Hundred Seventy Fifth 
Report on the Demands for Grants of Ministry of Culture (2012-13).  
2.  One Hundred Seventy Fifth Report of the Department-  related Parliamentary Standing 
Committee on Transport, Tourism and Culture was pre sented to the Parliament on the 7 th  May, 2012 in 
Parliament.  
3.  The Action Taken Replies on the recommendations of the Committee contained in its One 
Hundred Seventy Fifth Report were received from the Ministry of Culture, on 16 
th  October, 2012. 
4.  The Committee considered and adopted the Report as its meeting held on the 5 th  November, 
2012. 
 
 
 
SITARAM YECHURY 
NEW DELHI;                                            Chairman,  
November 5,,  2012                                            Department -related Parliamentary Standing  
Kartika 14,  1934 (Saka)                     Committee on  Transport,  Tourism and Culture.
