Human Resource Development
44. The IWT Policy also lays stress on the requirement of human resource development. The
trained manpower of the IWT sector can be classified into two groups. The first category consists
of professionals in various fields like hydrography, navigation, civil engineering, mechanical
engineering, naval architecture and transport economics for the development and management of
the waterways and operation of various supporting infrastructural facilities. The second category
of personnel would be required for operational purposes to man the inland vessels.
45. The Committee was informed that in order to meet the manpower requirement National
Inland Navigation Institute (NINI) was established by IWAI at Patna and has been functional from
February, 2004. Induction course for deck and engine ratings, preparatory course for srang and
drivers, basic and advanced dredging courses, refresher courses for hydrographic surveyors, repair
and maintenance of vessels etc. are conducted in NINI regularly. So far, over 1300 candidates (till
July, 2012) have been trained at NINI for IWT sector. The administration and management of the
Institute is done by M/s ARI, New Delhi. NINI has got ISO 9001:2008 certifications during
February, 2010. 100% placement has been achieved for the trainees of 13
th and 14 th batch and 50%
for 15 th batch. A scheme for placement of NINI trained candidates on board IWAI vessels under
Apprentice Act has also been implemented. An “Inland Vessel Manoeuvring Simulator” has been set
up and commissioned in March, 2010.
46. Further, Memorandum of Understanding has been signed between IWAI and M/s ARI for
setting up of a “Marine Simulator Centre” at NINI on 50:50 revenue sharing bases for which the
work is in progress, and the centre has trained 26 candidates so far. The Institution has been
approved by DG Shipping to conduct Navigational Watch keeping officers courses for manpower
for River Sea Vessels and Coastal Vessels. The first Course commenced on 15
th April, 2012. The
institute has also assisted the Government of Bihar in drafting and adopting Boat Rules 2010 and
IV rules for Government of Bihar. The approval process of Diploma Program in IWT from IMU
is also in progress.
Protocol with other Countries
47. The Committee was informed that the Government of India and Bangladesh have entered
into an arrangement for the use of their waterways for commerce between the two countries.
Under the arrangements certain IWT routes have been undertaken which are:– (i) Kolkata-Silghat-
Kolkata, (ii) Kolkata-Karimganj-Kolkata, (iii) Rajshahi-Dhulian-Rajshahi and (iv) Silghat-Karimganj-
Silghat. For inter-country trade, five ports of call have been designated in each country. These are;
Haldia, Kolkata, Pandu, Karimganj and Silghat in India, Narayanganj, Khulna, Mongla, Sirajganj and
Ashuganj in Bangladesh. This protocol has recently been extended up to 31.3.2014. More than
15 lakh tonnes of fly ash is transported between Kolkata/Haldia and Bangladesh every year under
this protocol.
48. During the Secretary level talks held in Dhaka between India and Bangladesh early July,
2012, it was proposed that the validity of the protocol should be co-terminus with the trade
agreement and the protocol has been reviewed by another two years till 31
st March, 2014. Other
issues which were discussed included:-

9
(a) Operationalisation of Trans-shipment at Ashuganj for movement of cargo to North
Eastern States.
(b) Protocol routes to be made navigable and extension of Protocol route.
(c) Twenty four hours/Night Navigation and Differential Global Positioning System
Facilities.
(d) New/Extended Ports of Call.
49. It was agreed at the Secretary level talks that the follow up on each item would be further
deliberated for implementation in the Standing Committee meetings held biannually.
Indo-Myanmar Kaladan Multimodal Transit Transport Project
50. This project was conceptualized by the Ministry of External Affairs to provide alternative
connectivity of Mizoram with Haldia/Kolkata ports through Kaladan river in Myanmar. The project
envisages Coastal Shipping/ Maritime Shipping from Haldia to Sittwe, IWT from Sittwe to Paletwa
(in Myanmar) and thereafter road from Paletwa to Mizoram. The project is piloted and funded by
the MEA which appointed IWAI as their Project Development Consultant (PDC) vide agreement
dated 19.3.09 for the IWT components. After updating of DPR for port and IWT components,
IWAI invited bids for construction of these facilities and gave its recommendations to MEA for
award of work to the successful bidder. Consequently, MEA has appointed an Indian contractor
[M/s ESSAR projects (I) Pvt Ltd] for construction of port and IWT components at a cost
Rs 342 crores. Contract was signed in May 2010. Construction of Sittwe port is in progress and
the work is likely to be completed by July, 2013.
51. Initially India had tried to persuade Bangladesh to offer transport and transit rights to the
northeastern states. However, Bangladesh has consistently refused to grant such rights, including
access to its Chittagong port, which is less than 200kms away from Agartala, the capital of
Tripura.
North East Region
52. The IWT Policy 2001 envisages that special emphasis would be laid on the development of
inland water transport facilities in the North-Eastern Region. The main bulk commodities which can
be considered suitable for inland water transport movement are coal, POL, food grains, limestone
and dolomite. The development of inland water transport facilities in the North-Eastern Region
would ensure cost effective transportation of the above mentioned commodities.
53. The Government in 2008-09 introduced a Central Sector Scheme for the development of
IWT in the NE States. The activities covered under the scheme include hydrographic surveys,
techno economic feasibility studies, preparation of DPR, bandalling, dredging provision of
navigational aids and setting up of terminal facilities for passenger and cargo handling. 100 % grant
is provided by the Central Government under this scheme. During the 11th Plan period, IWAI has
spent Rs.208.69 crores in the NE Region.
Connectivity of Waterways to Ports
54. IWT Policy Document 2001 gives that interlinking waterways and ports with coastal
shipping holds good prospects in respect of several river systems in India. For instance Ganga-
Brahmaputra- Sunderbans river system has the potential to be integrated with Haldia-Kolkata ports,
the Brahmani-Mahanadi river system with Paradip port, Krishna-Godavari-Buckingham Canal with
Chennai port, West Coast Canal with Cochin Port and the Manddovi-Zuari-Cumburjua Waterways

10
with Murmugao port. The development and connectivity of these waterways with the ports will not
only ensure development of the entire hinterland but will also help in relieving the pressure on the
other already congested modes of transportation. In this connection the Secretary, Ministry of
Shipping stated that “one more area which I did not touch and you had touched in your opening
remarks was connectivity of waterways to the ports. I think, this is another area which has not been
much talked about. This is very crucial. For example, in most of the countries like Holland,
wherever there is 30 to 40 per cent transportation by inland waterways, the river is also connected
to the port and there is only navigation lock –in between. So whatever cargo is coming through
the ships is straightway going into the river system. That is what we need to focus on, and we
have done that exercise. Today, we have started identifying that. Till now, we used to only talk
about road and rail connectivity gap in the port. Now we have widened that definition, we have
included waterways and there is a committee under my Chairmanship. We have already collected
information. Now, we are trying to identify those gaps and then we will see how to fill up those
gaps.”
Techno-Economic Studies and R&D
55. As per the IWT Policy Document 2001, it has been stated that due to nascent stages of
development of the IWT sector, research and development has to play a crucial role in the
development of the sector. Design of low-cost and shallow-draft vessel and introduction of
navigational aids are important factors for improving the economics of IWT. In view of this, during
the Ninth Plan, an R&D cell was set up in IWAI to act as a nodal agency to coordinate the R&D
activities required to be carried out in this sector.
56. The Committee was informed that preparation of Detailed Project Reports (DPR) for
Kakinada-Puducherry canals along with Godavari and Krishna rivers and East-Coast Canal along
with Brahmani River and Mahanadi delta were completed in 2009-10 and their EIA/EMP studies are
at advanced stage. In 2011-12 a few more technical studies have been completed. These are:
(a) DPR of Goa Waterways (b) DPR of Barak river (c) decongestion of Mumbai city through IWT
and coastal routes; and (c) identification of potential waterways of north-eastern region. Studies for
(a) design of prototype inland cum coastal vessel (b) Technical feasibility of providing 3 m LAD
in Allahabad-Ghazipur stretch of NW-1; and (c) review feasibility study for extension NW-3 in
north and south sides are in progress.
Central Inland Water Transport Corporation (CIWTC)
57. The Central Inland Water Transport Corporation, Kolkata set up in 1967 was the principal
inland water operator with the following activities:
• Transportation by inland waterways from Kolkata to Bangladesh and to Assam and
lighterage operations in the river Hooghly;
• Transportation from Kolkata to Allahabad;
• Construction and repair of small and medium sized vessels;
• Repairs of ocean-going vessels.
Merger of CIWTC with IWAI
58. The Committee came to know that IWAI in the past, since its formation in the year 1986
has been taking over various river terminals viz. Guwahati, Patna, Allahabad and Haldia, belonged
to the CIWTC without manpower. As a result thereof, the CIWTC got overburdened with excess
staff having no work. This situation has accelerated the loss making process by the CIWTC. In

11
addition to this, the IWAI has taken over some vessels belonged to CIWTC, viz. Tug MOT-III and
Bahika-IV for Re.1/- only, without the crew.
59. They have also taken over the following from CIWTC:–
(a) river conservation works in 2005-06 without the small vessels and manpower;
(b) the “competent authority” for Indo-Bangladesh Protocol in 2003 which CIWTC had
with them since 1973 for 30 years. No manpower was taken over.
All the above measures were being used only for the IWT sector.
Future of CIWTC
60. During the deliberations, the Secretary Shipping has stated that “Recently, we prepared an
inventory of the assets, moveable as well as immoveable, we have found that they own a lot of
land which is also useful for the development of the waterways, particularly in the North East. It
has already been sent to the IWAI. They are having a look at that, As far as the assets are
concerned, there should be no difficulty in the IWAI taking over those assets. They will be of use
to them in their operations. On man power, sir, we would, of course try to see how many can be
absorbed in the IWAI. At the same time we will also explore the possibility of coming out with
an improved voluntary retirement scheme. Even the existing one is accepted by some people. But
if possible we will try to come out with an improved voluntary retirement scheme with the approval
of the cabinet. Then we will move in that direction whereby some accept the voluntary retirement
scheme and the rest move to the IWAI, and the assets, by and large move to the IWAI. We are
trying to do that in an expeditious manner.”
Private Investment in the IWT Sector
61. India has a highly developed railways and roads network of considerable size and capacity
for transportation of goods and passengers. However, in spite of a strong case for development
of inland water transport, this sector remained neglected. The development of infrastructure and
services in the IWT sector needs mobilization of substantial resources to improve the efficiency
and quality of services. It is expected that private sector participation in the development of
infrastructure and services in the IWT sector would result in reducing gestation period for setting
up of the new facilities and services and bring the latest technology and improved management
techniques.
62. Government has decided to permit automatically Foreign Direct Investment up to 100 per
cent equity for infrastructure sector. This would be applicable to IWT sector.
Suggestions for Promoting Water Transport
63. FICCI has suggested that viability and means to attract more investment into the IWT
sector should be studied by creating an institutional frame work for it, IWT should also become
a part of the National Maritime Development Programme. More waterways should be identified for
development and those earmarked be given a push. Also for a viable project, government has to
ensure stable two-way traffic as even large volume of cargo in one direction cannot make a river
service economically viable.
64. The fuel used for the barges are mostly diesel and it has a negative impact on the
operational costs if diesel prices are hiked. The route identification is very important as in certain
stretches the land route is shorter than the river way route. The wide variation in the draft of
rivers is also a cause for concern. On NW-1, according to experts, there are stretches where

12
the draft is as deep as 6 m but there also stretches where its below 1.8 m. This can slow down
a barge.
65. Regarding navigable drafts, FICCI has commented that waterways are suffering from lack
of required depth, width and vertical (overboard) clearance which would allow vessels to pass
through easily. It should be noted that even if any point on the stretch of waterway to be used
is not navigable, the entire stretch becomes useless. Moreover, the waterways should have all-
weather operations. The width of the canals varies from 9m to 20m. It makes movement of the
barges (having width of around 9 meters) very difficult in the narrow stretches. Presence of low-
lying bridges across the canals causes hindrance for the movement of vessels with cargo.
66. Dredging is required for providing and maintaining the depth. Widening of canals require
land acquisition. The road/rail bridges constructed over the canals/waterways become hindrances
in passing of a loaded barge. For example, a bridge at Kovilthottam around half a km away from
Chavara towards Cochin side, posed problems for the free movement on waterway for Indian Rare
Earths Limited (IREL).
67. ONGC has submitted that enhanced usage of Inland Waterways infrastructure shall provide
a competitive and faster mode of transportation of large cargo of food items like wheat and rice,
construction material like steel and cement; coal for power generation and fertilizers. For developing
a robust infrastructure, upgradation of the waterways to enable their navigability around the year
need to be done. Government may consider restructuring of IWAI with authority vesting with
professional having domain knowledge of the sector with long term continuity in position, instead
of the current arrangements of the IWAI which is managed by the generalists drawn from civil
service, with a short term tenure.
68. FACT imports about 2.5 lakh MT of sulphur and 3 lakh MT of rock phosphate annually.
These solid raw materials are moved by barge and road to the production units at Udyogamandal
and Ambalamugal. FACT produces about 85 lakh MT of fertilizers annually.
69. In the wake of restrictions on road movement of these dangerous chemicals like ammonia,
FACT has drawn up plans for transport of ammonia and other raw materials by barges, also has
plans for expansion and diversification of its fertilizer production facilities. With the implementation
of these projects, the volume of raw materials handled and also the finished products transported
would increase considerably. Water transport requirements would need to be augmented to meet
these needs. Dedicated barges are required for transportation of goods like phosphoric acid, sulphur
etc. the major factor influencing success of these initiatives will be the availability of barges often
dedicated ones for transporting these materials. Government agencies like Kerala Shipping and
Inland Navigation Corporation and IWAI should play a more proactive role to support industries in
their requirement by partnering such ventures. The role of private players in water transport is vital
in making these endeavors a success.
70. Periodical dredging of the waterways wherever essential, needs to be carried out by the
authorities concerned to ensure that bulk cargoes can be handled safely and without delay leading
to demurrages. FACT is principally transporting its finished goods by road and rail at present could
also look at water transport as a new alternative especially to locations in Kerala. This would
reduce dependency on rail movement which is becoming more congested leading to delays.
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS
71. The Committee notes that Inland Water Transport (IWT) is a fuel efficient and
environment friendly mode of transportation. India is richly endowed with navigable
waterways, comprising rivers, canals, backwaters, creeks, etc. that can be developed as
alternate mode of transportation in the coming years.

13
72. This Committee has always stood for developing water transport in a big way which
also has some immense potential. It has been emphasizing this through its
recommendations given in various reports, latest being its 177
th Report on Demands for
Grants, 2012-13, of the Ministry of Shipping. This inter alia states that water transport has
various advantages compared to road transport. Water transport is cheaper, can handle huge
volumes of cargo and less impact on environment. The Committee had felt that a strong
inland water transport system would be able to handle an efficient, cheaper and
environment-friendly cargo transport system. The Committee, had strongly recommended to
make available adequate resources in order to have a well connected water transport
facilities throughout the country.
NATIONAL POLICY
73. India has inland waterways with a navigable length of 14,500 km, but the Committee
notes is constrained to state that even though National IWT Policy document prepared in
the Ninth Plan prescribed for making efforts for pooling the resources through captive users
and PSUs, with liberal investments in IWT sector, the Government have failed to implement
the vision of the policy document in actual terms over these years. On the contrary, water
transport has shrunk even in those areas with great potential. The Committee also notes
that lack of adequate policy support for the sector was also compounding the problems,
leading to IWT losing its competitive edge over other modes of transport. The other modes
of transport received policy support and huge investment in developing its infrastructure,
whereas the water transport seems to have been neglected or has not received the required
attention of the policy makers and the Government. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that Government of India should take necessary follow up actions on the
Inland Water Transport Policy Document of 2001 for the optimum utilization of our
potential in the water transport sector.
74. Having emphasized this, the Committee is of the views that IWT as a mode of
transportation cannot be considered in isolation. It needs to be integrated with other modes
of transportation to achieve maximum benefits. Centre-level coordination would be required
for this. The Committee also recommends that IWT operators should be given a level-
playing field vis-à-vis those in other modes – road and rail transports.
75. The Committee notes that national highways are contributing about 40% of the road
accidents and trucks being the major contributor in this. The water transportation being the
safest mode, can reduce the road accident and resulting casualties significantly. It also
reduces treatment and rehabilitation costs to a great extent. Moreover, the land acquisition
for the Highways/Roads have been a major problem which is not only sensitive issue, it is
highly time taking and costly exercise. There is shortage of free land for road construction.
Switching to water mode, therefore, would become the most viable option to reduce the
dependency on roads, particularly for bulk cargo transport. It has lot of tourist potential
especially for pilgrimage which is mainly located on river sides.
FUND ALLOCATIONS
76. Even in the operational waterways, the Committee notes, lack of maintenance and
sufficient funds are the main reasons for insignificant use of National Waterways. We have
five national waterways so far, of which only three are operational and rest of two are to
be started since last three years. The Committee recommends that adequate funds need to
be allocated separately for maintenance and development of the national waterways which
are presently in use. The Committee notes with dismay and express its unhappiness for not

14
being able to operationalise NW 4 and 5 so far. It is believed that these national waterways
will be operationalised on PPP mode as has been decided by the Planning Commission. This
Committee does not know why this have been kept languishing. The Committee feels that
Planning Commission is not much interested in the development of waterways in the
country as their reluctance to allocate adequate budget has resulted the two national
waterways NW-4 and 5 remain in mere papers. To avoid further delay, the Committee
recommends to allocate adequate financial support soon for operationalising these
waterways.
77. The Committee notes that severe dearth of infrastructure and lack of modernization
are the major factors bedeviling the Inland Water Transport sector in the country. The
Committee notes that Infrastructure creation requires continued efforts better planning and
larger quantum of funds.
78. The Committee also notes that not only the allocations made for IWT has been
inadequate, till the end of Eleventh Plan only an amount of Rs.1168 crore approximately
has been incurred. Further only an amount of Rs.1500 crore have been allocated by the
Planning Commission, whereas, the working group as projected requirement of funds to
the line of Rs.10,500 crore for the Twelfth Five year plan. This trend can be observed
in the previous plan periods like Eighth, Ninth and Tenth also. All the above periods,
the Budget Estimates and the actual expenditure incurred left huge gaps. It is a matter
of concern of the Committee that even the inadequate fund are also not being optimally
utilized. Besides, there is no specific planning and roadmap for mobilizing required
investment for the creation of infrastructure and modernization of the existing
waterways and also operationlising new ones that are pending. The Committee
recommends that government should come out with comprehensive projects for
development of IWT in the country in a time bound manner and sanctions for the same
should be made accordingly.
79. In this connection, the Committee would like to reiterates its recommendation
contained in its 130
th Report on the “National Waterway (Lakhipur-Bhanga stretch of the
Barak River) Bill, 2007”. The Committee had expressed its concern about the
discontinuance of the centrally sponsored scheme for IWT development in the country by
the Planning Commission, the Committee was of the view that the decision of the Planning
Commission to convert the centrally sponsored scheme (CSS) for IWT development into
central sector scheme would adversely affect the pace of development of Inland water
transport in the county. The Committee had recommended for the revival of the centrally
sponsored scheme for overall development of the IWT Sector.
80. The Committee would like to reiterate its recommendation made on its 130
th Report
which was about the proposed NW-6. The Committee was of the view that the proposed
NW-6 would boost the rural economy and provide IWT connectivity for movement of
commodities between the Port of Haldia/Kolkata through Indo-Bangladesh protocol route for
transit and trade in hinterland and Bangladesh. Besides decongestion of roads and fuel
saving, it would provide port-hinterland connectivity, better environment corridor and
generate employment among weaker sections and increase tourism activities in the region.
The Committee had recommended that the existing Protocol routes connecting NW-1 and
NW-6 and NW-2 and NW-6 may be taken up with the Bangladesh on an expeditious way to
convert these waterways into international waterways for effective transportation of inter-
country movement of goods between hinterland cities and Bangladesh. But in the process
the security concern should not be compromised in any way.

15
DREDGING, CHANNELS, TERMINALS AND NA VIGATION
81. The Committee notes that waterways do not have the required depth, width and
vertical (overboard) clearance which would allow vessels to pass through easily. It should be
noted that even if any stretch of waterway to be used is not navigable, the entire stretch
becomes useless. Moreover, the waterways should have all-weather operations. The
Committee also notes that the width of the canals varies from 9m to 20m. It makes
movement of the barges (having width of around 9 meters) very difficult in the narrow
stretches. Also the presence of low-lying bridges across the canals acts as hindrance for the
movement of vessels with cargo. The Committee, therefore, recommends that IWAI should
make a policy standard for all the navigable canals in order to ensure required depth and
width in all the waterways.
82. The Committee also recommends that periodical dredging of the waterways wherever
essential needs to be carried out by the IWAI/Major Ports to ensure that bulk cargoes can
be handled safety and without delay.
83. The Committee notes that the modern day navigation aids have been developed and
implemented by most of the major ports in the country. Therefore, the IWAI could seek
the expertise of the same from the major Ports like Mumbai Port Trust, Jawaharlal Nehru
Port Trust, etc., for making the navigation along the waterways hassle free. Also the GPRS
used by many agencies also can be applied in the NWs to monitor the vessels. The IWAI
may take the expertise from the agencies which are working under the Ministry of Shipping
in this field. The Committee also recommends that initiatives need to be taken to facilitate
night navigation in order to meet the quantity requirements of the industries along the
waterways.
84. The Committee recommends that the road/rail bridges constructed over the canals/
waterways should not become hindrances in passing of a loaded barge. As the Committee
has been informed that a bridge at Kovilthottam around half a km away from Chavara
towards Cochin side, which posed problems for the free movement on waterway for Indian
Rare Earths Limited (IREL). The Committee recommends that wherever possible, existing
bridges should be redeveloped for  providing the required vertical clearance .
85. The Committee also was informed that the fishing activities along the navigable
canals are causing hindrances to the vessel movements. The Committee notes that if the
fishing nets are removed from the waterways, it may cause conflict with the interests of the
fishermen. The Committee recommends that field visits should be organized to address the
concerns of fishermen and make them aware of the problems created by fishing nets.
OTHER USER AMENITIES
86. In order to ensure the optimum utilization of potential of waterways, it is necessary
that River Terminals are connected to the hinterland by proper road terminals. The
Committee recommends that on the lines of Pandu terminal, good quality road links may
be provided connecting all other terminals of the National Waterways. Similarly, feasibility
of rail connectivity to terminals on each NW also need to be worked out for a better cargo
movement to and fro using the waterways.
87. The Committee recommends that the terminal should have properly developed
facilities such as jetties for berthing of vessels, space for loading/unloading, storage area,
space for vehicles movement and parking, etc. These facilities are to be provided by the
government. Apart from these, the Government should encourage setting up of ancillary
infrastructural facilities such as custom bonded area within the terminals.

16
88. The Committee also observes that last mile connectivity is one of the major
hurdles in switching to IWT. While, services are available for moving the cargo from one
terminal to another terminal, finding a service provider for last mile connectivity is
difficult and not so cost-effective. The existing service providers have to evolve an
integrated logistics model wherein they take the responsibility for end-to-end movement.
This would remove the multiple interfaces with different transport service providers that
a shipper is subjected to. Moreover, the shipper would feel relieved and can focus on its
core business. The committee recommends for a holistic approach in providing such
facilities in various waterways.
CARGO HANDLING
89. The Committee is constrained to note that despite huge potential cargo
transportation by Inland Water Transport mode has not shown significant improvement on
these National Waterways as its share is only 0.15 per cent in the country compared to 32
percent in Bangladesh or 9 per cent of China. The Committee also expresses its displeasure
over the fact that no comparative cost-output evaluation for transportation of cargo through
this alternate mode of transport has been carried out by the Government. The Committee
is of the view that such evaluation would further establish the support of Inland Water
Transport over other mode of transports. Therefore, the Committee recommends that
realistic physical target for cargo transportation year-wise should be fixed and time-bound
action plan should be implemented in the IWT sector during the Twelfth Plan period. The
Committee hopes that the target of 15 billion tonne km by 2017 may, at least, be achieved
so as to rejuvenate this sector.
90. The Committee also notes that there are no regular services for movement of cargo
through IWT. Existing service providers cater to full shipload of cargo on charter basis.
However, entities with less than shipload, such as 1-2 TEUs, do not have the facility for
moving the cargo same day by IWT. For having the full load for a barge, the shipper would
have to wait for 7-10 days. This waiting time is not required in case of moving the
containers by road, as the shipper can move any number of containers same day. The
Committee is of the view that regular barge services between the ports and inland water
terminal can resolve this problem.
CARGO TRANSPORTATION OF PSUs
91. The Committee recommends that bulk cargoes like, raw materials, chemicals,
containers and finished products from various industrial units need to be promoted by the
IWT mode. Since many agencies are currently depending solely on the road and rail modes
of transports the new alternative will be able to reduce the road congestions, accidents and
dependency on rail movement which is now facing congestion, lack of stalks etc., leading
to delays.
92. The Committee observes that (National Thermal Power Corporation (NTPC) is
contributing to the IWT a good share of its raw material movement at many of its thermal
power stations. Since the road and railway networks are causing hindrances for imported
coal movement due to shortage of rakes and congestion at ports, the IWT mode is found
to be more suitable for NTPC. The Committee recommends that NTPC’s project at
Bongaigaon and Barah should be assisted with the IWT system for coal movement and IWAI
should complete the projects within the schedule.
93. The Committee, in view of the restrictions on the movement of dangerous raw
materials of Fertilizers and Chemicals Travancore Limited (FACT) by road like Ammonia,

17
Benzene, Sulphuric acid, etc., recommends that, the opportunity may be explored for
enhancing the cargo transportation in the NW-3. The Committee, therefore, recommends
that IWAI should play a more proactive role for promotion of national waterways and extent
its support to such industries in their requirements by partnering such ventures.
94. The Committee recommends that IWAI may take the matter with FACT so that bulk
movement of raw materials to its various plants could be carried out through the inland
waterway mode. The project will be able to handle the finished products of FACT also to
various parts of the country and to various sea ports. This mode will enable free movement
of materials in a more economic and hassle free manner and may be a mutual benefit for
both the agencies.
95. The Committee is of the view that Food Corporation of India (FCI) could be a
regular beneficiary of the water ways as they have food grain movement round the year.
The Committee notes the initiative taken for transportation of food grains in Kolata-Tripura
through Ashugang. The Committee recommends that IWAI should make a feasibility report
on the movement of food grains through IWT mode on other parts of the country and the
additional facilities required also should be identified so that FCI could be made an active
beneficiary of the waterways.
CONNECTIVITY TO PORTS
96. The Committee recommends that linking of ports in Karnataka, Gujarat and Tamil
Nadu also should be worked out as these states are having in-bound and out-bound bulk
cargo potential. The Committee recommends for developing the West coast – Kandla,
Mumbai, Murmogao, Kochi – and East coast – Kolkata, Paradip, Vishakhapatnam, Chennai–
coastal freight corridors. Investing in these corridors will augment scale and improve the
economics for coastal shipping, making it an attractive alternative to other modes. Also, it
will improve last mile road and rail connectivity to and from ports.
97. The Committee is of the view that there is a need to encourage inland water
transport for movement of containers from various ports. It also reduces the costs and
time, if the staking of the customs examined containers directly to the ship. This might
enable to decongest the already congested roads and the transaction costs.
98. The Committee is of the view that if Central and State Governments concerned take
the necessary steps for the promotion of coastal transportation, the free movement of cargo
in a cost-effective manner will benefit the EXIM trade in the country.
99. The Committee also recommends that as in the case of Vallarpadam Terminal, all the
other Ports including private ports of the country may be connected with the Inland Water
Transport System so that cargo movement from ports to other part of the territory can be
met in a cost effective manner.
INDO-BANGLADESH PROTOCOL ON IWT
100. The Committee is of the view that container mode of transport should be promoted
in the area using multi-modal transit route through Bangladesh, which may ease the
transport of essential commodities to the North Eastern States of the country. Already NE
Region is suffering connectivity handicap with the mainland India. The Committee observes
that the land route currently being used for the purpose through the chicken neck is over-
stretched. The Committee recommends that Containers Corporation of India (CONCOR)
may take the initiatives in establishing necessary terminals for the purpose.

18
101. The Committee also recommends that for establishing arrangements through
Bangladesh, the pre requisite is to develop a river port at Ashuganj, on the Meghana River.
The road network connecting Ashuganj with the check-posts also need to be widened for
ease of traffic there. Round the clock navigation facilities need to be provided in the
protocol routes, if feasible, in all aspects.
INDO-MYANMAR KALADAN MULTIMODAL TRANSIT TRANSPORT PROJECT
102. The Committee has been informed that Kaladan Multi-Modal Transit Transport
Project will connect the eastern Indian seaport of Kolkata with Sittwe port in Myanmar by
sea; it will then link Sittwe to Mizoram via river and road transport. This project will reduce
distance from Kolkata to Sittwe by approximately 1328 km and will reduce the need to
transport good through the narrow Siliguri corridor. The Committee recommends that Indo-
Myanmar Kaladan Multimodal Transit Transport Project may be considered for
implementation.
MERGING OF CIWTC WITH IWAI
103. The Committee observes that periodically the assets and work assignments of
CIWTC were taken over by the IWAI without absorbing the employees working on those
assets and work assignments. This has finally resulted in the accumulation of large
numbers of employees without any work. The Committee therefore recommends that the
IWAI should correct the mistake it has committed over these years and should come
forward to take the service of the experienced staff of CIWTC in the IWT sector.
104. In this connection the Committee has conveyed its concern to the Government from
time to time. In its 177 th Report, the Committee has again and again considered the matter
observed and the Committee had expressed its concern over the future of persons working
in CIWTC. The Committee hoped that the staff of CIWTC would not be forced to opt VRS
against individual’s will and CIWTC would be merged with IWAI if the assets of CIWTC
were taken over by it. The Committee also recommended that till the merger process is
completed adequate funds and manpower be made available to CIWTC to carry out its
operations.
HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT
105. The Committee notes that National Inland Navigation Institute (NINI) is providing
various courses required in the water transport and aquatic navigation, dredging repair and
maintenance of vessels, etc. The Committee hopes NINI is able to solve the shortage of
vessel pilots as faced by the Major Ports of the country also. The Committee recommends
that the curriculum and the courses offered must reflect the future requirements of the
country.
CRUISE TOURISM
106. River cruise tourism is a major tourist attraction with enormous potential for further
development in places like Guwahati, Goa, Mumbai, Kolkata and Kerala. The house boats and small
boats are also catering to the tourism needs. The Committee feels that the tourism will get
required boost when the waterways are fully developed and linked properly with various
Ports of the country. This factor, therefore, should be kept in mind while planning for
expansion and development of water transport in the country.

19
107. The Committee would like to draw attention in this respect towards development of
tourism circuit proposed in Alappuzha, which is a river/backwater tourism spot for which the
Government of Kerala has planned a mega circuit project for development of backwaters
and the same is under consideration of the Ministry of Tourism for the grant of central
financial assistance. The Committee would like to know response of the Union Ministry in
this regard.
108. The Committee observes that the river tourism offers multi faceted tourism potential
like hotel barges, river cruise ships, canal tourism, private boats, pilgrim tourism etc.
Currently only a very few stretches of the country are utilizing the potential in a limited
manner. The Committee recommends that states that have water transport potential may
be sensitized to come forward with more river tourism projects and IWAI may assist the
States and Ministry of Tourism for making the efforts a success. This may boost the
revenue earnings from the inland waterways in the country.
MANAGEMENT OF IWAI
109. The Committee observes that the current organizational set up of the IWAI is not
sufficient enough to fulfill its objectives in a wider prespective. The Committee therefore
recommends that the IWAI need to be strengthened with experts having sufficient
experience in the fields like hydrography, navigation, civil engineering, mechanical
engineering, naval architecture, transport economics for the development and management
of the waterways, rather than it be made a dumping ground for the Civil Servants.

20
20
OBSERV ATIONS/CONCLUSIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS — AT A GLANCE
The Committee notes that Inland Water Transport (IWT) is a fuel efficient and
environment friendly mode of transportation. India is richly endowed with navigable
waterways, comprising rivers, canals, backwaters, creeks, etc. that can be developed as
alternate mode of transportation in the coming years. (Para 71)
This Committee has always stood for developing water transport in a big way which
also has some immense potential. It has been emphasizing this through its
recommendations given in various reports, latest being its 177 th Report on Demands for
Grants, 2012-13, of the Ministry of Shipping. This inter alia States that water transport has
various advantages compared to road transport. Water transport is cheaper, can handle huge
volumes of cargo and less impact on environment. The Committee had felt that a strong
inland water transport system would be able to handle an efficient, cheaper and
environment-friendly cargo transport system. The Committee, had strongly recommended to
make available adequate resources in order to have a well connected water transport
facilities throughout the country. (Para 72)
NATIONAL POLICY
India has inland waterways with a navigable length of 14,500 km, but the Committee
is constrained to state that even though National IWT Policy document prepared in the
Ninth Plan prescribed for making efforts for pooling the resources through captive users
and PSUs, with liberal investments in IWT sector, the Government have failed to implement
the vision of the policy document in actual terms over these years. On the contrary, water
transport has shrunk even in those areas with great potential. The Committee also notes
that lack of adequate policy support for the sector was also compounding the problems,
leading to IWT losing its competitive edge over other modes of transport. The other modes
of transport received policy support and huge investment in developing its infrastructure,
whereas the water transport seems to have been neglected or has not received the required
attention of the policy makers and the Government. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that Government of India should take necessary follow up actions on the
Inland Water Transport Policy Document of 2001 for the optimum utilization of our
potential in the water transport sector. (Para 73)
Having emphasized this, the Committee is of the views that IWT as a mode of
transportation cannot be considered in isolation. It needs to be integrated with other modes
of transportation to achieve maximum benefits. Centre-level coordination would be required
for this. The Committee also recommends that IWT operators should be given a level-
playing field vis-à-vis those in other modes – road and rail transports. (Para 74)
The Committee notes that national highways are contributing about 40% of the road
accidents and trucks being the major contributor in this. The water transportation being the
safest mode, can reduce the road accident and resulting casualties significantly. It also
reduces treatment and rehabilitation costs to a great extent. Moreover, the land acquisition

21
for the Highways/Roads have been a major problem which is not only sensitive issue, it is
highly time taking and costly exercise. There is shortage of free land for road construction.
Switching to water mode, therefore, would become the most viable option to reduce the
dependency on roads, particularly for bulk cargo transport. It has lot of tourist potential
especially for pilgrimage which is mainly located on river sides. (Para 75)
FUND ALLOCATIONS
Even in the operational waterways, the Committee notes, lack of maintenance and
sufficient funds are the main reasons for insignificant use of National Waterways. We have
five national waterways so far, of which only three are operational and rest of two are to
be started since last three years. The Committee recommends that adequate funds need to
be allocated separately for maintenance and development of the national waterways which
are presently in use. The Committee notes with dismay and express its unhappiness for not
being able to operationalise NW 4 and 5 so far. It is believed that these national waterways
will be operationalised on PPP mode as has been decided by the Planning Commission. This
Committee does not know why this have been kept languishing. The Committee feels that
Planning Commission is not much interested in the development of waterways in the
country as their reluctance to allocate adequate budget has resulted the two national
waterways NW-4 and 5 remain in mere papers. To avoid further delay, the Committee
recommends to allocate adequate financial support soon for operationalising these
waterways. (Para 76)
The Committee notes that severe dearth of infrastructure and lack of modernization
are the major factors bedeviling the Inland Water Transport sector in the country. The
Committee notes that Infrastructure creation requires continued efforts better planning and
larger quantum of funds. (Para 77)
The Committee also notes that not only the allocations made for IWT has been
inadequate, till the end of Eleventh Plan only an amount of Rs.1168 crore approximately has
been incurred. Further only an amount of Rs.1500 crore have been allocated by the
Planning Commission, whereas, the working group as projected requirement of funds to the
line of Rs.10,500 crore for the Twelfth Five year plan. This trend can be observed in the
previous plan periods like Eighth, Ninth and Tenth also. All the above periods, the Budget
Estimates and the actual expenditure incurred left huge gaps. It is a matter of concern of
the Committee that even the inadequate fund are also not being optimally utilized. Besides,
there is no specific planning and roadmap for mobilizing required investment for the
creation of infrastructure and modernization of the existing waterways and also
operationlising new ones that are pending. The Committee recommends that government
should come out with comprehensive projects for development of IWT in the country in a
time bound manner and sanctions for the same should be made accordingly. (Para 78)
In this connection, the Committee would like to reiterates its recommendation
contained in its 130 th Report on the “National Waterway (Lakhipur-Bhanga stretch of the
Barak River) Bill, 2007”. The Committee had expressed its concern about the
discontinuance of the centrally sponsored scheme for IWT development in the country by
the Planning Commission, the Committee was of the view that the decision of the Planning
Commission to convert the centrally sponsored scheme (CSS) for IWT development into
central sector scheme would adversely affect the pace of development of Inland water

22
transport in the county. The Committee had recommended for the revival of the centrally
sponsored scheme for overall development of the IWT Sector. (Para 79)
The Committee would like to reiterate its recommendation made on its 130 th Report
which was about the proposed NW-6. The Committee was of the view that the proposed
NW-6 would boost the rural economy and provide IWT connectivity for movement of
commodities between the Port of Haldia/Kolkata through Indo-Bangladesh protocol route for
transit and trade in hinterland and Bangladesh. Besides decongestion of roads and fuel
saving, it would provide port-hinterland connectivity, better environment corridor and
generate employment among weaker sections and increase tourism activities in the region.
The Committee had recommended that the existing Protocol routes connecting NW-1 and
NW-6 and NW-2 and NW-6 may be taken up with the Bangladesh on an expeditious way to
convert these waterways into international waterways for effective transportation of inter-
country movement of goods between hinterland cities and Bangladesh. But in the process
the security concern should not be compromised in any way. (Para 80)

vertical (overboard) clearance which would allow vessels to pass through easily. It should be
noted that even if any stretch of waterway to be used is not navigable, the entire stretch
becomes useless. Moreover, the waterways should have all-weather operations. The
Committee also notes that the width of the canals varies from 9m to 20m. It makes
movement of the barges (having width of around 9 meters) very difficult in the narrow
stretches. Also the presence of low-lying bridges across the canals acts as hindrance for the
movement of vessels with cargo. The Committee, therefore, recommends that IWAI should
make a policy standard for all the navigable canals in order to ensure required depth and
width in all the waterways. (Para 81)
The Committee also recommends that periodical dredging of the waterways wherever
essential needs to be carried out by the IWAI/Major Ports to ensure that bulk cargoes can
be handled safety and without delay. (Para 82)
The Committee notes that the modern day navigation aids have been developed and
implemented by most of the major ports in the country. Therefore, the IWAI could seek
the expertise of the same from the major Ports like Mumbai Port Trust, Jawaharlal Nehru
Port Trust, etc., for making the navigation along the waterways hassle free. Also the GPRS
used by many agencies also can be applied in the NWs to monitor the vessels. The IWAI
may take the expertise from the agencies which are working under the Ministry of Shipping
in this field. The Committee also recommends that initiatives need to be taken to facilitate
night navigation in order to meet the quantity requirements of the industries along the
waterways. (Para 83)
The Committee recommends that the road/rail bridges constructed over the canals/
waterways should not become hindrances in passing of a loaded barge. As the Committee
has been informed that a bridge at Kovilthottam around half a km away from Chavara
towards Cochin side, which posed problems for the free movement on waterway for Indian
Rare Earths Limited (IREL). The Committee recommends that wherever possible, existing
bridges should be redeveloped for  providing the required vertical clearance . (Para 84)

23
The Committee also was informed that the fishing activities along the navigable
canals are causing hindrances to the vessel movements. The Committee notes that if the
fishing nets are removed from the waterways, it may cause conflict with the interests of the
fishermen. The Committee recommends that field visits should be organized to address the
concerns of fishermen and make them aware of the problems created by fishing nets.
(Para 85)

Committee recommends that on the lines of Pandu terminal, good quality road links may

movement to and fro using the waterways. (Para 86)
The Committee recommends that the terminal should have properly developed
facilities such as jetties for berthing of vessels, space for loading/unloading, storage area,
space for vehicles movement and parking, etc. These facilities are to be provided by the
government. Apart from these, the Government should encourage setting up of ancillary
infrastructural facilities such as custom bonded area within the terminals. (Para 87)
The Committee also observes that last mile connectivity is one of the major hurdles
in switching to IWT. While, services are available for moving the cargo from one terminal
to another terminal, finding a service provider for last mile connectivity is difficult and not

wherein they take the responsibility for end-to-end movement. This would remove the
multiple interfaces with different transport service providers that a shipper is subjected to.
Moreover, the shipper would feel relieved and can focus on its core business. The committee
recommends for a holistic approach in providing such facilities in various waterways.
(Para 88)

transportation by Inland Water Transport mode has not shown significant improvement on
these National Waterways as its share is only 0.15 per cent in the country compared to 32

this alternate mode of transport has been carried out by the Government. The Committee

Transport over other mode of transports. Therefore, the Committee recommends that
realistic physical target for cargo transportation year-wise should be fixed and time-bound
action plan should be implemented in the IWT sector during the Twelfth Plan period. The
Committee hopes that the target of 15 billion tonne km by 2017 may, at least, be achieved
so as to rejuvenate this sector. (Para 89)
The Committee also notes that there are no regular services for movement of cargo
through IWT. Existing service providers cater to full shipload of cargo on charter basis.

24

moving the cargo same day by IWT. For having the full load for a barge, the shipper would
have to wait for 7-10 days. This waiting time is not required in case of moving the

Committee is of the view that regular barge services between the ports and inland water
terminal can resolve this problem. (Para 90)

containers and finished products from various industrial units need to be promoted by the
IWT mode. Since many agencies are currently depending solely on the road and rail modes

dependency on rail movement which is now facing congestion, lack of stalks etc., leading
to delays. (Para 91)

contributing to the IWT a good share of its raw material movement at many of its thermal
power stations. Since the road and railway networks are causing hindrances for imported
coal movement due to shortage of rakes and congestion at ports, the IWT mode is found
to be more suitable for NTPC. The Committee recommends that NTPC’s project at
Bongaigaon and Barah should be assisted with the IWT system for coal movement and IWAI
should complete the projects within the schedule. (Para 92)
The Committee, in view of the restrictions on the movement of dangerous raw
materials of Fertilizers and Chemicals Travancore Limited (FACT) by road like Ammonia,
Benzene, Sulphuric acid, etc., recommends that, the opportunity may be explored for
enhancing the cargo transportation in the NW-3. The Committee, therefore, recommends
that IWAI should play a more proactive role for promotion of national waterways and extent
its support to such industries in their requirements by partnering such ventures.
(Para 93)
The Committee recommends that IWAI may take the matter with FACT so that bulk
movement of raw materials to its various plants could be carried out through the inland
waterway mode. The project will be able to handle the finished products of FACT also to
various parts of the country and to various sea ports. This mode will enable free movement
of materials in a more economic and hassle free manner and may be a mutual benefit for
both the agencies. (Para 94)

regular beneficiary of the water ways as they have food grain movement round the year.
The Committee notes the initiative taken for transportation of food grains in Kolata-Tripura
through Ashugang. The Committee recommends that IWAI should make a feasibility report
on the movement of food grains through IWT mode on other parts of the country and the
additional facilities required also should be identified so that FCI could be made an active
beneficiary of the waterways. (Para 95)

The Committee recommends that linking of ports in Karnataka, Gujarat and Tamil

25
Nadu also should be worked out as these states are having in-bound and out-bound bulk
cargo potential. The Committee recommends for developing the West coast –
Kandla,Mumbai, Murmogao, Kochi – and East coast – Kolkata, Paradip, Vishakhapatnam,
Chennai – coastal freight corridors. Investing in these corridors will augment scale and
improve the economics for coastal shipping, making it an attractive alternative to other
modes. Also, it will improve last mile road and rail connectivity to and from ports.
(Para 96)

transport for movement of containers from various ports. It also reduces the costs and
time, if the staking of the customs examined containers directly to the ship. This might
enable to decongest the already congested roads and the transaction costs. (Para 97)
The Committee is of the view that if Central and State Governments concerned take
the necessary steps for the promotion of coastal transportation, the free movement of cargo
in a cost-effective manner will benefit the EXIM trade in the country. (Para 98)
The Committee also recommends that as in the case of Vallarpadam Terminal, all the
other Ports including private ports of the country may be connected with the Inland Water
Transport System so that cargo movement from ports to other part of the territory can be
met in a cost effective manner. (Para 99)

MINUTES

30

31
II
SECOND MEETING
The newly constituted Committee met at 3.30 P.M. on Thursday, the 18 th October, 2012 in
Room No. 074, Ground Floor, Parliament Library Building, New Delhi.

2. * * *
3. Thereafter, the Committee heard the Secretary, Ministry of Shipping and Inland  Waterways
Authority of India on the “Development of Inland Water Transport System in the country”. The
Ministry made a power point presentation regarding the present status of the National Waterways
I to 5 as well as its proposals in this regard during the Twelfth  Five Year Plan. The present

India using water transport system and the Committee was informed that Bangladesh Protocol

INTRODUCTION
I, the Chairman, Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport,
Tourism and Culture, having been authorized by the Committee, do hereby present on its behalf this
One Hundred Ninetieth Report on ‘Development of Tourism in Darjeeling and Sikkim’.
2. The Committee, in continuation of its special focus on promotion of Tourism in India, took
up the North-Eastern Region for studying various issues related to promotion of tourism sector in
that region. The Committee undertook a study visit to Guwahati, Aizawl, Shillong and Agartala from
9
th to 15 th February, 2011 and presented its 172 nd Report to the Parliament.
3. The Committee further visited Darjeeling and Gangtok from 26 th February to 2 nd March,
2012 to study the difficulties that came in the way of promotion of tourism in the Region such
as restriction on entry of tourists, poor infrastructure, lack of transport facility, poor security and
insufficient road-rail-air network etc.

rd January, 2013.

REPORT
CHAPTER-I
INTRODUCTION
The eight States of the North-Eastern Region form part of the East Himalayan region, which
includes Sikkim that embraces the Darjeeling Hills of West Bengal. The rich natural beauty, serenity
and exotic flora and fauna of the area are invaluable resources for the development of eco-tourism.
The Region is endowed with several tourist attractions, each State having its own distinct features.
Such attractions are scattered all over the region largely located in remote areas within highly
fragile environments.
2. Despite abundance of natural beauty, snow peaked mountains and white water rivers,
forests and wild life, the flow of incoming tourists has been marginal mainly due to lack of
infrastructure in this region. All our efforts for the development and promotion of North East
Region, that includes allocation of 10% of the Plan fund all the Ministries has had no desired
impact. An amount of Rs.110.00 crore has been earmarked in B.E. 2011-12 for the region. The
financial assistance being given to North East States includes assistance for development of tourist
infrastructure, promotion of fairs/festivals and tourism related events in the region, Information
Technology related projects, publicity campaigns, market development assistance, human resource
development, promotion and marketing etc.
3. Realizing that certain aspects/areas of the region did not get required emphasis in its earlier
report, the Committee decided to look into those aspects relating to North-Eastern Region, the
Committee decided to take up the issues relating to development of tourism for detailed
consideration and make a report to Parliament. The Committee undertook an on-the-spot study of
the region and visited Guwahati (Assam), Aizawl (Mizoram), Shillong (Meghalaya) and Agartala
(Tripura) where it interacted all the stakeholders including State Governments and local people. The
Committee has been quite concerned about the lack of infrastructure and other facilities for a long
time reflected in its observations/recommendations in its various Reports from time to time. So
much so, it had earlier made a study of the region and presented its 172
nd Report on the
Development of Tourism in North Eastern Region on 17 th August, 2011.
4. The Committee visited Darjeeling and Sikkim with the view to see, discuss and find
solutions to the problems and bottlenecks confronting the promotion of Tourism in the region.
It comprehensively studied the two major aspects of the Infrastructure Development in the two
areas, commutation; viz. development of roads, roadways, railways, airways, ropeways,
helicopter services, bridges; and (ii) Hospitality; viz ., development of hotels, homestays,
development of areas of tourist interest and to provide facilities like telescopic Himalayan
mountain views, trekking and adventure tourism, parks, monuments, etc. With these aspects in
mind, the Committee held interaction with the transport operators, hoteliers and other
stakeholders in the private sector as well as with the Ministries of Tourism, Civil Aviation, RTH,
Culture, and organizations like ASI, BRO, Airports Authority of India, Air India, and the State
Governments of West Bengal and Sikkim.
5. Darjeeling  in West Bengal is one of the most magnificent hill resorts in the world. It
conjures visions of snow peaks, serenity of vibrant green hills steeped in splendor, a land of

2
breathtaking beauty crowned by the majestic Himalayas and attracts young, adventurous and
enthusiasts across the age groups. The tourist spots and attractions in the region are serene,
pristine and hub of adventure, leisure and special interest tourism. The tourism products of
Darjeeling and adjoining areas are Tea Tourism, Toy Train—a World Heritage product, Trekking,
Water Rafting, Bird Watching Tour, Butterflies Tours, Forest Safaris and Wellness Tourism.
6. Sikkim  is a small State in the North-Eastern Himalayas, surrounded by vast stretches of
Tibetan plateau in the North, the Chumbi valley of Tibet and the kingdom of Bhutan in the East,
Darjeeling district of West Bengal in the South and the kingdom of Nepal in the West. The State
being a part of the inner ranges of mountains of Himalayas has no open valleys, and no plains but
varied elevation ranging from 300 to 8583 mtrs. consisting of lower hills, middle and higher hills,
alpine zones and snow bound land. The highest elevation of 8583 mtrs. is at the top of the
Mt. Kanchenjunga. This Hill State is a bio-diversity hotspot endowed with unblemished natural
beauty with lush green forest and abundant flora and fauna.
7. Sikkim also famous for its unique culture, ethnic heritage, pilgrimage tours, sites of
archeological interest and more so, a perfect option for adventure lovers. This hill-station, popular
as ‘Nature’s own Garden’, is one of the most sought after hill destinations. As a showcase of
nature-tourism, the hills of Sikkim offer multiple options for those in search of authentic natural
splendor away from hustle of city atmosphere.
8. These factors are supporting these hill stations to have a regular upward growth in the case
of tourist arrivals over the years.
