OBSERV ATIONS/CONCLUSIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS — AT A GLANCE
Development of Tourism related Infrastructure in Darjeeling
The Committee notes that various tourism development schemes have been proposed
for the development of Darjeeling and adjoining areas. The Committee was informed that
approximately 4000 people visit Tiger Hill every morning to watch the sunrise. The
Committee is of the view that augmentation of facilities at the observation with latest
telescopes and such aids will attract more tourists to this place. To cater to the requirement
of influx in tourists, the Committee recommends that projects initiated for the promotion
of tourism in Darjeeling and the adjoining areas may be completed within the proposed
time-frame. (Para 12)
Darjeeling Ropeway
The long pride of Darjeeling has been the ‘Singla Ropeway’, which once connected the
Darjeeling town to the other side of Sikkim, making transportation much easier has been recently
opened but with only one station. The Committee during its field visits has seen the most scenic
ropeway that has the backdrop of the snow-capped mountains, tea gardens and the Rangeet River.
The Committee hopes that this may be connected to Singla as served earlier and later it
can be extended to the other side of the river to Jorethang in Sikkim and taking it to
Namchi, making this a Darjeeling-Sikkim Ropeway, which would be a major tourist
attraction in both the places. (Para 14)
Darjeeling Himalayan Railway
The Committee, therefore, recommends that renovation/restoration of all stations
from Siliguri station to Darjeeling station should be taken up. Not only the Railway
Stations, but the adjoining areas with tea estates, old buildings, etc. should be brought
under ‘Tourism and Heritage Park’. Siliguri Town, Sukna, Tindharia, Kurseong, Sonada,
Ghoom and Darjeeling station need to be provided with tourist information and felicitation
centre and other amenities. (Para 15)
Neighbouring Country Borders
The Committee was informed that there are 3 major border points which are used by
tourists; viz., Kakkarvitta-Panitanki border with Nepal, Chengrabandha-Burimari border with
Bangladesh and Phuentsholing-Jaigaon border with Bhutan. These points need to be immediately
upgraded to facilitate tourists, which are completely unorganized at the present State. The
Committee, therefore, takes the view that all-weather single window facility like customs
and immigration clearances, foreign exchange and other information should be available to
the tourists at these spots. Inter-country reciprocal arrangement with Nepal and Bhutan
with regard to taxis, permits, foreign exchange, etc. for tourists between India-Bhutan and
India-Nepal were demanded by the tour operators. The Committee recommends that the
matter may be taken up with the Ministry of External Affairs. (Para 16)

34
Celebration of Tourism Day
The Committee was also informed that in order to create awareness about Ministry of
Tourism, Darjeeling tourism celebrates World Tourism Day on the Mall. However, last year (2010-11)
they did not get funds and the event was not organized. The Committee, therefore, recommends
that ‘Tourism day’ should be celebrated with festivity to encourage tourism sector on
regular basis and adequate allocation of funds should be provided by the Government.
(Para 17)
Streetlights and Footpaths
The Committee was informed by the stakeholders that they are not allowed to put
streetlights and build footpaths. The Committee, during the visit witnessed itself
darkness on the streets and lack of proper walking space in the roads. The Committee
notes that such measure would only enhance the market capacity of the place and
recommends that efforts should be made to put proper streetlights and build footpaths.
(Para 18)
Development of Parks
The Committee notes that Bankim Chandra Park is an important component of
tourism in Kalimpong. For development of tourism in Darjeeling and adjoining region, the
development of Kalimpong is crucial. The Committee, therefore, recommends that
immediate steps for the development of Kalimpong and also Bankim Chandra Park should
be taken. The Committee notes that the Ministry of Tourism has proposed setting up of
horticultural park, orchard garden and creation of infrastructure facilities for gliding in
Kalimpong. The Committee also recommends that the State Government may be consulted
and sensitized to submit new proposals in this regard. (Para 21)
The Committee was also informed that the Janmukti Park situated in the heart of
Kalimpong town is built on land where the Kalimpong Arts and Crafts once functioned. It is a
small Open Air Park with flowerbeds, pathways, benches, small lawns with a panoramic view of
the Himalayas. The Committee was, however, surprised to find that its view is obstructed and
obscured by concrete structure and the entrance to the park is through a historic section of
Kalimpong town where the original pagoda style enclosure that once housed the bust of Queen
Victoria still stands besides the original structure of Coronation dispensary. The Committee
recommends for the proper maintenance and upkeep of the park by the concerned agencies.
(Para 22)
Maintenance of Lakes
The Committee takes a serious view of the utter neglect of Mirik lake. The
Committee, therefore, recommends that there should be a proper sewage disposal mechanism
for the area so that the process of polluting the Mirik lake could be checked. The Committee
also recommends that de-silting should be done in Mirik Lake and, thereafter, proper
maintenance work should be carried out at regular intervals. (Para 23)
Observatories
The Committee recommends that telescopes and such facilities enabling the tourists
to get clear view of the mountain may be arranged at the Tiger Hills. (Para 24)

35
Tea Tourism
Darjeeling is famous for its beautiful Tea Gardens spread far and wide having
immense potential for tourism. The concept of ‘Tea Tourism’ should be explored for tourism
purposes. The Committee was informed during the discussions with the stakeholders that
for this purpose Lease agreement is to be reviewed to include tourism in it. The Committee
recommends that the State Government may be consulted for taking necessary steps in this
regard. (Para 26)
MICE tourism
The Committee notes that these two places have immense potential for this purpose.
There are no facility for holding conference in Darjeeling, as such, the corporate sector is
not interested in visiting the place. In Sikkim also the situation is more or less the same.
The Committee therefore recommends that the State Governments of West Bengal and
Sikkim should take benefit from the above mentioned scheme as so far they have not sent
any proposal for setting up convention centres in these places. (Para 28)
Hotel Accommodation and Amenities
The Committee recommends that subsidy should be provided to smaller and Budget
hotels on priority basis. The Committee is of the strong view that there is need to give
special status to Darjeeling and keep it at par with NE States so that it can also get
exemption in taxes, etc. If timely action is not taken the tourist flow will gradually decrease
and this will affect the economy of the region as the major source of employment is tourism
related services. (Para 29)
The Committee also visited the West Bengal Tourism hotel at Mirik. The place is
situated atop a hill with scenic beauty and the rooms are very spacious. However the facility
was not opened for visitors. The Committee noted that the place away from the crowd can
be a good staying option if properly maintained. The Committee recommends that the
possibility of opening the hotel for the public may be explored. (Para 30)
Rural Tourism
The Committee recommends that scheme for subsidy to Home Stays should be
included in the subsidy scheme for building tourist accommodation in villages. The
Committee recommends that there is an immediate need to formulate a rural tourism
policy and support for development of some model tourism villages in the Darjeeling and
Sikkim region. (Para 31)
Removal of Eyesores
The Committee was also informed of the towers which have been installed on the
rooftops and the hills which is an eyesore on the beauty of Darjeeling. There is urgent need
for relocating them. Further, there are BSNL cables lying all over the city in a haphazard
manner. These cables are potential danger and also destroy the beauty of the place. The
Committee recommends that local authorities should take corrective measures to solve the
problem. (Para 32)

36
Drinking Water Supply
The Committee recommends that drinking water should be arranged on priority basis
and special schemes for the purpose should be formulated. The Committee hopes that the
project will be completed within a period of 1½ year as informed to the Committee.
(Para 34)
Sanitation and cleanliness
The Committee also noted that sanitation and cleanliness is lacking in Darjeeling which has
to be taken up as utmost important.  Since Ministry of Tourism is already holding the “clean
India” campaign, the Committee recommends that Darjeeling should be included in the
campaign. The Committee also recommends that local bodies and NGOs may be involved the
‘Clean India’ campaign at the field levels. (Para 35)
Erratic supply of LPG
The Committee also got complaints of erratic supply of LPG cylinders to hotels which had
led to price hike and black marketing. The Committee recommends that the matter may be
taken up with concerned Ministries/agencies to ensure that hospitality sector does not face
the shortage of LPG cylinders. (Para 36)
The Committee notes that at present, Sikkim primarily is seen as a standalone
destination. However, it can be a unique combination of various products of tourist interest.
These include culture, nature and adventure tourism products. The ultimate aim is to develop
Sikkim as a part of Buddhist Circuit and an eco-tourism destination in the country. The
Committee recommends that efforts should be made to integrate all the tourism products.
The Committee hopes that these adversities like poor connectivity, under developed roads,
expensive travel costs, etc. should be met with proper study on the actual problems and
implementing modern technologies for the construction works, etc. (Para 40)
The Committee has observed that many projects sanctioned during 2008-09 and 2009-10
are still to be completed. The Committee recommends that efforts should be made to
complete these projects at the earliest. (Para 42)
The Committee also recommends that ropeway between Namchi to Samdruptse may
be considered to take tourists from Namchi which will not only save time but will also to
have a panoramic view of the place. The Committee during its field visits to the Char-Dham
temple complex has seen the well organized facilities for the pilgrim tourists there. The
Committee is also impressed with the simulator aided film show which is a major tourist
attraction there. The Committee recommends that such initiatives need to be developed at
other tourist locations in Sikkim as these places will be on must visit places by a tourist
once landed there. (Para 43)
The Committee recommends for constructing of steps for approaching the Relli river
and the pathways. The sandy beach area below the bridge could be cleaned up and
permanent picnic spots could be set up. The drive down to Relli village is through
picturesque villages. Suitable viewing points should be constructed with facilities for
drinking water, toilets and refreshments kiosks. (Para 44)
Across the Relli bridge, a small hamlet is situated the Gorkha Village complex with
cottage and a restaurant maintained by DGHC Tourism. These facilities should be opened
round the year for the sake of the tourists. (Para 46)

37
The Committee recommends that development of Relli Village as a potential tourist
spot should be initiated by the Ministry of Tourism and the wayside inn, situated in an
excellent location on a small hillock just beyond the bridge needs to be spruced up and
remain open on all occasions for the service of tourists and guests. (Para 47)
Human Resource Development
The Committee also recommends that Institute of Travel and Tourism Management
in Sikkim on the lines of the Tourism Management Institute at Gwalior for serving the
interest of tourism industry of North East may be established. (Para 49)
The Committee notes that Darjeeling district and Sikkim, both have the potential for
capacity building. They have huge manpower resources which should be tapped for the
tourism industry in the States and also for seeking placement outside the States. Trained
manpower presents positive image in the tourists mind and helps for flourishing the tourism
industry. The Committee recommends that the States should seek the benefit from the
scheme of capacity building to exploit human resources. (Para 51)
In the case of hospitality education, which is equally important for the tourism
development of Sikkim, the Committee has come to know that there is no proposal from
the State Government. The Committee recommends that Ministry of Tourism may consult
the State Government for a suitable location for establishment of an Institute of Tourism
Studies and the project may be taken up. (Para 52)
The Committee during deliberations noted that Mirik can be a potential tourist
destination. They should be made aware of the tourism potential in the area so that they
could make a better earning from it in the days ahead. There is also potential for Home
stays in Mirik town which can be explored. For exploiting the resources the local people
should be trained under some schemes. (Para 53)
STUDIES AND SURVEYS
The Committee recommends that the studies/surveys should be completed in time
and action should be taken on the study to improve various aspects of tourism. The
Committee also recommends identifying the source markets and carrying out intensive
market research through qualified consultants. The Committee also recommends that
collection of tourism data should also be made for Darjeeling. (Para 55)
RAILWAYS
The Committee is of the view that the increased transport connectivity to the Sikkim
would be a major boost for attracting travelers to the region. The Committee recommends
that Ministry of Tourism may take up the issues with the Railway Board for introducing
more trains, increasing frequency of existing trains and introduction of new trains to this
sector. (Para 59)
AIR CONNECTIVITY AND AIRPORTS
Bagdogra Airport is the only airport which supports a large area, including the States
of West Bengal, Sikkim, Bihar and Assam. It also caters to countries like Bhutan, Nepal
and Bangladesh. This is the only profitable terminal for Northeast India. Bagdogra needs to

38
be better connected to the rest of the country with flights for Mumbai, Bangalore,
Dibrugarh, Gaya etc. Also, a facility to connect most of the South and Southeast Asian
capitals. (Para 64)
The Committee, keeping in view the limitations for operating civil flights at a
Defence airport, has suggested that Air India flights need to be increased for linking
Bagdogra with major cities of the country. Since the LTC package is open to the North East
Region, the passenger rush is peak during the summer holidays and so the Air India should
make arrangements for getting more passengers accommodated by ensuring extra flight/
seat availability in the sector. (Para 65)
The Committee is also of the view that this sector has good tourist potential due to
Buddhist connection and that needs to be explored in a big way. The Travel Agents
Association also suggested for operating international flights from Bagdogra to Paro
(Bhutan) and Bangkok (Thailand). The Committee, therefore, recommends that the
commercial viability may be assessed in these sectors. (Para 69)
The Committee hopes that the efforts in enhancement of the tourist’s visits to these
areas, the commercial viability will be improved and profitable flights could be operated in
future. (Para 70)
The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Civil Aviation/Airports Authority of
India may take up with the Ministry of Defence and Indian Air Force in getting the airport
facilities upgraded as per the above proposal. The matter may also be taken up with
Government of West Bengal for making available additional land for expansion of the
Bagdogra Airport. (Para 74)
Keeping in view the culture of the area a suggestion has been made to rename Bagdogra
Airport as ‘Kabiguru Rabindranath Tagore International Airport’. The Committee desires that
the Ministry of Civil Aviation may look into the possibility of renaming the airport.
(Para 75)
Airports Authority of India has also briefed the Committee about constructing a new
Greenfield Airport at Pakyong in Sikkim for operation of ATR72 type of aircraft. The Project is
funded by the Central Government and is being taken up in phases. The total cost of the project
is Rs.309.46 crores and will be completed in 2013. The tourist inflow will be boosted up in Sikkim
after the new airport is made operational. The Committee was also informed that the runway is
6000 feets and further expansion is not possible due to steep hills. The Committee was also
informed that the Airport is suitable for smaller aircrafts. As such the Committee desires
that the frequency of the aircrafts is to be increased to be able to lift more tourists.
Keeping in view the density of international tourists, the airport should be made to
international standards with all the facilities. The Committee also came to know that two
lane road is to be constructed by State Government to connect Pakyong airport to Ranipool
to Gangtok city to facilitate smooth movement of traffic. The Committee recommends that
the work on the road should be completed before the airport becomes functional so that the
passengers do not face problem of congestion on the road. (Para 76)
Taxi operators have submitted many complaints as regards the tax structures, plying of
unauthorized vehicles, unjustifiable parking fee etc. at Bagdogra airport . The Committee desires
that the Government of West Bengal and Airports Authority of India should look into the
grievances and take remedial measures. (Para 77)

39
CONNECTIVITY BY HELICOPTER
The Committee notes the various initiatives proposed by Ministry of Tourism and the
proposal of Government of Sikkim Government which is trying to promote heli-tourism in
the State. However, the connectivity in Darjeeling is yet to be explored. As such the
Committee recommends that the Ministry of Tourism should make plan with the West
Bengal Government to cover the Darjeeling area also by heli services and provide financial
assistance for the same. The Committee recommends that adequate numbers of helicopters
as per the requirement may be procured or leased from Pawan Hans Ltd. for the purpose.
Besides this the Army may also be taken into confidence for the smooth functioning of
helicopter operations in the region. (Para 84)
Taking into consideration the extent of subsidy in Helicopter journeys being enjoyed
by the tourists, the Committee is of the opinion that tourism activities should be aimed at
bringing revenue to the exchequer and not be made a burden on the tax payers. The
Committee, therefore, recommends that Pawan Hans Ltd. should make a detailed study on
how the heli tourism can be made a profitable business without seeking any-subsidies, on
the lines of the heli-taxi services started by a private operator at nominal rates in Kerala
recently. (Para 85)
ROAD CONNECTIVITY AND CONSTRUCTION OF ROADS
The Committee notes various steps taken to provide an alternative highway for
Gangtok which is very essential so that it is well connected with the country. Since it is
surrounded by international borders, the need is more also from the strategic point of view.
The Committee, therefore, recommends that keeping in view its strategic location the
alternate highway should be given top priority. The Committee hopes that the proposed
highway will be completed as per schedule overcoming all the shortcomings. (Para 96)
To expedite forest clearance regular review meetings are being held at Ministry of Defence,
last meeting was held on 23 rd December, 2011 and State official were advised to expedite the
pending cases. The Committee notes the initiatives taken by the Ministry to get required
clearances. The Committee is, however, constrained to note that out of the 72 projects only
19 have got the clearances and 49 projects are found to be under process at various stages.
Maintenance and development of NH is crucial not only for the economic development of
Sikkim and Darjeeling and surrounding region, but also for the security of the country. The
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Forests Departments of West Bengal and
Sikkim may be impressed upon to take strategic and economic interest of the region while
considering the proposals received for clearances. The Committee hopes that the projects
will be cleared and started soon. (Para 105)
The Committee is aware of the constraints in proper maintenance of the road
conditions in the Darjeeling and Sikkim region. The Committee also recommends that the
BRO should be given modern equipment and adequate funds for the roads maintained by
them. The Committee is surprised to observe that BRO, in addition to its main work of
construction and maintenance of NH has to engage itself in the task of seeking clearances
from the State Governments. The Committee recommends that BRO should concentrate its
efforts in the construction of roads and the rest of the formalities should be completed by
the Ministry in consultation with the concerned State Governments. (Para 106)
The Committee has noted that the road connecting Bagdogra Airport to Darjeeling is
in a dilapidated State, which is a major bottleneck for the growth of tourism in Darjeeling

40
and Sikkim. The Committee, therefore, recommends that since different authorities are
involved in the maintenance work at various stretches, a coordinated action is required to
maintain the highway from Bagdogra to Darjeeling. (Para 107)
The Committee had witnessed the road damages at various places as a result of the
recent earth quake. The Committee finds that at many places, lack of water drains are
causing over flow of water on the roads and sliding of the sides. It, therefore, recommends
that BRO/NHAI need to take up the matter at the time of road design itself. The
Committee has the opinion that all the roads in the Sikkim and in the North East should
be provided with proper culverts so that the rain water and mud should not come to the
roads as a result of rain or for other reasons. (Para 108)
The Committee recommends that at the entry point of Sikkim i.e Rengpo check post,
the concerned authorities and the transport officials should monitor the movement of
trucks to ensure that they do not carry extra load. Otherwise, they should be directed to
move through roads which can sustain extra load. (Para 109)
The Committee notes that the maintenance of roads is an expensive task in the hilly
terrain because of high rainfall and topographical conditions. It, therefore, recommends that
some long-term financial solutions be evolved to create a fund dedicated to the maintenance
of roads for Darjeeling and the North East including Sikkim so that modern technology may
be better utilized for improving the pace and quality of work. (Para 110)
The Committee also recommends for strengthening of the existing bridges so that
the carrying capacity may be increased for higher loads. With these objectives in view,
special emphasis may be given to the improvement of low cost roads and bridges and
construction of new roads in new areas. (Para 111)
Having regard to the importance of roads network in the overall economic
development of the State in general and the need for connectivity for the growth of tourism
in particular, the Committee recommends for granting adequate funds and timely release
of the same, which will go a long way in improving the construction/replacement/repair of
roads at various stages/locations. (Para 112)
The Committee got complaints that NH-55 is closed for traffic since last 20 months and
NHAI is neither taking any steps nor the State PWD who is entrusted with its maintenance is
utilizing the services of NHAI. The Committee recommends that proper coordination with the
two agencies may be ensured so that the road maintenance and construction works should
not be trapped in red tapes. (Para 113)
The Committee also noticed the insufficient and deficient road signage which is a major
cause of accidents. The Committee recommends that proper signage and road markings
should be provided at important points. (Para 114)
ROAD PERMIT
To overcome the bottlenecks of multiple inter–State road transport barriers, the Ministry of
Tourism informed the Committee that they have been advocating implementation of seamless travel
for commercial tourist vehicles. It was felt that that there is a need for a system which would
ensure single window payment of taxes for seamless travel, through which tax can be collected
centrally and apportioned to States. This would facilitate smooth movement of vehicular traffic and

41
avoid delays and inconvenience to tourists. The system was implemented for Delhi–Jaipur–Agra
Sector. The Committee is of the view that there is a need to adopt the same approach for
seamless travel in Darjeeling and Sikkim in consultation with the Ministry of Road
Transport and Highways. The Committee recommends that the taxi fare and road taxes
should be rationalized in consultation with the stake holders concerned by the State
Governments. (Para 116)
The Committee recommends that the problem of road permit in Darjeeling should be
considered by the Ministry of Tourism on priority in consultation with the concerned
Departments to give them a level playing field. The State Government should also take the
benefit from the scheme for construction of modern, state-of-the-art, dedicated parking lots
for which financial assistance is provided by the Ministry of Tourism. (Para 117)
The Committee agrees with the State Government’s view on the importance of
strengthening the public transport facilities. The Committee is of the view that with new
initiatives for enhancing the tourist inflow to the State, immediate attention is required for
proper road connectivity and vehicles. Since the public transport is able to minimize the
road congestions, strengthening of the State transport facilities and passenger amenities
should be taken up on priority basis. (Para 120)
The Committee notes the initiatives taken by the ASI in restoring the monuments
Dubdi Monastery which was damaged by the earthquake in September, 2011 has been
repaired. Since these monuments major tourist attractions, it is equally important that
tourist amenities are also made available in these sites. The Committee recommends that
adequate funds and manpower should be provided to these monuments as most of them do
not have proper maintenance staff. The Committee also recommends that illumination of
monuments should also be considered by ASI on priority in these places. (Para 127)
As per the data provided by ASI, the Committee is constrained to note that the
Horticulture Department is almost absent in Sikkim and out of the 14 sanctioned posts at
various levels including Garden Attendant and Chowkidar, the man in position is NiL. At
present the works are being supervised by Horticulture Assistant Grade I, Cooch Behar. The
Committee would like to know the reasons accounting for utter neglect of the region and
non-filling up of posts. The Committee recommends that immediate steps be taken to fill
up the vacant posts of the Horticulture Branch cater to the need of Sikkim. (Para 129)
VISA-ON-ARRIV AL
The Committee recommends that the Visa on Arrival facility should be provided at
Bagdogra airport to facilitate international tourists. Extension of the ‘Visa on Arrival’
facility at the border adjoining Darjeeling and Sikkim may also be considered. (Para 132)
Inclusion of the Darjeeling Hills in ambit of DoNEAR for allocations of 10% of the Union
Budget
The Committee while going through different areas in and around Darjeeling and
Sikkim, could notice a strong sense of deprivation and discrimination amongst the people
in Darjeeling. The argument being that both the areas are adjacent and have same
topography, etc. The Darjeeling area is also affected by the same problems and has all the
considerations based on which other adjoining areas are getting special help, but same
treatment is not being given to them. There are no special projects either by the Union or
the State Government to boost the economy of areas. Darjeeling has had enjoyed traditional

42
glory and has lot of memories of the past. There is a threat of loosing the heritage status
of the Darjeeling Himalayan railways. Besides this, the permit system for taxi operators in
Darjeeling is different from the rest of the State and the Operators have to make
unnecessary rounds of RTO office to get the permit. In fact the tourists in the earlier days
only talked about Darjeeling and were fascinated by the place. But with no developmental
work taking place in the region, the Darjeeling area has lagged behind other States and has
been left to remain only in our memories. (Para 133)
The said resentment in the areas was also about the exclusion of the Districts of
Darjeeling, Jalpaiguri and Coochbehar from the Northeast Tourism Development schemes.
It was said to be mainly due to regional discrimination meted out to them. The Committee
also feels that the people of Darjeeling are also facing the same vagaries of nature and
difficulties of life as that of the North-Eastern States. The Committee also feels that these
arguments have merit that deserve to be considered seriously as earlier as possible. Why
not include Darjeeling Hills also in the category of NE region so that it gets the benefit of
10% of the funds through the Ministry of DoNEAR. The Committee recommends that for
the integrated development of the NE region, benefits of the 10% tourism budget for the
NE Region should be extended to the three north eastern districts of the West Bengal.
These areas should be considered along with Sikkim for the purpose of development of
tourism facilities, subsidies, reorganization, tax benefits etc. of Ministry of DoNER. The
Committee also recommends that Darjeeling should be included in the “Incredible India”
campaign. The Ministry of Tourism should take the desired steps and lay special emphasis
on the publicity campaign by including Darjeeling in all the campaigns. (Para 134)
LTC facility in lieu  of Hometown granted to Central Government Employees
The Committee also notes that Darjeeling is excluded from the LTC facility in lieu
of Hometown granted to Central Government Employees. The Committee recommends that
the matter should be taken up with the DoPT to grant the same status to Darjeeling.
(Para 135)
Strict norms for construction and abiding the building rules in the Region
The Committee notes that Sikkim and Darjeeling lies in the seismic zone and are
prone to earthquakes. During the deliberations in Darjeeling the Committee was informed
that there is no framework/guidelines for construction in the area. The Committee
recommends that strict norms for construction and abiding the building rules in the Region
should be followed in all the projects involving concrete structures. The Committee is also
of the view that keeping in view the hill areas, there is need for a Technical Institute who
can frame guidelines and help the hill people in constructing in the area keeping in view
the ecological balance. (Para 137)
Connectivity by telecommunications and internet
To facilitate tourists to remain connected with their people, connectivity by
telecommunications and internet is very important. The internet service and mobile signals
are very weak in most of the places in Darjeeling and Sikkim. This may be causing
difficulty in proper communication especially at times where immediate assistance is
required. The Committee recommends that this matter may be taken on a priority basis
with the concerned agencies i.e. Ministry of Communications and IT. (Para 138)

43
Special holiday railway concession during festival seasons
The Committee also recommends for special holiday railway concession during
festival seasons. Permission should be given to use chartered flights for NE package tours.
Special steps should be taken to attract tourists through advertisements by tourist offices,
travel agencies and airlines. (Para 139)
Special Incentives for film industry
To promote tourism in the region, the Cine producers may be invited and facility
provided for shooting in Darjeeling and Sikkim. The movies which are shot in these areas
should be screened in festivals also, to create awareness about the rich beauty of the place.
(Para 140)

1
REPORT
The Indian Civil Aviation sector has witnessed a tough time during the recent years. Hit by
rising fuel costs, uncertain cost regime, rupee depreciation and general slow down in India’s
economy resulting slump in passenger traffic. While the international traffic grew at the rate of
4.3%, the domestic traffic recorded a negative growth of 4.8% during the year 2012. Despite the
fact that the airlines charged higher airfare, most of the airlines incurred losses during this period.
Some of the Government’s initiatives like allowing FDI in civil aviation sector and permission to
import ATF have not yielded the expected results so far. The year also saw the closure of
operations of a private carrier and long labour unrest in the history of national carrier.
2. The Ministry of Civil Aviation is responsible for the formulation of national policies and
programmes for the development and regulation of civil aviation in the country and for devising
and implementing schemes for orderly growth and expansion of civil air transport. Its functions
also extend to overseeing the provision of airport facilities, air traffic services, carriage of
passengers and goods by air, safeguarding civil aviation operations, regulation of air transport
services, licensing of aerodromes, air carriers, pilots and aircraft maintenance engineers. In addition
to framing policies, the Ministry also provides guidance to the organizations in the implementation
of policy guidelines.
3. The Ministry of Civil Aviation has the following organizations under its administrative
control:–
(i) Attached/Subordinate Organizations
– Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA)
– Bureau of Civil Aviation Security (BCAS)
– Commission of Railway Safety (CRS)
– Airports Economic Regulatory Authority (AERA)
(ii) Autonomous Body
Indira Gandhi Rashtriya Uran Akademi (IGRUA)
(iii) Public Sector Undertakings
– Air India and its subsidiaries viz., Hotel Corporation of India Limited, Air India
Charters Limited, Air India Transport Services Limited, Air  India Engineering
Services Limited, Airline Allied Services Limited and Vayudoot Limited
– Airports Authority of India (AAI)
– Pawan Hans Helicopters Limited (PHHL)

and operational performance of Air India. The Company’s net losses for the period April–December

15. When asked about the status of turnaround plan for Air India, it was informed that the

Air India under which there would be equity investment in Air India spread over 10 years.

58. To a specific query on the steps taken to decongest major Indian airports, it was informed
that to avoid peak hour congestion due to bunching of flights, slots are allocated to airlines based
on notified runway, parking stands and terminal capacity in a transparent manner.
59. As regards congestion in the airspace, the following steps have been taken:
Performance Based Navigation (PBN), Standard Instrument Departures (SIDS) and Standard
Terminal Arrival Routes (STARS) have been implemented at metro airports to streamline air
traffic and reduce delays to arriving and departing flights to minimal.
Central Air Traffic Management (CATFM) is planned to be implemented which will result
in balancing the air traffic capacity and demand, thereby eliminating delays to flights in air
and on ground.
Reducing spacing of 3 nm in the terminal airspace at Delhi, Mumbai, Bangalore and
Hyderabad has resulted in elimination of delays to flights in air and on ground.
Improved procedures, reduced separation minima due to enhanced surveillance, reduced
runway occupancy time (ROT) and provision of ground surveillance at busy airports with
Advanced Surface Movement Guidance Control System (ASMGCS) and reduction in Radio
telephony congestion due to introduction of Data Link Clearance etc., have improved
capacity and significantly reduced aircraft holding on ground and in the air thereby easing
out congestion.

FDI in aviation sector
77. The Committee was informed that the private airlines in the country are in dire need of funds
for their operations and service upgradation to compete with other global carriers. Denial of access to
foreign capital could result in the collapse of domestic airlines, creating a systemic risk for the financial
institutions, and a vital gap in the country’s infrastructure. Hence, Government has decided to permit
foreign airlines to invest in the capital of Indian companies operating scheduled and non-scheduled air
transport services, up to the limit of 49 per cent of their paid-up capital. The purpose of removing the
existing restriction on investment by foreign airlines is to bring in strategic investors, as few private
equity investors would be willing to invest in a risky business like civil aviation.
78. Government has permitted FDI by foreign airlines in domestic scheduled and non-scheduled
carrier up to 49% of their paid up capital. The provision for investment by foreign airlines has been
made subject to conditions which include:
(i) It would be made under the Government approval route;
(ii) The 49 per cent limit will subsume FDI and FII investment;
(iii) The investments so made would need to comply with the relevant regulations of
SEBI;
(iv) A Scheduled Operator’s Permit can be granted only to a Company:
(a) that is registered and has its principal place of business within India;
(b) the Chairman and at least two-thirds of the Directors of which are citizens of
India and;
(c) the substantial ownership and effective control of which is vested in Indian
nationals.
79. When it was asked about the number of proposals received so far, it was informed that
one proposal for FDI by foreign airlines has been received under the new FDI guidelines from
M/s Air Asia Investment Ltd., a company incorporated under the laws of Malaysia, to make an
investment upto 49% amounting to US$ 15 million (equivalent to INR 80.98 Crore approx.) in the
total paid up equity share capital of a joint venture company to be incorporated in India together
with Telestra Tradeplace Private Limited and Tata Sons Ltd. to undertake the business of operating
Scheduled Passenger Airlines in the domestic civil aviation sector.
80. The Committee finds that the much fancied decision of allowing FDI in civil aviation
sector has not find many takers so far, except the one. The Committee desires to know
whether any study had been carried out by the Government before taking such an
important policy decision. The Committee feels that the Government should assess the
consequences of the new policy in the context of problems faced by Indian domestic airlines
particularly the AI. The Committee recommends that FDI may be allowed in such a way
that it should not affect the operational viability of India’s national carrier – Air India and
various airports of India. The FDI in civil aviation sector should aim at developing aviation
hubs within the country and any policy on the contrary should be discouraged.

18
Bilaterals
81. The Committee understands that the Government has increased the bilateral weekly seats
between India and Abu Dhabi to 36,670 seats a week from 13,330 at present. The Committee also
notes that the announcement has come in the backdrop of Ethihad paying huge premium of 32%
over the market price to pick up just 24% equity in Jet Airways.
82. The increase in bilateral capacity put the premium that Ethihad paid in perspective.
The Committee is aware that bilateral negotiations between two countries for increasing
airline seats take place only when the existing allotments become insufficient. The
Committee understands that concerned domestic Airlines have not exhausted those allotted
seats. In such a situation, the Committee is surprised to see this increase in the bilateral
to 36,670 seats a week by the Government. Prime facie this move appears to facilitate one
airline to strike a deal with a foreign Airline for its stake sale at a huge premium. The
Committee feels that the huge premium could be a backhanded way of obtaining access to
the huge Civil Aviation market in India.
83. The increase in the bilateral are questionable especially in view of the fact that the Indian
carries are not in a position to use increased seat capacity due to fleet constraint. In such a situation,
the foreign airline may try to catch up passenger traffic headed to destinations in North America,
Europe, Africa and Middle East resulting in huge losses to Air India and various airports of India.
84. The Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport, Tourism and
Culture in its 151
st Report on Merger of Indian Airlines and Air India had categorically
recommended that no more bilateral may be allowed till the home carriers are capable of utilizing
their quota. The Committee feels that this has put our National Carrier and other domestic airlines
at great disadvantage including our airports. The Committee as well as CAG has already commented
about lucrative routes of Air India generously given away to other foreign carriers on bilateral
agreements resulting in huge national losses. It should not be repeated.
85. The air service access and capacity entitlements are typically defined at a country level, that
is, between India on one hand and other countries as a whole on the other. Accordingly, India has
exchanged air access and capacity rights with more than 100 countries. UAE however seems to
have been accorded a special status as India has exchanged access and capacity rights with each
Emirate of the UAE, viz., Dubai, Sharjah, Abu Dhabi and Ras Al Khaimah.
86. The creation of Emirate’s specific capacity entitlements, coupled with unbridled access to all
major cities in India for the airlines of the UAE, has already resulted in Dubai establishing itself as
the primary hub for Indian traffic. Already Emirates Airline is being called the “national airline’ of
India, as it operates more flights and carries more passengers to/from India than Air India, our
national carrier. More than 70% of the passengers carried by Emirates Airlines however travel to
points beyond Dubai, on Emirates’ network. Now, Abu Dhabi is also keen to emulate the success
of Dubai and Emirates Airline, and is keen to establish Abu Dhabi as another hub airport on the back
of Etihad Airways, and for this reason, is aggressively seeking an increase in capacity entitlements.
87. The Committee finds that already, India is struggling to create a world class hub at
Delhi, faced with competition from airports like Dubai and Doha in the Gulf and Bangkok,
Hong Kong and Singapore in South East Asia and despite leading airports like Delhi and
Mumbai having been privatized. While Delhi and other private airports along with the
Government of India have made huge investments in upgrading infrastructure and building
new world class terminals, they are hampered by the competition posed by these well-
established hubs and their aggressive mega carriers. Allowing Abu Dhabi to come up as
another hub  which is only about three hours flight away from the major Indian metros
might have adverse impact on our efforts to establish a world class hub in India.

19
88. The Committee feels that creating hubs needs time and also a home carrier with a
critical size to be able to sustain the hub. Air India has just started to create a hub in Delhi
as its chosen hub, which needs to be encouraged/supported  in its endeavour. The development
of events will, no doubt, have adverse impact on Air India’s efforts in this regard.
89. The Committee finds that Air India is already struggling to make a turn around as
Indian passengers prefer to travel via the foreign hubs. Rs.30,000 crores of taxpayer’s
money is being pumped into it by the Government to keep it afloat and signs of certain
turnaround is already visible.
90. The Committee is of the opinion that in this way, Air India will be denied the ability
to establish direct services to long haul destinations with the B787 Dreamliner that they
have ordered for this very purpose. If the Ministry supports the development of more and
more hubs outside India, thousands of crores of taxpayer’s money will go waste, not to
mention the investment of thousands of crores made by private enterprise along with the
Government in developing world class airports in Delhi and other major metros.
91. The Committee, therefore, calls upon the Ministry to reconsider the Agreement for
bilateral with the UAE, which may be kept frozen at the current level of 13,330 seats and
any bilateral may be opened only after the capacity of the Indian carriers is increased.
Moreover, this Committee has always maintained that Air India being the national carrier
must have the first right of refusal for any bilateral.
92. The Committee notes that no sound Civil Aviation Policy exists in India which is the
need of the hour. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government should
come out with a clear Civil Aviation Policy with an aim to provide growth to the national
carrier and national airports.
93. The Committee recommends that the bilateral arrangement with the Abu Dhabi may
be reconsidered by the Government to protect our national carrier and the airports of India.
Sale of bilateral by Jet Airways
94. The Committee was informed that Jet Airways sold three of its slots in London to
the Ethihad Airlines and the Secretary, Ministry of Civil Aviation has confirmed that the
Ministry is aware of the development. The Committee feels that carriers have no right to
sell the bilateral allotted to them to other airlines that too foreign airline. The Committee
recommends that the Government should take away the slots from Jet Airways and the
airlines should be penalized for selling the national property – bilateral.
Setting up of Aranmula Airport in Kerala
95. The Committee was informed that Gov ernment of India has granted ‘in-principle approval in
September 2012 for setting up of the Greenfield airport at Aranmula in Kerala. Aranmula International
Airport is to be built by M/s KGS Infra Ltd. in two phases on about 900 acres in three years. The
airport will be able to handle Airbus A-320/Boeing 747 like aircraft. Approx. 905 acres of land is
required, out of which, 600 acres has already been acquired. The total project cost is approx. Rs.2,000
crores. The project cost for the first phase has been estimated at Rs.550 crores while another Rs.1450
crores will be invested in the second phase. The runway length will be 3100x45 metres with PCN 45
F/B/W/T. The terminal building is designed to handle 1000 passengers at a time. The airport will be
privately owned and managed. The necessary approvals from various nodal agencies such as site
clearance by AAI, NOC from Government of Kerala, NOC from Ministry of Defence, environment
clearance from Ministry of Environment and Forests and site clearance for international operations from
MoCA, have been obtained. Further the project site has been declared as “Industrial Area”.

20
96. As regards traffic projection, capacity, environmental impact etc., these details are to be
given by the promoters.
97. When asked about the existing guidelines for setting up a second new airport within
an airport limit and whether the guidelines differ from airport to airport, it was informed that
Chapter 8 (Greenfield airports) specified in the Policy on Airport infrastructure indicates that no
Greenfield airport will normally be allowed within an aerial distance of 150 kilometres of an existing
airport. A Greenfield airport may be permitted where an existing one is unable to meet the projected
requirements of traffic or a new focal point of traffic emerges with sufficient viability. It can be
allowed both as a replacement for an existing airport or for simultaneous operation. This aspect
will have to be clearly spelt out in the notice inviting tenders.
98. However, in case a proposal is received by Government for consideration of a new
Greenfield airport within 150 kilometres of an existing Civil airport or Civil Enclave, the proposal
is to be cleared by the Steering Committee under the Ministry for inprinciple approval.
99. The Committee finds that the proposed Greenfield airport in Aranmula (Kerala) is
120 km. from Trivandrum and 90 km. from Cochin, both are international airports and it is
violative of the Government policy of not allowing an airport within 150 km. Moreover, the
Kochin International Airport and Thiruvananthapuram Airport are brand new airports and there
is no scope for saturation of capacity in these airports in near future. The Committee notes that
the proposed Aranmula Airport is violating the principles of 150 kms. distance rule and the
saturation of the nearby existing airports. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the
proposal for construction of Aranmula Airport may be reconsidered by the Government.
100. The Committee in its 131
st Report on the Closure of Bangalore and Hyderabad Airports
expressed its apprehensions over the closure of existing Government owned airports to facilitate
the private Greenfield airports there. The Government took shelter behind the Concession
Agreement signed with the two private airport operators to justify the closure of Government
owned airports in Bangalore and Hyderabad. In this backdrop, the Committee fails to
understand the logic behind granting ‘in principle’ approval by the Central Government for
Aranmula Greenfield Airport project. The Committee feels that the Government should come
out with a clear policy decision on new airports within 150 km. radius of existing one.
General Observations
101. The Committee finds that except equity boost for Air India, the Union Budget 2013
has nothing special to offer for the Indian aviation sector. The industry’s most vociferous
demand of reduction of sales tax on ATF which varies from 4-25 from State to State and
‘declared goods’ status for ATF could not be addressed by the Government in this year’s
budget also. ATF price in the country remains among the highest and this is the main cause
for higher cost operations of air service providers.
102. The Committee feels that the much hyped creation of Civil Aviation Authority to
take care of all the regulatory and investigative needs of the aviation sector with more
powers is still pending with the Ministry. The Ministry had been informing the Committee
for couple of years now that they are contemplating the Civil Aviation Authority to bifurcate
and delineate the functions of policy maker, regulator and investigator in civil aviation
sector. The Committee hopes that the draft Bill for the purpose would be taken on priority
to give the authority required shape.
103. The Committee hopes that allocation of additional funds for Air India and Airports
Authority of India at RE level will help these organizations to carry on their programmes/
projects for the betterment of aviation industry in the country.

OBSERV ATIONS/CONCLUSIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS — AT A GLANCE
ANNUAL PLAN 2012-13
The Committee finds that the spending pattern of Plan funds has been poor during
2012-13 which needs a lot of improvement. The Committee hopes that the Ministry of Civil
Aviation will impress the concerned organizations/undertakings to spend the allocated fund
with proper planning and coordination with respective stakeholders. The Committee notes
that except the investment in Air India, all other organizations were allocated substantially
reduced allocations at RE stage which also could not be optimally utilized. The Committee
feels that reduction of funds at RE stage does not augur well for the much beleaguered
aviation sector. Most of these under-utilizations have been mainly due to finalization of
schemes. The Committee expresses dismay over non-finalization of building plan for BCAS
and DGCA that are pending for so many years. Slow progress in case of NER projects is
a cause of concern to the Committee. The Committee recommends the Ministry to take
necessary steps urgently to finalize/approve these Plan schemes at the earliest to spend the
allocated funds during the current year. (Para 7)
ANNUAL PLAN 2013-14
The Committee notes that the Ministry of Civil Aviation was able to get only 56%
of the projected plan allocations for the current fiscal. The Committee feels that such
inadequate allocation will definitely hamper progress of ongoing infrastructure projects and
other aviation related programmes. The Committee hopes that the Ministry will expedite
the approval of various Schemes and persuade Planning Commission for allocation of more
funds at RE stage. The Committee also hopes that the allocated funds will be utilized
judiciously to avoid any reduced allocation at RE stage. (Para 10)
Air India Limited
Ground Handling SBU:
The Committee notes that despite many labour unrests witnessed during the last
year, the national carrier was able to improve its performance notably both financially and
operationally. It recorded positive EBITDA of Rs.19 crores during the year 2012-13 as
against a negative EBITDA of Rs.2237 crores during the year 2011-12. Air India’s on-time
performance was 84.8% in the case of domestic sector and 74% for international sector as
against the turnaround plan benchmark of 85%. The passenger load factor of Air India was
72% as against the target under turnaround plan of 69.5%. The turnaround plan
benchmark on yield per kilometer was 3.53, against which Air India achieved 3.76.
(Para 36)
The Committee finds that Air India was able to get Rs.5000 crores as against the
requirement of Rs.8574. The Committee finds that as part of the FRP and as approved by
the Cabinet, the Government of India had given a commitment to infuse the Equity as per
the FRP. Any delay or shortfall in the infusion of the equity would adversely affect the
implementation of Turn Around Plan and FRP, since Air India would be compelled to borrow
short term loans from Banks in order to bridge the equity gap which would entail payment

22
of interest, which may adversely affect the profitability of the company. In fact, one of the
conditions under which, the regulator (RBI) and the consortium of Banks supported the
FRP, entails timely equity support to Air India by Government of India. (Para 37)
The Committee feels that since Air India has started achieving the milestones as
prescribed in the TAP during the last year, further allocation of Rs.3574 crores as equity
infusion will help the national carrier to implement the turnaround plan smoothly and carry
forward the improved performance in the coming years also. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that the Government should provide the promised equity infusion which has
been accumulated without any interruption during the course of the financial year.
(Para 38)
The Committee feels that Air India with its wide range of aircraft in its kitty should
expand its operations beyond metro cities. Since majority of the non-metro airports have
been modernized/developed by Airports Authority of India, the national carrier should make
efforts to penetrate those unexplored markets. When the private carriers are in a position
to offer air services to Tier-II and Tier-III cities, Air India should explore offering its
services to such cities using smaller aircrafts. The Committee still feels that Air India’s
entry into LCC segment will definitely strengthen its business. The Committee recommends
that the Air India should try to provide better service and products to the passengers which
have lot of scope for improvement. (Para 39)
The Committee also hopes that Air India’s entry into ground handling operations will
add much needed financial fillip for the company. The Committee notes that process of
operationalising the MRO SBU is going on in a snail’s pace and the Government and the
Air India do not appear to be taking adequate initiatives to speed up the process. The
Committee is confident that the MRO SBU and the Ground handling activity of AIATSL, if
planned and executed properly, can bring lot of revenue to Air India. The Committee
recommends that the Government should, if need be, make necessary policy changes to
enable these two agencies to function on proper business and commercial prudence. The
Committee notes significant headway in implementing the human resources merger
programmes. The Committee recommends that all the outstanding issues must be settled as
early as possible to enable Air India to function as a single entity. (Para 40)
The Committee further recommends that before taking any policy decision in respect
of AI, proper study and analysis of its impact on the functioning and viability of Air India
should be carried out. Air India is our national carrier in which thousands of crores of
rupees of taxpayers’ money has been invested. The Committee, therefore, calls upon the
Ministry and AI to keep this fact always in mind while taking any decision. (Para 41)
The Committee feels that with a committed annual Government equity, Air India can
improve its performance more than the parameters mentioned in TAP in the coming years
and reaffirm its status of ‘Maharaja’. (Para 42)
Hotel Corporation of India
The Committee finds that Hotel Corporation of India was allocated Rs.25.00 crores
(BE) for 2012-13 which was reduced to Rs.I0.00 crores at RE level. HCI was able to spend
the entire revised allocation for its various schemes. Now, it has been allocated with a paltry
sum of Rs.5.00 crores for 2013-14 for all the four units. The Committee feels that such a
nominal investment for these units under HCI does not inspire any confidence. If the idea
is to do away with these properties, Committee does not know. The Committee hopes that
allocation of funds will be mainly utilized to renovate/upgrade Centaur Hotel Srinagar and

23
Chefair Flight Catering Delhi and more funds would be demanded at RE stage and complete
the same within the fixed time-frame. (Para 47)
Airports Authority of India
The Committee finds that the AAI was allocated a budgetary support of Rs.280 crores
(BE) for the year 2012-13 while it has been reduced to Rs.42.00 crores in BE 2013-14. Out
of this, Rs. 32.00 crore is exclusively for development works at airports in Pakyong and
Tirupati. The Committee was informed that AAI’s requirement for various projects under
Grant-in-Aid Schemes is to the tune of Rs.460.21 crores. The Committee feels that such a
drastic cut in budgetary support for the airport infrastructure developer of the country will
definitely slow down the ongoing projects especially in North-Eastern Region. The
Committee hopes that necessary funds will be allocated to AAI at the RE stage so that its
ongoing as well as future projects are not delayed for want of funds. The Committee also
recommends that pending balance of Rs.77 crores be released for the GAGAN project at the
earliest opportunity. (Para 61)
The Committee also finds that out of the required 3500 ATCs to control the Indian
skies only 2300 personnel are available. The Committee hopes that AAI  will take necessary
steps to address the issue by augmenting its training facilities at Allahabad. (Para 62)
The Committee was informed on the deadlock persisting over the development of
Patna airport. The Committee reiterates its observation/recommendation contained in its
174
th Report in respect of Patna Airport last year and hopes that the AAI will pursue the
matter with the State Government of Bihar for ensuring some viable alternate plan taking
into consideration impending danger for the air travelers to Patna. The Committee would
like to have a status note including efforts made, alternate proposals and the results
thereof. (Para 63)
Pawan Hans Helicopters Limited
The Committee finds that as against the projected demands of Rs.5.00 crores under
plan, the Pawan Hans Helicopters Limited was not able to get any budgetary support from
the Government. The Committee feels that necessary budgetary support, if given to PHHL
at RE stage, it can take up its capacity building and skill development/expansion projects
without delay. The Committee feels that PHHL should expand its business beyond off-shore
operations and present itself as a viable air service provider in unexplored tourist
destinations. The Committee also hopes that heliport project at Rohini, Delhi is completed
as per its schedule. (Para 69)
Directorate General of Civil Aviation
The Committee finds that DGCA was allocated Rs.60.00 crores (BE) under plan head
for the year 2012-13 which was reduced to Rs.13.00 crores at RE level. However, an amount
of Rs.4.27 crore only was spent out of the allocated amount. The main reason attributed to
the non-utilization fund was the non-finalization of headquarters building for DGCA. The
Committee hopes that all the land related issues for the building project will be sorted out
with the concerned agencies and the project is taken-up further. The Committee further
hopes that the spending pattern of DGCA will improve during the current fiscal. The
Committee recommends that the process of filling-up of vacancies in DGCA should be
expedited so that the day-to-day functioning of the principal regulatory body of the country
is not affected. (Para 73)

1
REPORT
Indian culture, one of the most ancient cultures of the world, is a treasure trove of
innumerable tangible and intangible cultural heritage. The role of the Ministry of Culture,
Government of India is extremely important as they shoulder the responsibility to preserve and
protect the country’s ancient, vibrant, continuous and vast cultural resources. Promoting country’s
culture while preserving its unique diversity becomes all the more a daunting task. The vast
functional spectrum of the Ministry also includes generating cultural awareness at the grassroots
level to promoting cultural exchanges at international level. In order to fulfill its mandate the
Ministry of Culture undertakes the following activities:
➢ Managing ancient sites, monuments, museums, libraries, archives, cultural
organizations;
➢ Literary, visual, performing arts, institutional and individual initiatives;
➢ Commemoration and celebration of important events and personalities.
2. The above mentioned activities spanning from conservation, preservation and promotion of
Indian heritage both tangible and intangible, are carried out through the two attached offices, i.e.,
Archaeological Survey of India and National Archives of India; six subordinate offices and thirty-
four autonomous institutions working under the Ministry.
3. The budget allocations of the Ministry of Culture for the financial year 2013-14, contained
in the Demand No. 19 was taken up for consideration by the Department-related Parliamentary
Standing Committee on Transport, Tourism and Culture in its meeting held on the 2
nd April, 2013.
The Secretary and other officials of the Ministry of Culture made a presentation on various aspects
of the budget and functioning of the Ministry. Several important aspects as detailed in the
Secretary’s deposition, replies to the questionnaire sent by the Ministry, Out-come Budget and
several other Budget (2013-14) documents have been examined by the Department-related
Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport, Tourism and Culture and recommendations made
thereon are given in the succeeding paragraphs.
4. The Ministry during the financial year 2013-14 has been allocated Rs. 2062.00 crore, out
of which Rs. 1435.00 crore is planned budgetary allocation and Rs. 627.00 crore is non-plan
budgetary support. Further, the plan component of Rs. 1435.00 crore also includes Rs. 39.00 crore
for capital works.

was 92.78% of its total funds provided at RE stage. The Committee in fact, found that the

9. The Committee was informed that the Ministry has to adopt during the Twelfth Five Year
Plan, a “new approach and appropriate policies which are less dependent on Government financing
and catalyze local partnerships”. The Programmes of the Ministry must be integrated into strategies
for sustainable development at every level and take into account the needs and aspirations of the
community where cultural assets are found. Sustainable heritage conservation depends upon the
commitment and involvement of local communities. Conservation policies, to be successful, need
to promote local community stewardship of the heritage as well as to provide socio-economic
benefits for local communities. Therefore, a direct link must be established between safeguarding
the heritage and socio-economic development. This calls for the “deliberate recasting of heritage
conservation as a development activity that brings economic opportunities, creates jobs and
generates income based on traditional technologies and know-how”. This new programme is aimed
at complementing and extending those efforts by moving heritage conservation beyond the exclusive

3
sphere of high technology and elite specialization and to become the concern and responsibility of
every citizen and transform heritage conservation into grassroots movement, which will return the
heritage to the communities that created it and who rely on it as the foundation for their future
development.
10. Due to the increased awareness about the need to protect monuments, the ASI is under
great strain so as to not only protect their own monuments but also to take over new monuments.
The issue of huge developmental scope in Archaeology is the main priority area for the Ministry
of Culture. Since the State Governments are not in a position to take up maintenance of their
monuments for want of funds, central intervention is imperative for maintenance of large number
of such monuments. As such, archaeological sites protected by the State Governments/UTs are
scattered all over the country.
11. During the Twelfth Plan period, the Ministry has laid stress on strengthening and upgrading
State Museums and modernizing and upgrading central museums as well for bringing them at par
with the international standards. The Ministry plans to undertake digitization, networking, access,
etc. of our Libraries, Archives and Museums. Conservation of monuments, manuscripts, and other
art objects too can scale new heights by the application of modern technology.
12. During the Twelfth Five Year Plan, 21 new schemes are proposed to be introduced under
various sectors of Art and Culture by the Ministry in addition to 24 ongoing schemes being
implemented from Eleventh Five Year Plan (2007-12). On the direction of the Planning Commission
regarding reduction in number of schemes or heads by clubbing the existing schemes, a number
of new as well as old schemes proposed for Twelfth Plan have been merged with the ongoing
schemes/organizations under the Ministry of Culture during the year 2013-14. In the year 2013-14,
a total of 26 Plan schemes including ongoing/new schemes will be implemented by the Ministry
as against 45 schemes proposed for implementation during 2012-13.

16. The Committee was informed that 150 th Anniversary of Swami Vivekananda, centenary of
famous painter Amrita Sher Gil will be celebrated in 2013 and the committed liabilities from
previous commemorations will also be taken care of under the head centenary celebrations.
17. As regards the strategies for the Twelfth Five Year Plan, the Committee is of the
firm view that these are more of vision than strategies, as these are vague and do not
provide a clear road map for the organizations working under the aegis of the Ministry. The
Committee has strong reservation about the Government’s commitment to privatise
heritage conservation activities. Moreover, the Committee also fails to understand the
meaning of the “new approach and appropriate policies which are less dependent on
Government financing.” The Committee feels that these could be high on ideal but low on
implementation on ground and therefore, less practicable. The Twelfth Plan strategies
reflect a paradigm shift in the heritage conservation activities, but the Committee did not
find specific initiatives/intervention in keeping with the said “new approach and appropriate
policies”. Instead, these are vague and high sounding ideals only which do not inspire
required confidence. It turns out to be an attempt to obfuscate the real issues and practical
problems faced by the Ministry and different stakeholders. The Committee finds a critical
disconnect in the approach of the Ministry towards heritage conservation vis-à-vis the people
and community. The view that conservation of our ancient cultural heritage would become
the concern and responsibility of every citizen appears to be too idealistic. The Committee
understands that excavation, recording of excavation findings, chemical and physical
conservation of our monuments require a certain level of knowledge, expertise and deft
handling. The Committee agrees in principle with the need for involving community in this
exercise but it appears to be better said than done. The Committee is surprised to note that
the linkage between culture and economic growth has not been properly reflected in the
strategy outlined by the Planning Commission and feels that because of this, the Ministry
may not be able to harness the Cultural resources for economic development of the
Country.
18. The Committee notes with satisfaction that there has been about two fold increase
in the allocation to the Ministry right from the Eighth Plan onwards, the Committee also
appreciates the fact that Ministry was able to spend about 90% of all its allocation
throughout the Eleventh Five year Plan and the first year of the Twelfth Plan.
19. The Committee also appreciates the constraints under which the Ministry has to
function and notes that the actual Plan allocation for the Twelfth Plan is about 38.97% of
the projected outlay. The Committee observes that although there has been a constant
increase in allocations to the Ministry of Culture right from the Eighth Plan onwards and
every year thereafter, it is of the firm view that even these increased allocations are highly
inadequate in comparison to the ambitious task the Ministry has to undertake during the
Twelfth Plan. Resultantly, protection and promotion of our culture and heritage which are
highly significant to the identity and existence of India, will suffer. The Committee
sincerely feels that apart from protecting our existing heritage, adequate cultural
infrastructure also needs to be created for promoting and projecting our heritage and
culture, for that we need appropriate plan/programme and adequate funds. In the absence
of adequate allocation, the country would not be able to protect and reap the benefits of
such vast cultural resources.
20. The Committee feels that inadequate budgetary provision will certainly hamper the
progress of works underway as well as new programmes to be undertaken by the Ministry.
Creation of infrastructural facilities, modernization of Museums, Archives and Libraries are
long overdue. Heritage conservation/protection is becoming capital intensive. Akademis also

7
need adequate funds to carry forward their work. The Committee sincerely feels that much
more things are required to be done in the core area other than making arrangements for
peripheral activities to keep things going.
21. Therefore, the Committee strongly recommends that the overall allocation for the
Twelfth Plan period should be increased and the Ministry of Culture may take it up with
the Planning Commission and Ministry of Finance. Since, the Ministry has been consistently
utilizing its allocations above 90%, the Committee feels it is a good case for incentivizing
the Ministry by increasing their allocation.
22. The Committee would like to point out the under-utilization of funds under the heads
– Archaeology, Archives and Archival Libraries, Museums, Public Libraries and International
Cultural relations. The Committee finds a dichotomy  between the Ministry’s claim of
spending more than 90% during the last many years and reporting under utilization in the
areas which constitute a large share in the Ministry’s allocation. The Committee would like
to have a clarification about this.
23. The Committee feels that almost all proposed schemes of the Ministry may be
adversely affected due to inadequate funds. A total of 26 planned schemes, including
ongoing/new schemes, will be implemented from 2013-14 by the Ministry. The Archaeological
Survey of India will now implement one centrally Sponsored Scheme (CSS) from the year
2013-14 as two proposed CSSs have also been merged. Accordingly, the Committee
recommends that proper monitoring of the Schemes/Plans should be done on regular basis
and proposals of the Plans/Schemes should be made after thorough planning to ensure that
the allocated funds are expended uniformly throughout the plan period.
24. The Committee expects that special allocation of Rs. 485 crore made for five areas
as shown in Table 5 would be judiciously and adequately utilized.
ARCHAEOLOGICAL SURVEY OF INDIA (ASI)
(a) General Functioning
25. Archeological Survey of India, an Attached Office of the Ministry of Culture, was
established with the primary object of surveying antiquarian remains in this country and their study.
The prime task of the ASI is conservation, preservation and maintenance of the centrally protected
monuments. Presently ASI which has jurisdiction over the whole country has 24 circles,
6 Excavation Branches, 2 Temple Survey Projects, 1 Building Survey Project, 1 Science Branch
(with many sub-offices located in different parts of the country), 1 Epigraphy Branch (two offices
located at Mysore and Nagpur) and 1 Horticulture Branch, with its divisional offices located at
strategic points in the country.
26. Plan allocation was increased in BE 2012-13, basically to strengthen the conservation and
development of site museums activities and also to implement new schemes proposed during 12th
Five Year Plan including one Centrally Sponsored Scheme. The provision has now again been
increased in 2013-14 for undertaking various activities/programmes of ASI, including conservation
of ancient monuments, archaeological exploration and excavation, development and maintenance of
Central Archaeological Museums, National Mission on Monuments and Antiquities, Setting up of
Competent Authorities for operation of Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Monuments Sites
and Remains (Amendment and Validation Act, 2010), Implementation of Centrally Sponsored
Scheme and new schemes proposed in the Twelfth Plan period, etc.
27. The Committee specifically wanted to know from the Ministry about the policy of the
Government on restoration and conservation of monuments. The Ministry informed that

8
Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) protected 3678 protects monuments of national importance.
The conservation and preservation work of these monuments is attended to as per the
archaeological norms and principles laid out in John Marshall’s Conservation Manual of 1923 and
International Charters recognized by the UNESCO. The Ministry informed that keeping in view the
new developments including that in technology, a new draft National Policy on Conservation has
been prepared which is being finalized for adoption.
28. The Committee notes that though the budgetary support to ASI has been consistently
increasing since the last three years, the present Budgetary allocation of Rs. 250.00 crore
is insufficient in view of the increasing cost of conservation and preservation and huge
responsibilities to be discharged by the ASI in terms of safety, security, protection and
upkeep of the monuments.
29. The Committee also feels that number of protected monuments under the ASI at
present is far too less and lakhs of our ancient monuments are languishing. As a result,
large numbers of them have either vanished or encroached or illegally occupied. The
Committee emphasizes the urgent need to bring most of them under protected category.
Therefore, the Committee strongly recommends that number of protected monuments
should be increased on priority and in a phased manner for which we should have a
roadmap and realistic allocation of funds required.
30. For taking our monuments scattered all over the country under archaeological
protection, we will have to take State on board, who it appears are not able to pay required
attention to this aspect. The Committee is of the view that our National Policy must provide
