(d) Encroachment of Monuments
38. As per the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remain (Amendment and
Validation) Act, 2010 no new construction is allowed within prohibited area (100 mtrs. Zone) of
monument/site and new construction is permitted in regulated areas (200 mtrs. Zone further beyond
regulated area) only with the approval of Competent Authority on recommendation of the National
Monuments Authority. Any new construction raised in prohibited area is illegal construction and any
new construction in regulated area, raised without permission from Competent Authority is
unauthorized. Any construction or installation within the protected area or protected limit of a
monument of national importance is encroachment.
39. On report of unauthorized construction within prohibited or regulated areas of protected
monuments, complaints with the Police are filed and notices are issued to defaulters for removal
of the said illegal or unauthorized construction. If no action is taken, demolition order is issued
under Rule 38(2) of the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remain Rules, 1959 with
a request to the Collector to cause to remove the said illegal/unauthorized construction. Recourse
is taken to courts of law as a last resort.
40. Following the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remain (Amendments and
Validation) Act in 2010, about 780 notices/demolition orders have been issued under Rule 38(1) and
38(2) of the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remain Rules, 1959. No demolition
has been carried out so far. However, Archaeological Survey of India has been persistent in its
efforts to tackle encroachment and has succeeded in removing encroachment from 24 monuments.
41. The Committee is surprised to note that not a single encroachment could be
demolished on the archaeological sites out of 780 demolition notices/orders issued in this

10
regard. The Committee is also aware of the apathy of the civic authorities, local Police and
other agencies in the matter. ASI has no power to ensure compliance for such orders from
them. Even court orders were also ignored at times. The Committee is aware that
encroachment, unauthorized occupation and illegal construction near our monuments is a
problem about which we have not been able to do much so far. The Committee feels that
possibility of a nexus between the vested interests, private parties and civic and police
authorities cannot be ruled out in this context. Defacing of our national monuments is
another serious problem. Therefore, strong action should be taken against not only the
encroachers/offenders but also the agencies/officials of the concerned departments if these
do not obey/cooperate. The Committee may be informed about the efforts made and
responses of the concerned authorities in this regard.
42. The Committee understands that creation of mechanisms under the provisions of
Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remain (Amendment and Validation) Act,
2010 has been very slow so far. These are essential for the implementation of the Act. The
Committee was not informed about the reasons for this and the efforts made in this regard.
The Committee would like the Ministry to be proactive for putting the required mechanism
in place at the earliest in order to save our ancient sites/ monuments and the Ministry may
also apprise the Committee about it through an explanatory note.

th Report of the Committee on “The

89. The Committee has been emphasizing/raising some important issues relating to

in a time bound manner and the Committee would like to be informed of the

and also the head of the organization, these premier institutes are functioning.

the purview of UPSC that takes a lot of time. The Committee reiterates its

OBSERV ATIONS/CONCLUSIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS — AT A GLANCE
As regards the strategies for the Twelfth Five Year Plan, the Committee is of the
firm view that these are more of vision than strategies, as these are vague and do not
provide a clear road map for the organizations working under the aegis of the Ministry. The
Committee has strong reservation about the Government’s commitment to privatise
heritage conservation activities. Moreover, the Committee also fails to understand the
meaning of the “new approach and appropriate policies which are less dependent on
Government financing.” The Committee feels that these could be high on ideal but low on
implementation on ground and therefore, less practicable. The Twelfth Plan strategies
reflect a paradigm shift in the heritage conservation activities, but the Committee did not
find specific initiatives/intervention in keeping with the said “new approach and appropriate
policies”. Instead, these are vague and high sounding ideals only which do not inspire
required confidence. It turns out to be an attempt to obfuscate the real issues and practical
problems faced by the Ministry and different stakeholders. The Committee finds a critical
disconnect in the approach of the Ministry towards heritage conservation vis-à-vis the people
and community. The view that conservation of our ancient cultural heritage would become
the concern and responsibility of every citizen appears to be too idealistic. The Committee
understands that excavation, recording of excavation findings, chemical and physical
conservation of our monuments require a certain level of knowledge, expertise and deft
handling. The Committee agrees in principle with the need for involving community in this
exercise but it appears to be better said than done. The Committee is surprised to note that
the linkage between culture and economic growth has not been properly reflected in the
strategy outlined by the Planning Commission and feels that because of this, the Ministry
may not be able to harness the Cultural resources for economic development of the
Country. (Para 17)
The Committee notes with satisfaction that there has been about two fold increase
in the allocation to the Ministry right from the Eighth Plan onwards, the Committee also
appreciates the fact that Ministry was able to spend about 90% of all its allocation
throughout the Eleventh Five year Plan and the first year of the Twelfth Plan. (Para 18)
The Committee also appreciates the constraints under which the Ministry has to
function and notes that the actual Plan allocation for the Twelfth Plan is about 38.97% of
the projected outlay. The Committee observes that although there has been a constant
increase in allocations to the Ministry of Culture right from the Eighth Plan onwards and
every year thereafter, it is of the firm view that even these increased allocations are highly
inadequate in comparison to the ambitious task the Ministry has to undertake during the
Twelfth Plan. Resultantly, protection and promotion of our culture and heritage which are
highly significant to the identity and existence of India, will suffer. The Committee
sincerely feels that apart from protecting our existing heritage, adequate cultural
infrastructure also needs to be created for promoting and projecting our heritage and
culture, for that we need appropriate plan/programme and adequate funds. In the absence
of adequate allocation, the country would not be able to protect and reap the benefits of
such vast cultural resources. (Para 19)
The Committee feels that inadequate budgetary provision will certainly hamper the
progress of works underway as well as new programmes to be undertaken by the Ministry.

22
Creation of infrastructural facilities, modernization of Museums, Archives and Libraries are
long overdue. Heritage conservation/protection is becoming capital intensive. Akademis also
need adequate funds to carry forward their work. The Committee sincerely feels that much
more things are required to be done in the core area other than making arrangements for
peripheral activities to keep things going. (Para 20)
Therefore, the Committee strongly recommends that the overall allocation for the
Twelfth Plan period should be increased and the Ministry of Culture may take it up with
the Planning Commission and Ministry of Finance. Since, the Ministry has been consistently
utilizing its allocations above 90%, the Committee feels it is a good case for incentivizing
the Ministry by increasing their allocation. (Para 21)
The Committee would like to point out the under-utilization of funds under the heads
– Archaeology, Archives and Archival Libraries, Museums, Public Libraries and International
Cultural relations. The Committee finds a dichotomy between the Ministry’s claim of
spending more than 90% during the last many years and reporting under utilization in the
areas which constitute a large share in the Ministry’s allocation. The Committee would like
to have a clarification about this. (Para 22)
The Committee feels that almost all proposed schemes of the Ministry may be
adversely affected due to inadequate funds. A total of 26 planned schemes, including
ongoing/new schemes, will be implemented from 2013-14 by the Ministry. The Archaeological
Survey of India will now implement one Centrally Sponsored Scheme (CSS) from the year
2013-14 as two proposed CSSs have also been merged. Accordingly, the Committee
recommends that proper monitoring of the Schemes/Plans should be done on regular basis
and proposals of the Plans/Schemes should be made after thorough planning to ensure that
the allocated funds are expended uniformly throughout the plan period. (Para 23)
The Committee expects that special allocation of Rs.485 crore made for five areas as
shown in Table 5 would be judiciously and adequately utilized. (Para 24)
ARCHAEOLOGICAL SURVEY OF INDIA (ASI)
The Committee notes that though the budgetary support to ASI has been consistently
increasing since the last three years, the present Budgetary allocation of Rs. 250.00 crore
is insufficient in view of the increasing cost of conservation and preservation and huge
responsibilities to be discharged by the ASI in terms of safety, security, protection and
upkeep of the monuments. (Para 28)
The Committee also feels that number of protected monuments under the ASI at
present is far too less and lakhs of our ancient monuments are languishing. As a result,
large numbers of them have either vanished or encroached or illegally occupied. The
Committee emphasizes the urgent need to bring most of them under protected category.
Therefore, the Committee strongly recommends that number of protected monuments
should be increased on priority and in a phased manner for which we should have a
roadmap and realistic allocation of funds required. (Para 29)
For taking our monuments scattered all over the country under archaeological
protection, we will have to take State on board, who it appears are not able to pay required
attention to this aspect. The Committee is of the view that our National Policy must provide
adequate emphasis on this aspect to make conservation and protection as a joint effort with
adequate financial and other support for the culture. (Para 30)

23
With changing times and technology as well as increasing threat perceptions to our
monuments, works concerning ASI are acquiring newer dimensions and they have to keep
up with them. Therefore, our strengths and weaknesses need a detail examination and the
Committee hopes that the Ministry will keep such aspects in mind while adopting National
Conservation Policy. (Para 31)
The Committee also notes that ASI cannot undertake renovation work during
monsoon months which restricts time as well as its fund utilisation capacity. Due to this,
the RE allocation is reduced as it is made on the basis of the BE utilisation and as a result,
their fund lapses. The Committee realises that this is the major reason for their inability
to complete capital work. The Committee strongly recommends that the ASI may be
exempted from the BE utilisation restriction while deciding RE. The Ministry of Finance is
requested to give a favorable consideration to this so that ASI activities do not suffer and
their funds do not lapse. The Committee reiterates its recommendation made in its (Para
30 and 31) 175
th Report for creation of a non-lapsable fund for ASI activities. (Para 32)
The Committee is aware that National Culture Fund has not received the required
response, neither from the corporate sector nor from the private sector. It could be made
attractive for Corporates/PSUs, if culture and heritage are included in the list of activities
under CSR. These may be an added attraction for them to put their plaque, etc. to be
noticed by the visiting public thereby, enhancing their image-building. The Committee
appreciates that the Ministry of Culture has taken up the issue with the Ministry of
Corporate Affairs as well as with Prime Minister himself. The Committee strongly
recommends incorporating “heritage and culture” in the Indian Companies Bill as a CSR
activity. The Committee may be apprised about the progress made in this matter.
(Para 35)
The Committee finds a strong case for allocating the fund raised on the entry tickets
to ASI to be used for the conservation, protection, preservation, etc. of our monuments. The
Committee strongly recommends that the Ministry of Finance should appreciate the value
of our heritage and allow the amounts collected out of entry fee at monuments to be
allocated to ASI for its activities and it should be made a non-lapsable fund. The matter
may be pursued at apex level and the response of Ministry of Finance should be informed
to the Committee. (Para 37)
The Committee is surprised to note that not a single encroachment could be
demolished on the archaeological sites out of 780 demolition notices/ orders issued in this
regard. The Committee is also aware of the apathy of the civic authorities, local Police and
other agencies in the matter. ASI has no power to ensure compliance for such orders from
them. Even court orders were also ignored at times. The Committee is aware that
encroachment, unauthorized occupation and illegal construction near our monuments is a
problem about which we have not been able to do much so far. The Committee feels that
possibility of a nexus between the vested interests, private parties and civic and police
authorities cannot be ruled out in this context. Defacing of our national monuments is
another serious problem. Therefore, strong action should be taken against not only the
encroachers/offenders but also the agencies/officials of the concerned departments if these
do not obey/cooperate. The Committee may be informed about the efforts made and
responses of the concerned authorities in this regard. (Para 41)
The Committee understands that creation of mechanisms under the provisions of
Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remain (Amendment and Validation) Act,
2010 has been very slow so far. These are essential for the implementation of the Act. The
Committee was not informed about the reasons for this and the efforts made in this regard.

24
The Committee would like the Ministry to be proactive for putting the required mechanism
in place at the earliest in order to save our ancient sites/monuments and the Ministry may
also apprise the Committee about it through an explanatory note. (Para 42)
The Committee takes strong exception to the fact that the dossiers sent to the
UNESCO for including our Heritage sites in the List of World Heritage Sites are generally
found not to be in order. As a result, these are sent back for corrections, etc. This has
happened several times in respect of our different sites. The Committee has taken up this
issue earlier also with the Ministry and had expressed its concern about this. It feels that
with the kind of vast technical and other expertise that we have in this regard, we are
unable to present our case properly to the UNESCO. It appears we do not do our homework
seriously and send dossiers to UNESCO casually. It is alleged that dossiers are deliberately
not processed properly for unknown reasons. It is a serious matter that our dossiers have
been returned several times. The Committee recommends that a “Dossiers Committee”
should be constituted comprising eminent persons from relevant areas as well as other
professionals for the purpose so that Nation does not have to hear again about our proposals
being returned. (Para 45)
The Committee emphasizes the urgent need for strengthening of all wings of
Archaeological Survey of India like Monument, Conservation, Exploration and Excavation,
Epigraphy, Chemistry, etc. due to increase in the quantum as well as nature of these works.
The Committee observes that the workload of Horticulture Wing has increased manifold
with the increase in number of gardens under maintenance from 100 to 500 with no
corresponding increase in the manpower. As a result, sites, monuments, etc. are not being
properly maintained and landscaped. Their upkeep is generally not upto the mark. The
Committee, therefore, recommends that there should be a commensurate increase in the
workforce engaged in all the Departments of ASI, particularly in Horticulture for
showcasing our heritage sites. The Committee also recommends that vacancies at all levels
should be filled up on priority and revival of posts whenever necessary also be expedited
with the Ministry of Finance. It is taking lot of time. The Committee desires the Ministry
to keep it informed about the recommendations of the Manpower Management and Planning
Consultants and status of its implementation. (Para 50)

Museums
The Committee finds that the renovation of the galleries of the National Museum,
New Delhi has taken unduly a long time and we are not sure when are these going to be
completed/opened. Prolonged closure of these Galleries will also cause revenue loss to the
National Museum apart from the public not being able to see them. Therefore, these
Galleries should be opened without any further delay. (Para 60)
The Committee notes that advertisement for the post of Director, National Museums
on deputation basis has been given. It recommends that efforts be made to fill it up very
soon. Further, the National Museum is not acquiring new objects for so many years owing
mainly to the lack of storage space. This itself is a cause for serious concern to the
Committee as well as our culture-loving people. In the absence of Government acquisition,
all rare art and antiquities might go into the hands of private and foreign hands. It may
encourage illegal activities like smuggling etc. causing huge national loss. The Committee,
therefore, recommends to constitute the acquisition committee which is remaining defunct
for a long time, and start the process of acquisition at the earliest. (Para 61)
The Committee observes that Rs.60 crore has been allocated to the National Museum
as approved outlay for the Twelfth Five Year Plan, which, the Committee feels, is by all
means inadequate for the works to be undertaken. The Committee notes that our museums
are in bad shape. Only 10% of the acquisitions are put to display and those are not even
rotated regularly. Museum stores and galleries are in poor condition and lot of improvement
has to come in all these spheres in order to bring our museums at par with global standard.
The Committee recommends that allocation should be increased in museum sector and
hopes that the present amount allocated would be fully utilized for the earmarked projects/
work. (Para 62)
The Committee appreciates the new initiatives for digitization of the Museums and
master pieces, thorough increased professionalism, recruitment of staff and capacity
building programmes would no doubt bring in necessary fillip.  But, the outreach in terms
of foot-fall in the museums and recognition as national heritage are both the tangible
aspects that should be the yardstick in measuring the initiatives and the allotment of
funds. The Ministry of Culture should not lose sight of this target in their endeavor.
(Para 63)
The Committee appreciates the signing of Memorandum of Understanding with the
three world famous Museums and feels that our association with them would bring
necessary fillip to the working of our Museums. (Para 64)

Modernization of Indian Museum, Kolkata
The Committee recommends that due care be taken while renovating this heritage
building and conservation and restoration work should be given priority in view of our

Archives and Archival Libraries
The Committee expresses concern about under utilization of funds/unspent balances
of previous years. It hopes that the allocations to the tune of 67.44 crore for the archives
and archival libraries for 2013-14 will be fully spent particularly on upgradation and

The Committee notes that our capital city lacks class integrated infrastructure
facility of international standards. The Committee recommends that we may have such a
centre located near Indira Gandhi National Centre for Arts at Rajpath, the most

1
REPORT
Road and Highways is a critical infrastructure for economic development of a country. In
India, road infrastructure is utilized to transport over 60% of total goods and 85% of total
passenger traffic. Therefore, India has taken up ambitious programmes for developing National
Highways and other roads in a big way. Our focus is on developing roads of international standards
to create facilities for faster and smooth flow of traffic with enhanced safety features including
better riding surface, better road geometry, better traffic management, adequate signage, divided
carriageways, service roads, grade separators, over bridges and underpasses, bypasses and wayside
amenities as well as medical facilities.
2. The National Highways in India, although comprise only 1.7% of the entire road network,
carry about 40% of the total road traffic. India has one of the largest road networks consisting
of National Highways, Expressways, State Highways, Major District Roads, Other District Roads
and Village Roads.
3. The Ministry of Road Transport and Highways is responsible for the development and
maintenance of National Highways. Out of the total length of 79,116 km. of National Highways,
38,800 km. is with the State Public Works Departments (State PWDs), 30,046 km. with the
National Highways Authority of India (NHAI) and 2,905 with Border Roads Organization (BRO),
balance length of 7,365 km. is yet to be entrusted to the executing agencies.
4. The Ministry of Road Transport and Highways primarily follows the agency system to
develop and maintain the National Highways. Besides, the State Governments, the Border Road
Organization and National Highways Authority of India, an autonomous organization under this
Ministry, act as agencies of the Central Government. The Ministry has undertaken the National
Highways Development Project which is being implemented in phases and envisages the
improvement of more than about 54,500 km of arterial routes of National Highways network to
international standards.
5. The budget allocations of the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways under Demand
No.81 for 2013-14 were considered by the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee
on Transport, Tourism and Culture at its meeting held on the 2
nd April, 2013. During the meeting,
performance of various projects and programmes relating to construction/maintenance of Highways
and road transport, details of the budget allocations, the major achievements of the Ministry and
various aspects of budget utilization were examined.

8. When asked about the performance of road sector during the year 2012-13, the Secretary,
Ministry of Road Transport and Highways informed the Committee that it was a difficult year for
the sector. The slide back in the GDP had a very direct impact on the road construction activity.
The market sentiment was extremely poor. There was serious distress in the market, both in terms
of equity and debt. The road building sector witnessed obstacles in terms of environment and
forest clearances. As a result, 13 projects bid out by NHAI did not receive any bid.
9. The Committee finds that funds under both plan and non-plan outlays have seen
substantial reduction at RE stage for the year 2012-13. The Committee is not convinced of
the reasons for such drastic reduction of funds especially under plan head from Rs.23000
crores at BE stage to Rs.17773.54 crores at RE stage. The Committee found that reduction
of funds at RE stage is happening every year due to one reason or the other. The
Committee feels that the Ministry should strive to utilize the allocated money. The
Committee also feels that major modification of allocation at the stage of revised estimate
should be avoided as it delays the implementation of sanctioned projects.
Twelfth Plan (2012-17)
10. The Secretary, Ministry of Road T ransport and Highways (RTH) informed the Committee
on the investment pattern in road sector during the Eleventh and Twelfth Plan periods. He informed
that the total investment during Eleventh Five Year Plan was of the order of Rs.1.58 lakh crore,
out of which private sector investment was Rs.65,000 crore (about 42%) and the GBS and
borrowings was Rs.92,400 crore.
11. As regards, Twelfth Plan the Committee was informed that the Working Group
recommended for an outlay of Rs.5.29 lakh crore comprising Rs.2.64 lakh crore as GBS and cess,
Rs.64,800 crore as borrowing and Rs.2 lakh crore as private investment. In this, the private sector
investment was approximately 38 per cent. The 42 per cent investment in the Eleventh paln was
sought to be unsustainable for this expanded programme. However, the actual allocation for the
Twelfth plan is Rs.3.97 lakh crore consisting of Rs.1.44 lakh crore of GBS and cess, Rs.64,834
crore of borrowings and Rs.1.87 lakh crore of private sector investment. The private sector
investment as a percentage to the total allocation stands at 47 percent.
12. When asked about the private sector investment in the first year of Twelfth plan, it was
informed that it was not encouraging. It was further informed that expecting the private sector
investment to the order of 47 per cent in the road sector in the current plan period is a tall order.

Rs.1,44,769 crore including central transport sector as against the projected requirement of
Rs.2,64,080 crore excluding central transport sector. The Committee feels that this
reduction in allocation will certainly deter the Ministry in taking-up the new projects/
schemes envisaged for the Twelfth plan period. Projects like connectivity to 50 minor ports,
connectivity to 24 airports and implementation of special packages for J&K and North-
Eastern Region have to be dropped by the Ministry for want of funds from the Government.
The Committee also notes that Rs.6,400 crore has been allocated against the requirement
of Rs.37,540 crore for works NH(O) for the entire plan period, which is unsustainable

projects/schemes apart from the on-going ones do not suffer.

33. During the discussion the role of the Planning Commission in certain crucial aspects of
highways construction/development also came up. The Committee was informed that the Ministry
of Road Transport and Highways and NHAI have to go for approval to the Union Cabinet on many
of the issues vexing the road sector. The Chairman NHAI submitted before the Committee
“the Planning Commission has got the approval of the Cabinet for everything. It is
surprising that model concessionaire agreement which is evolving over a period of time and
we do not have much of experience on that, you straightaway get the stamp of the Cabinet.
If any minor tweak is required, you have to go to Cabinet. People are generally averse to

MCA like that. It is an uncalled for thing.......... I am doing the contract management
through a document which is evolved in the Planning Commission based on experience of
some Western countries”.
34. The Committee, in view of the complicated and long procedure involving multiple
agencies at different levels coupled with strict norms, legal, administrative, financial etc.
that are required to be followed at different stages, appreciates the constraints under
which highways projects have to be executed. Then there are problems with land
acquisition and environmental clearances that are time taking. But, the Committee feels
that such infrastructure projects as highways have to be taken up and completed in this
setting only; there in no escape from the constraints as these are built into the system.
Real challenge, therefore, before the Ministry of Road Transport & Highways is to
expedite the projects in minimum time and to maximum possible extent, by having a
robust monitoring and coordination mechanism at different level/stages. Every important
agency involved in the process like financial institutions such as Banks and RBI, State
Governments, other Ministries and particularly Planning Commission will have to realize
the urgency and importance of faster development of Highways and will have to make it
a joint effort.
35. The Committee hopes that certain measures taken recently in respect of making
loans from Banks as secured loans; separating forest clearance from the environmental and

9
efforts made to revise Concession Agreement will certainly go a long way in expediting our
highways development programmes.
36. In this regard, a disturbing aspect about Planning Commission’s approach towards
highways construction came to notice of the Committee. To Committee’s utter dismay, the
Planning Commission instead of promoting and facilitating highways construction is alleged
to have been exceeding its brief. The Committee feels that the Commission’s overbearing
attitude was causing unease amongst the line Ministries/Departments. It is the considered
opinion of the Committee that documents/papers prepared by the line Ministries for
implementing a project may be seen by the Commission just as is done by the Department
of Law and Department of Expenditure; it should refrain from commenting upon
engineering & technical aspects and should confine itself to planning and allocation/
management of resources only. Moreover, the ultimate accountability for anything done or
not done rests with Ministry and not with the Planning Commission. For example, in the
case of Ministry of Road Transport and Highways, the Committee learnt that even
Concessionaire Agreements are being finalized in the Commission on the basis of models
being followed in Western Countries. If it is true, the Committee feels that Planning
Commission by doing so was going beyond its original mandate visualized by Pandit
Jawaharlal Nehru, whose idea was to have such a body which could facilitate faster growth
and development in planned manner. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the
Concessionaire Agreement devised by the Planning Commission should be reformulated in
concurrence with the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways to address the local
conditions and changing circumstances. The Committee feels the Western models will not
work in our country because we have our own peculiarities and constraints.
37. The Committee has strong reasons to conclude that PPP as a model for the
development of road projects needs to be reviewed seriously in the light of our experience
so far in this regard. That the private capital is mainly for profit is borne out by the fact
that the profitable projects are being bid out fast. A vast country which needs faster
connectivity to its length and breadth has to adopt an alternative model of project
development which is development driven and not profit driven. Since profitable projects are
sold out first, the Government is facing problem in getting bidders for such non-profitable
road projects as those in LWE and North-East Areas. India needs faster construction of
roads and the Committee, therefore, recommends that all such projects without bidders
should be developed with the budgetary support from the Government and Planning
Commission needs to be more practical and careful about its role and function.
National Highways Development Project (NHDP)
38. National Highways Authority of India is mandated to implement National Highways
Development Project (NHDP) which is India’s largest ever Highways Project in a phased manner.
Rapid expansion of passenger and freight traffic makes it imperative to improve the road network
in the country. Accordingly, Government of India launched major initiatives to upgrade and
strengthen National Highways through various phases of National Highways Development Project
(NHDP). NHDP consists of the following components:
• NHDP Phase-I: Four laning of 7498 km. at an approved cost of Rs. 30,300 crore in
December, 2000 and NHDP Phase-II: Four laning of 6,644 km. at an approved cost
of Rs. 34,339 crore in December, 2003. These two phases comprise of Golden
Quadrilateral (GQ), North-South and East-West Corridors (NS-EW), Port Connectivity
and other projects. The GQ (5,846 km.) connects the four major cities of Delhi,
Mumbai, Chennai and Kolkata. The NS-EW Corridors (7,300 km) connect Srinagar in

10
the North to Kanyakumari in the South, including spur from Salem to Kochi and
Silchar in the East to Porbandar in the West.
• Government has approved upgradation of 12,109 km under NHDP Phase-III at an
estimated cost of Rs. 76546 crore.
• Government on June 18, 2008 has approved upgradation/strengthening of 5,000 kms. of
national highways to two lane with paved shoulders on BOT (Toll/Annuity) basis under
NHDP Phase–IV A at a cost of Rs. 6950 crore. Moreover, a unified programme of the
entire length of 20000 Kms envisaged in NHDP Phase-IV has also been approved by
Cabinet Committee on Infrastructure (CCI) in its meeting dated 2
nd Feb., 2012.
• Government on October 5, 2006 has approved six laning of 6,500 km. of national
highways comprising 5,700 km. of GQ and balance 800 km. of other sections under
NHDP Phase-V at a cost of Rs 41,210 crore.
• Government on November 2, 2006 has approved construction of 1000 km. of
expressways with full access control on new alignments at a cost of Rs.16,680 crore
under NHDP-Phase-VI.
• Government has approved construction of 700 kms. ring roads and bypasses besides
grade separators, flyovers, elevated roads and tunnels etc. at a cost of Rs.16,680 crore
under the NHDP Phase-VII.
39. NHAI is implementing National Highway Development Programme (NHDP) and some other
allied projects in accordance with the mandate approved by the Government. The development and
maintenance of National Highways is financed by following modes:–
(a) Government of India’s Gross Budgetary Support (GBS) and Additional Budgetary
Support (ABS).
(b) Dedicated accruals under the Central Road Fund (share in the levy of cess on fuel)
allocated through Union Budget.
(c) External Assistance in respect of International Institutions (World Bank; ADB; JBIC)
funded projects allocated through Union Budget.
(d) Ploughing back of toll revenue including toll collection, negative grant, premium and
revenue share deposited by NHAI into Consolidated Fund of India and in turn
equivalent amount released to NHAI for development, maintenance and management of
National Highways entrusted to it.
(e) Private financing under PPP frameworks
(i) Build Operate and Transfer (BOT)-Toll/Design Build Finance Operate and Transfer
(DBFOT)-Investment by private agencies and return through levy and retention of
user fee;
(ii) BOT (Annuity)-Investment by private agencies and return through semi-annual
pre-determined payments from NHAI as per bid; and
(iii) Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV)-with equity participation by NHAI.s
(f) Funding of the NHDP Projects under SARDP-NE and in J&K with Additional
Budgetary Support (ABS) over and above cess allocation; and
(g) Market borrowings (including funds raised through Capital Gain Tax Exemption Bonds
under section 54 EC of Income Tax Act and Tax free Bonds) as authorized by
Government of India on year to year basis.

44. One of the research organizations informed the Committee that there are silence/ignorance
about several facts which lead to the problems being faced by the road developers/concessionaires/
NHAI in carrying out the construction work on the projects acquired by them in past 2-3 years.
45. It was further informed that it was naïve on the part of road developers, if true, that traffic
on highways shall be consistently growing at 15% annually, GDP growth shall remain robust at
8%-9%, 20 km. per day highway construction announced in the year 2009 shall have to be
achieved, cost escalation will stop and environmental clearances shall be coming with a dispatch.
Most of the long stretch national highway development projects in previous two years were
cornered by leading road infrastructure developers of the country by offering premium to the NHAI
because the expert international rating agencies hired by road developers have validated their
expectation and targets of financial closure and revenue recoveries through Toll collections over a
period of 25-30 years.
46. However, most of the road developers, even after grave economic slow down of year
2008-09, have gambled to quote high premium in acquiring national highway road development
projects. Even now in the existing operational national highway stretches, due to manual collection,
there is a large scale under reporting of the traffic and therefore, the lower revenue recovery at
Toll plazas by the concessionaires. Fact of the case is that these big construction firms had
wrongfully offered premium in their road construction bidding process before NHAI and at the
same time the policy makers have forgotten that the burden of so called premium shall ultimately
be borne by the road users and now since the excitement has fizzled out the sympathies and noises
for the infrastructure players are being blow out of proportion by their well entrenched interest in
Government and outside.
47. The bankers are now weary of backing new projects because exposure to these big
infrastructure players has far exceeded capital adequacy ratio as they have plunged into non-road
construction projects like power, which are not taking up due to various reasons. As a matter of
fact, a sound long term investment project like road building always discounts the fluctuation in
traffic growth, cost overrun, shrinking GDP and passing through policy/environmental bottlenecks
rather than using them a ‘fig leaf’ to back out of their legal commitment.
48. It seems that ground work is being undertaken by NHAI and other official agencies to work
out so called settlement and conciliation mechanism to bail them out and holding back any penal
action against them for backing out of their commitment to start work on highway construction
in which they have committed through tender process premium payment to the NHAI in acquiring
the work. It is feared that in the end, as has been happening, it will be the road users, hapless
stakeholder, who shall be paying the price for acts of omissions and commissions committed by
road developers, NHAI and policy makers.
49. Though these observations of the research organization were forwarded to the Ministry for
their Comments, the Ministry has not bothered to furnish any comments to the Committee.

II. Road Transport
96. The Committee was informed that more than 60 per cent of freight and 85 per cent
passenger traffic are carried by road. Although National Highways constitute only about 1.7 per
cent of the road network, it carries 40 per cent of the total road traffic. Ministry claimed that easy
availability, adaptability to individual needs and the cost savings are some of the factors which go
in favour of road transport. Road transport also acts as a feeder service to railway, shipping and
air traffic. The number of vehicles has been growing at an average pace of around 10 per cent
per annum. The share of road traffic in total traffic has grown from 13.8 per cent of freight traffic
and 15.4 per cent of passenger traffic in 1950-51 to an estimated 62.9 per cent of freight traffic
and 90.2 per cent of passenger traffic by the end of 2009-10. The rapid expansion and
strengthening of the road network, therefore, is imperative, to provide for both present and future
traffic and for improved accessibility to the hinterland. In addition, road transport needs to be
regulated for better energy efficiency, less pollution and enhanced road safety.
97. The Ministry of Road Transport and Highways is responsible for formulation of broad
policies relating to regulation of road transport in the country, besides making arrangements for
movement of vehicular traffic with the neighbouring countries. The Ministry frames policies and
undertakes activities for improving road safety so as to minimise road accidents. The important
schemes formulated and managed by the Road Safety Cell of the Ministry include publicity
programmes, road safety awareness programmes through print and electronic media, Setting up of
Institute of Driving Training and Research, National Highways Accident Relief Service Scheme
(NHARSS), refresher training to heavy vehicle drivers in unorganized sector etc.

Publicity Measures and Awareness Campaigns
102. Publicity campaign is one of the best means of raising awareness about road safety among

OBSERV ATIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS/CONCLUSIONS— AT A GLANCE
Annual Plan 2012-13
The Committee finds that funds under both plan and non-plan outlays have seen
substantial reduction at RE stage for the year 2012-13. The Committee is not convinced of
the reasons for such drastic reduction of funds especially under plan head from Rs.23000
crores at BE stage to Rs.17773.54 crores at RE stage. The Committee found that reduction
of funds at RE stage is happening every year due to one reason or the other. The
Committee feels that the Ministry should strive to utilize the allocated money. The
Committee also feels that major modification of allocation at the stage of revised estimate
should be avoided as it delays the implementation of sanctioned projects. (Para 9)
Twelfth Plan (2012-17)
The Committee notes that the total GBS outlay provided during the Twelfth plan is
Rs.1,44,769 crore including central transport sector as against the projected requirement of
Rs.2,64,080 crore excluding central transport sector. The Committee feels that this
reduction in allocation will certainly deter the Ministry in taking-up the new projects/
schemes envisaged for the Twelfth plan period. Projects like connectivity to 50 minor ports,
connectivity to 24 airports and implementation of special packages for J&K and North-
Eastern Region have to be dropped by the Ministry for want of funds from the Government.
The Committee also notes that Rs.6,400 crore has been allocated against the requirement
of Rs.37,540 crore for works NH(O) for the entire plan period, which is unsustainable
considering the length of roads taken-up for improvement under this scheme. This reduced
allocation for the NH(O) will affect the NH(O) works adversely and ultimately result in
diversion of cess towards development of non-NHDP projects from NHDP projects. The
Committee is concerned to note that such diversion of cess meant for NHDP projects has
been taking place for the last three years which is alarming. The Committee feels that the
Ministry should take-up the enhancement of GBS during mid-term plan review so that new
projects/schemes apart from the on-going ones do not suffer. (Para 13)
Annual Plan 2013-14
The Committee finds that the GBS component for the Ministry has seen only a
marginal increase of Rs.500 crore, from Rs.23,000 crore in 2012-13(BE) to Rs.23,500 crore
for 2013-14 (BE). As against the projected requirement of Rs.26,450 crores, the Ministry has
been allocated Rs.23,500 crore only as GBS for 2013-14 which is about 88% of the projected
requirement. The Committee feels that static allocation forces the Ministry not to take up
new projects/schemes and it also affects the progress of the sanctioned projects adversely.
The Committee finds that Rs.3,024 crores meant for financing of NHDP will be diverted to
NH(O) works resulting in various schemes under NHDP being delayed. The Committee feels
that the Ministry should find ways to check such diversions in consultation with the
Planning Commission so that major national highway projects are not delayed for want of
funds. Implementation of our road transport Schemes/programmes are not visible/felt at the
ground level at all and, therefore, these may be supported in a big way. (Para 18)

31
The Committee also expresses its concern over the reduction in allocation of funds
for Road Transport Sector from Rs.400 crore in 2012-13(BE) to Rs.200 crore for 2013-14
(BE). (Para 19)
National Highways Authority of India
The Committee, in view of the complicated and long procedure involving multiple
agencies at different levels coupled with strict norms, legal, administrative, financial etc.
that are required to be followed at different stages, appreciates the constraints under which
highways projects have to be executed. Then there are problems with land acquisition and
environmental clearances that are time taking. But, the Committee feels that such
infrastructure projects as highways have to be taken up and completed in this setting only;
there in no escape from the constraints as these are built into the system. Real challenge,
therefore, before the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways is to expedite the projects
in minimum time and to maximum possible extent, by having a robust monitoring and
coordination mechanism at different level/stages. Every important agency involved in the
process like financial institutions such as Banks and RBI, State Governments, other
Ministries and particularly Planning Commission will have to realize the urgency and
importance of faster development of Highways and will have to make it a joint effort.
(Para 34)
The Committee hopes that certain measures taken recently in respect of making
loans from Banks as secured loans; separating forest clearance from the environmental and
efforts made to revise Concession Agreement will certainly go a long way in expediting our
highways development programmes. (Para 35)
In this regard, a disturbing aspect about Planning Commission’s approach towards
highways construction came to notice of the Committee. To Committee’s utter dismay, the
Planning Commission instead of promoting and facilitating highways construction is alleged
to have been exceeding its brief. The Committee feels that the Commission’s overbearing
attitude was causing unease amongst the line Ministries/Departments. It is the considered
opinion of the Committee that documents/papers prepared by the line Ministries for
implementing a project may be seen by the Commission just as is done by the Department
of Law and Department of Expenditure; it should refrain from commenting upon
engineering & technical aspects and should confine itself to planning and allocation/
management of resources only. Moreover, the ultimate accountability for anything done or
not done rests with Ministry and not with the Planning Commission. For example, in the
case of Ministry of Road Transport & Highways, the Committee learnt that even
Concessionaire Agreements are being finalized in the Commission on the basis of models
being followed in Western Countries. If it is true, the Committee feels that Planning
Commission by doing so was going beyond its original mandate visualized by Pandit
Jawaharlal Nehru, whose idea was to have such a body which could facilitate faster growth
and development in planned manner. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the
Concessionaire Agreement devised by the Planning Commission should be reformulated in
concurrence with the Ministry of Road Transport & Highways to address the local conditions
and changing circumstances. The Committee feels the Western models will not work in our
country because we have our own peculiarities and constraints. (Para 36)
The Committee has strong reasons to conclude that PPP as a model for the
development of road projects needs to be reviewed seriously in the light of our experience
so far in this regard. That the private capital is mainly for profit is borne out by the fact
that the profitable projects are being bid out fast. A vast country which needs faster

32
connectivity to its length and breadth has to adopt an alternative model of project
development which is development driven and not profit driven. Since profitable projects are
sold out first, the Government is facing problem in getting bidders for such non-profitable
road projects as those in LWE and North-East Areas. India needs faster construction of
roads and the Committee, therefore, recommends that all such projects without bidders
should be developed with the budgetary support from the Government and Planning
Commission needs to be more practical and careful about its role and function. (Para 37)
National Highways Development Project (NHDP)
The Committee observes that performance of NHDP from 2006 onwards has not been
very good. For instance out of the 1000 km. envisaged in NHDP-VI in 2006, the Government
could not award even a single contract till March, 2013. Likewise, out of the 19,800 km.
envisaged in the NHDP IV , just 187 km. could be completed till March 2013. Apart from the
stated reasons such as poor market conditions, economic slow down, strict stipulations of
RBI for funding projects, poor response of bidders for projects, the Committee feels that
poor performance of NHDP projects may be due to reasons narrated in previous paragraphs.
The Committee, therefore, feels that the Government should look into such aspects and try
to curb such practice to prevent breakdown of implementation of projects. (Para 50)
The Committee feels that environment and forest clearance are necessary
components of any development. However, there is no point in delaying the clearance or
keeping it in abeyance for unduly long, affecting the viability of the projects. The
Committee recommends that the Government should fix a specific time-frame within which
the concerned authorities have to take a decision on such clearances. There should be an
effective coordinating mechanism with different Government agencies to give clearances in
a time bound manner. (Para 56)
The Committee after examining all the information provided by the Ministry as well
as the National Highways Authority of India expresses its concern over the status and
progress of development of national highways in the country. The NHAI’s ability to spend
only Rs.7780 crores as against the allocated amount of Rs.20780 crores (RE) during the year
2012-13 certainly does not inspire confidence with regard to development of national
highways. When the concessionaires who have awarded projects under BOT, are withdrawing
from various projects due to funding issues, the public sector agency is not able to spend
even half of the allocated money. The replies submitted by the Ministry are not convincing.
(Para 61)
The Committee was informed about the poor condition of Rewa-Katni-Jabalpur
section of NH7 and also the non-availability of approach roads to NH-60 of GQ in
Medinipur(WB). Poor condition of NH 25 between Kanpur and Jhansi was also brought
before the Committee. The Committee hopes that NHAI will take-up with State Government
of Tamil Nadu on the pending issues relating to completion of Chennai port-Maduravoyal
connectivity project. The Committee was also informed about the delay in acquisition of land
for national highways projects and release of share of central funds to Kerala. The
Committee also hopes that the development of Dehradun-Gangotri national highway via
Harsil will get the due importance from the implementing agencies and the project will be
completed within the stipulated time. (Para 62)
The Committee feels that the model Concession Agreement prepared by the Planning
Commission is acting as an impediment in awarding projects as there is no flexibility to
accommodate the local Conditions. The Committee is of the opinion that the NHAI may be
allowed to have its own Concession Agreement depending on the local conditions for the

33
roads to facilitate greater amount of private participation. The Committee also feels that
NHAI should not keep on adding projects in its kitty without completing the existing
projects. The Committee hopes that NHAI should fix its target levels based on ground
realities involved in road projects. (Para 63)
National Highways (Original) Works: NH(O)
The Committee feels that development of non-NHDP highways is not getting much
attention from the Government. Reduced allocation of Rs.5421.83 crores - 2013-14 against
that of Rs.6,042 crore for the year 2012-13 (BE) clearly shows the reduced emphasis of
Government this sector. The Committee notes with concern that to meet this shortfall of
fund money; out of cess meant for NHDP, was being diverted under the head. This diversion
of cess increased to Rs.5,719 crore in 2012-13 from Rs.l,162 crore diverted in 2011-12. The
Ministry has the planning to divert Rs.3,024 crore during the current fiscal. The Committee
finds that achievement of targets fixed under the development of non-NHDP is also not
encouraging. The Committee feels that dedicated allocation of funds for this head is a
necessity for strengthening the core non-NHDP national highways. (Para 68)
Road Projects in Left Wing Extremism affected areas
The Committee is of the view that developing road network in LWE areas forms a
strategic and economic significance to connect them with the rest of the country. The
Committee feels concerned to note that out of the 5477 km. road proposed in LWE areas
only 2267 km. could be completed till February, 2013. The Government machinery need to
be activated to involve all the agencies to ensure adequate security for doing the road
projects in the regions. The Committee observes that the relaxation of eligibility conditions
is a welcome step to implement the road projects in Left Wing Extremism affected areas.
(Para 71)
Maintenance and Repairs of National Highways
The Committee notes that over the past six decades, the volume of traffic on Indian
roads has increased exponentially. The vast network of roads and of National Highways,
notwithstanding, there are serious concerns about their quality and capacity. (Para 72)
The Committee feels that allocation of funds for maintenance and repair of national
highways is highly inadequate considering the damages etc. in the existing Highways and
new national highways added every year. The Committee learnt that what is allotted is just
1I3
rd of the requirement of funds for maintenance of National Highways. The Committee

REPORT
The Ministry of Shipping has been mandated with the responsibility of formulating policy
framework concerning the shipping industry as a whole, devise programmes in keeping with the
policy and to implement the programmes through appropriate delivery mechanism. The functions
of the Ministry are broadly divided into two wings — ports and shipping. Since India has a long
coastline of about 7517 km., functioning of the Ministry assumes critical importance from
economic as well as strategic points of view. Indian Shipping Industry has, over the years played
a crucial role in the transport sector of India’s economy. Approximately 90% of the country’s trade
by volume and 70% by value are moved through Maritime Transport. In the global context,
shipping continues to remain unchallenged as the world’s most efficient means of transportation
and there is no doubt that our Country has to strive hard in order to compete with global shipping
giants.
ORGANISATIONAL STRUCTURE OF THE MINISTRY OF SHIPPING
2. The Ministry of Shipping has the following subordinate and attached offices under it:
(i) Director General of Shipping, Mumbai (including Minor Ports Survey Organisation,
Mumbai)
(ii) Directorate General of Lighthouses and Lightships, Noida (U.P.)
(iii) 12 M ajor Ports
(iv) Inland W aterways Authority of India, Noida
(v) Indian Maritime University, Chennai
(vi) Shipping Corporation of India Limited, Mumbai
(vii) Cochin Shipyard Limited, Kochi
(viii) Central Inland Water Transport Corporation Limited, Kolkata
(ix) Dredging Corporation of India Limited.
(x) Hooghly Dock and Ports Engineering Limited, Kolkata
3. Demand No.88 containing the details of budgetary provisions of the Ministry of Shipping
for the financial year 2013-14 was scrutinized by the Department related Parliamentary Standing
Committee on Transport, Tourism and Culture at its meeting held on the 18
th April 2013. The
Secretary, Ministry of Shipping along with the senior officials explained to the Committee on
various aspects of the Demands for Grants. The Committee also sought information through a
questionnaire discussing various issues related to the subject.
TWELFTH FIVE YEAR PLAN (2012-17)
4. The Ministry of Shipping proposes to adopt a strategy for the Twelfth Five Year Plan to
ensure adequate investment in the Port Sector; to meet the growing capacity needs and improve
the efficiency of ports by reducing ‘dwell time’ and ‘turn around time’. One of the major
objectives is to increase the draft of all the ports to at least 14 meters by the end of the 12th Five
Year Plan . The Twelfth Plan is also focusing on increasing the share of containerized cargo in ports
with a view to capture higher share of international trade. Competitive mode of tariff fixation,

2
efficient environment clearance and land acquisition, integrating the port community system,
capacity augmentation through PPP mode, institutional reforms, etc. are the other strategies
proposed during the Plan period.
5. Planning Commission has approved a Gross Budgetary Support (GBS) of Rs.6960 crore for
the Ministry for the Twelfth Five Year Plan period. This is a 108.5% increase in over the GBS for
the Eleventh Plan period, which was Rs.3337.58 crore. Out of the total GBS approved for Twelfth
Plan, the share of Ports, Shipping and Inland Water Transport (IWT) sectors are Rs.3057.47 crore,
Rs.2402.53 crore and Rs.1500.00 crore respectively. The Committee was also informed that the
total actual expenditure incurred during the entire Eleventh Plan Period stood at Rs. 2151.53 crore only.
6. The Committee appreciates 108% increase in Twelfth Plan allocation but takes a
serious note of the fact that during the Eleventh Plan period, of the total Gross Budgetary
Support of Rs.3337.58 crore, the Ministry could incur actual expenditure of Rs.2151.53 crore
only. With such a poor spending during Eleventh Plan, 108% enhancement in the
allocations for the Twelfth Plan, throws a big challenge before the Ministry to optimally
utilize the enhanced amount during Twelfth Plan. The Committee recommends that the
Ministry may take necessary steps right from the beginning itself to ensure that the on-
going as well as proposed projects go as per the schedule. No expenditure should be incurred
hurriedly at the fag end of the year and it should be as per the guidelines in this regard.
Moreover, delay should also be avoided as it ultimately results into cost and time overruns.
There should not be any compromise on the quality of works.
ANALYSIS OF ANNUAL PLAN 2012-13
7. The Budget Estimate for the Ministry for Financial Year 2012-13 was Rs.817.00 crore
which was reduced to Rs.502.00 crore at RE stage. IEBR for 2012-13 of Rs.4858.47 crore,
however, was enhanced to Rs.5051.30 crore at the RE stage.
8. Ministry of Shipping has informed that against the RE allocation of Rs.502.00 crore, actual
expenditure as on 31.12.2013 is Rs.377.63 crore. While the Ports and Shipping sectors have
utilized their RE amount, Inland Waterways Authority of India (IWAI) lagged a little bit as its
expenditure is seasonal in nature, which generally would pick up from January onwards.
9. The Secretary, Shipping informed the Committee that the reduction in allocations during the
RE stage was mainly on two accounts. Firstly, the ship-building subsidy had a provision of Rs.400
crore out of Rs.817 crore. This was an old scheme which, actually, expired in 2007. As per the
assessment made at that time, the requirements were not more than Rs.200 to Rs.220 crore.
Therefore, this had to be reduced from Rs.400 crore to Rs.200 crore at the R.E. stage. Thus, there
was a straight reduction of Rs.200 crore on account of this only. Secondly, Kolkata Port Dredging
Subsidy backlog was still being cleared for 2010-11 and 2011-12, which was about Rs.332 crore.
It was reduced to about Rs.71 crore at the R.E. stage.
10. The Committee notes with concern that the Ministry was not able to utilize its funds
mainly due to ship-building and dredging subsidy schemes. It could have been avoided with
proper assessment and foresight as these schemes are not new. Underutilization, in fact,
defeats the purpose of having a planned budget and allocations itself. The Ministry has
claimed that except IWAI, the Shipping and Port sectors have expended the allocations
satisfactorily. Whereas, compared to the BE, the expenditure incurred in the Port Sector is
only 54.77% and 33.56% by the other organizations like DCI, ALHW, SCL, etc., altogether
in the Shipping sector the expenditure is about 71.77%.
11. The Committee further observes that the B.E. allocations had been reduced in
many sectors and there are under-utilizations as well. Major reductions have taken place

3
in Ports, Ship Building and Inland Water Transport. Only exception was Light Houses,
allocation for which was marginally increased. The Committee once again recommends
that, the Ministry should project a realistic demand, prepare right estimate and also
execute its plans properly.
ANNUAL PLAN 2013-14
12. Total Plan allocation for the Ministry of Shipping during the year 2013-14 stands at
Rs.7087.30 crore, out of which the share of GBS and IEBR each is Rs.852.00 crore and
Rs.6235.30 respectively. While replying to a questionnaire on the projected demand and allocations
during 2013-14, the Ministry of Shipping mentioned that they had projected a Plan allocation of
Rs.1329.42 crore for 2013-14 whereas, the Planning Commission has allocated Plan Budget of
Rs.852 crore only. Out of the GBS of Rs.852.00 crore, Rs.80.20 crore has been earmarked for
the North Eastern Region. Sector wise projected demand and allocation of GBS during 2013-14 is

(a) Ports Sector:

15. An outlay of Rs. 399.00 crore has been allocated to Shipping Sector for the Financial Year

• Inland Waterways Transport (IWT): 200.00 crore which also includes the provision of
Rs. 80.20 crore ( i.e. 10% of total Plan outlay excluding EAP component) for North-
East region;
• Directorate General of Lighthouse and Lightships (DGLL): Rs. 103.00 crore for DGLL
for development of Lighthouses and Lightships;
• Directorate General of Shipping (DG(S)): Rs. 12.00 crore out of which an amount of
Rs. 6.00 crore is placed at the disposal of Ministry of Urban Development. and

• Indian Maritime University (IMU): Rs. 80.00 crore;
• Shipbuilding and Repair (SBR): Rs. 3.00 crore for Shipbuilding and Repairs which is

Industry;
• Coastal Shipping: Rs. 1.00 crore.
16. The Committee observes that the GBS of 2012-13 at the BE stage was Rs. 817 crore
which was reduced to Rs. 502 crore in the RE. The actual spending was Rs.494.83 crore. The
Committee feels that due to reduction/under-utilization of the allocations, the Planning
Commission had to peg the GBS during 2013-14 to Rs. 852 crore even though the projected
demand by the Ministry was Rs. 1329.42 crore. It can be seen that about 30% of the
projected demand has been cut by the Planning Commission. The Committee is of the view
that such a cut in allocation to the Ministry of Shipping could have been avoided if the
funds were expended optimally during 2012-13 as the Plan allocations have been decided on
the basis of actual expenditure made in the previous year. The Committee recommends that
the Ministry may make it sure that its proposed plan expenditure during 2013-14 may be
kept as per schedule so that the present allocation of Rs. 852 crore may not be reduced at
the RE stage as done in the previous years, leading to more cuts in the succeeding years.
17. The Committee feels concerned about the planning and execution of the Plan projects
of the Ministry of Shipping. Out of the Rs.6960 crore approved allocation for the Twelfth
Plan; so far the allocation made to the Ministry is only Rs.1354 crore in the first two years.
(RE of 2012-13 Rs.502 crore + BE of 2013-14 Rs.852 crore). The Committee fails to
understand as to how far the Ministry will be able to achieve the targets. The Committee
recommends that Ministry of Shipping should review the pace of the on-going works and
necessary corrective measures should be taken at the earliest.
PORT SECTOR
18. Ports are considered as the Country’s gateways to the world, facilitating ocean borne

going vessels/ships. India has 12 Major ports and about 187 minor ports. These major ports are

19. The Eleventh Five Year Plan envisaged an increase in capacity of major ports to 1,016.55
Million Tonne (MT) by the end of 2011-12 from the pre-plan base level of 504.75 MT. Average
annual growth in capacity addition was envisaged at 15 per cent. Actual capacity addition during
the plan (2006-07 to 2011-12) was, however, moderate and showed a growth of 6.65 per cent per
annum. The cargo handling capacity at the end of March, 2012, was 696.53 MT .
20. As per Twelfth Plan projection, Ministry of Shipping has planned to increase the capacity
of Major Ports in the country during 2012-13 to 745.86 million tonnes from 670.13 million tonnes
and for Non-Major ports it is expected to increase to 447.15 million tonnes from 391.66 million
tonnes. Major Ports have identified various projects/schemes or implementation during 2012-13 to
create the targeted capacity. The Ministry of Shipping has submitted that by the end of Twelfth
Plan ( i.e. March, 2017), it is proposed to enhance the capacity of Major Ports to 1229.21 million
tonnes and Non-Major Ports to 1457.342 million tonnes. In the Maritime Agenda 2010-20 prepared
by the Ministry of Shipping, a target of 3,130 MT port capacities has been set for the year 2020.
More than 50 per cent of this capacity is to be created in the non-major ports as the traffic
handling by these ports is expected to increase to 1,280 MT.
21. The Secretary Shipping during the evidence informed that the total capacity at major ports
stood at 750 million tons on 31
st March, 2013 and the non-major ports as on 31.3.2013 was 630
million tons, the total becoming 1380 million tons at the end of the last financial year in terms of
capacity.
22. The Secretary Shipping also stated that during the year 2012-13 a record number of 32 port
projects were awarded resulting in a capacity addition of 136.75 MMTPA involving an estimated
investment of Rs. 6765.63 crore. Out of these 32 projects, 13 are on the basis of PPP and an equal
number of 13 are non-PPP and six are captive projects, with the PSUs. The PSUs will spend the
money and create those berths. The ports do not have to spend the money.

7
23. On being asked about the reasons for negative growth in the certain ports and the
requirement of starting two new major ports, the Secretary stated that in the last two years, some
of the Major Ports like Mormugao, Chennai, Kolkata and Vishakhapatnam have registered poor
growth because of ban on iron ore mining by the Supreme Court. Moreover, the slow down and
recession in the global market has also adversely impacted the traffic growth of the Major Ports
in recent times. However, the emerging global economy has opened up new avenues for the
maritime sector. Given India’s high GDP growth in the last decade, it is necessary to build adequate
infrastructure in the port sector to cope with this growth. The Maritime Agenda for the period
2010-20 prepared by the Ministry of Shipping has indicated that the traffic at Indian Ports is likely
to grow at CAGR of about 11% from 849.89 million tonnes (during 2009-10) to about 2485 million
tonnes by 2019-20. The traffic at Major Ports is likely to grow at a CAGR of about 8% from
561.09 million tonnes in 2009-10 to about 1215 million tonnes by 2019-20. Therefore, there is a
need to augment the capacity in the port sector through all means – through non-Major Ports,
additional berths/terminals in the Major Ports and setting up new Major Ports.
24. The Secretary, Ministry of Shipping confirmed that Government has taken the decision to
establish two new major ports, one at Sagar Island in West Bengal and the other in Andhra
Pradesh. These will create an additional capacity of around 100 million MMTPA. Sagar Port is at
a more advanced stage because the location has also been identified already. The State Government
of West Bengal have agreed to take 26 per cent equity in an Special Purpose Vehicle(SPV) and
remaining will be with the Kolkata Port and this SPV will then find the partner for development
of the port. There is no land acquisition involved in the development of this major port because
the land has to be reclaimed. There will be small land acquisition of about 70 hectares, which
would be required for providing road and rail connectivity from the main land to the Sagar Island.
In the case of Andhra Pradesh, there are two locations being considered right now. The proposal
that has been moved to the Cabinet is to commission the feasibility report for both these locations
and the model is again the same. There will be an SPV jointly by the concerned State Government.
They have given their consent and for the Vishakhapatnam port.
25. In addition, a new outer harbour will be developed in the Tuticorin Port at Thoothukkudi,

42 million tones of capacity.

Kolkata and Haldia Port System
35. The Secretary Shipping during the evidence explained that Kolkata Port, is a combination
of Haldia Dock System and Kolkata Dock System. The Haldia Dock System is served by one
channel, called Haldia channel. The main problem of dredging is really in the Haldia channel. 98%
of total subsidy which the Government of India gives is spent on the Haldia channel, which has
a draft of usually 6-7 metres. Even to maintain that draft that much money has to be spent. The
Kolkata Dock System is served by the Rangfala channel which has a better draft and less
siltation.
36. In the Haldia Dock System, the capacity of available lock through which the ships pass is
already exhausted. Thus, an alternative has to be developed through a new project which is outside
the lock system. At Haldia, two major projects have already been approved. One is called the Haldia
Dock South and North, Haldia Dock-II. Like the existing dock, port is trying to develop Haldia
Dock-II which is upstream of the existing Haldia Dock, about 15 kms. off shore. It is outside
the existing dock system. Here, there will be trans-shipment. Smaller vessels will go to Haldia
Dock-II because they can’t go to Haldia Dock-I. The capacity of Haldia Dock-I is already
exhausted.
37. On the Kolkata Dock, there is not much dredging required, as the Rangfala channel is better
on this account. In 2013-14, the major project proposed is Diamond Harbour Container Terminal.
This will be on the Rangfala channel on the Kolkata Dock System. The project will be awarded
this year. This is for the development of the Kolkata Dock System.
38. Even after these developments at Kolkata and Haldia, still there will be a gap of about 52
MT because Kolkata Port has a large hinterland. Once upon a time the entire State of West Bengal,

11
Bihar, Jharkhand, and land-locked countries like Nepal, Bhutan, all used to depend on Kolkata Port.
But, now, they are getting their cargo from Paradip Port, from Visakhapatnam Port because the
Kolkata Port is not working due to lack of adequate draft. The eastern freight corridor will be
connected to the proposed Sagar Port. Once that connectivity is available, the difficulties faced by
Bihar and Jharkhand will also be solved.
39. The Ministry informed that there is a scope for development of port at Rasulpur. The
Rasulpur Port can also supplement whatever cargo we are handling at Haldia and Kolkata. The
Kolkata Port Trust was approached by the State Government in 2008 for carrying out
oceanographic survey and data. Since the Chairman of the Kolkata Port Trust is also the
conservator of the entire navigation channel for Hooghley River, they had to take permission
from the Ministry and it was immediately granted. Kolkata Port Trust will be very willing to
extend any kind of help if the State Government wants to develop it in the minor ports sector.
Whatever help was sought for by the State Government has been given to them by the
Ministry.
40. The Committee welcomes the new initiatives taken for establishing two new Major
Ports in the country. The Committee also observes that the Kolkata Port has been running
in losses and the Haldia Port is earning much more and the Ministry is collecting money
from the Haldia Port and spending it on Kolkata Port. However, the Haldia Port is not being
developed, as is required. The Committee recommends that Haldia Port may be developed
to an independent port.
41. The Committee feels that like so many Ports abroad including the Shanghai Port,
which is the number one port in the world, the Kolkata Port has the potential to grow. But,
for this the port needs to be extended to deep sea. This will enable the port to pick up the
cargo from deep sea from mother ships and then to bring in through the barges into the
mainland. For this, the facilities/manpower with the CIWTC can also be meaningfully
utilized.

Cabotage Law
45. The Ministry informed the Committee that recently certain modifications were made in the
cabotage law pertaining to ICTT. The relaxation of Cabotage for transhipment of EXIM containers
to and from ICTT, Vallarpadam was approved by the Union Cabinet on 6.9.2012. The approval was
subject to certain security-related conditions suggested by the Ministry of Home Affairs and the
Ministry of Defence. This relaxation is also subject to a review after a period of three years. The
order to implement the relaxation of cabotage policy, as above, was issued to Directorate General
of Shipping on 21.9.2012.
46. The Committee was informed that more than 50% of the Indian container traffic is being
transhipped at ports outside India, mainly at Colombo and also at Singapore, Salalah and Jebel Ali.
The Cochin Port Trust, with the objective of attracting more mainline vessels to India, had
approached the Ministry for a relaxation of Cabotage for transhipment of EXIM (Export-Import)
Containers to and from ICTT, Vallarpadam. The cabotage relaxation is expected to reduce the need
for transhipment at foreign ports and thereby reduce transaction cost for Indian Exim trade.
47. The Committee feels that change in Cabotage Law is a welcome step and hopes that
Cabotage regulations at the ICTT would attract more vessels thereby increase the revenue
earning of the Cochin Port.
The Tariff Authority for Major Ports (TAMP)
48. The Tariff Authority for Major Ports (TAMP) – an autonomous body – regulates the tariff
structure for all the activities of the Major Ports including private terminals, etc., located within
them. There has been a major bottleneck, both for our major ports as well as for the investors
because TAMP has to fix tariff on cost plus basis only for our major ports, whereas for non-major
ports they are not governed by TAMP. The private ports and the non-major ports are not governed
by TAMP due to which there is no level playing field and the Major ports are adversely affected
because of being governed by TAMP.
49. The Committee recommends that the review of the TAMP should be done on priority
so that the Major Ports may be able to get a level playing field as compared to its counter
parts in the non major ports.

scientific assessment, followed inappropriate purchase procedure for sourcing the
requirement, did not determining competitive prices for procurement of fuel and lubricants
and had inadequate internal control procedures for procurement of fuel and lubricants.

waterways.

90. The IWAI was set up on 27 th October, 1986 vide Inland Waterways Authority of India

navigation. IWAI is primarily responsible for development, maintenance and regulation of National

the respective State Governments.
91. As of now, there are five National Waterways. IWAI undertakes development and
maintenance of IWT related infrastructure facilities on first three NWs. Various projects for
developing and maintaining following infrastructure on these NWs have been completed and some
are in progress.
92. At the initiative of IWAI, the concerned Ministries of Home Affairs, Department of Revenue,

has been made operational w.e.f. 1
st June, 2011, within a short span of 5 months. Besides helping
in the preservation of the flora and fauna of the unique biosphere reserve of the Sundarbans, it
will prevent poaching; illegal infiltration and facilitate enhanced vigil on Indo-Bangladesh border by
Border Security Force.
93. Kaladan Multimodal Transit Transport project was conceptualized by the Ministry of
External Affairs to provide an alternative connectivity of Mizoram with Haldia/Kolkata ports through
Kaladan river in Myanmar. The project envisages road transport from Mizoram to Paletwa
(Myanmar), thereafter from Paletwa to Sittwe (Myanmar) by IWT and from Sittwe to Haldia by
Maritime Shipping. The project is piloted and funded by the MEA which appointed IWAI as their
Project Development Consultant (PDC). Based on IWAIs recommendations, MEA awarded the work
to the successful bidder [M/s ESSAR projects (I) Pvt Ltd.] for construction of port and IWT
components at a cost Rs. 342 cr. The construction work of Sittwe IWT terminal is in progress
and the entire work targeted to be completed by June, 2013.
