PIRACY, SAFETY AND SECURITY
108. The menace of piracy continues unabated in spite of increased naval presence in the Gulf
of Aden region and merchant ships being asked to comply with best management practices which
includes establishment of “Citadel”.
109. Shipping Ministry has stated that there are reports of more and more shipowners deploying
security guards on their ships while transiting piracy infested waters of Gulf of Aden and Arabian
sea. It has been estimated that about 35% of the total number of ships transiting these waters,
deploy armed security guards. A merchant ship arriving with weapons on board, in a commercial
port of a coastal state, would also invoke concern for customs, police and other security agencies
tasked with law enforcement and coastal security. Therefore, International Maritime Organization
(IMO) has left the decision to the concerned flag States.
110. The subject has been deliberated at length in the Ministry of Shipping and it is noted that
decision to employ armed security guards is complex one and whilst not endorsing the use of
armed guards on merchant ships, given the present serious danger to shipping from the pirates,
the Indian ship owners may deploy armed security guards, subject to their risk assessment
particularly for ships which bear slow speed and have low freeboard, and in pursuance of section
86 “Transit and transshipment of stores” 77- “Declaration by owner of baggage” and
80-Temporary Detention of Baggage of Customs Act, 1962 and section 45 A of the Indian Arms
Act, 1959.
111. The Ministry of Shipping has informed that the incidence of piracy has been of great
concern to the Government. The Government has deployed naval vessels for assistance to
merchant vessels in the piracy-affected areas. The government has also been raising the issue of
piracy and the need for more concerted international action at the meetings of the United Nations
and the International Maritime Organization (IMO). (In 2011, 237 vessels were attacked, 28 vessels
were hijacked and 1,118 crew members were taken hostage (of which 24 seafarers were killed).
As on date, there are a total 37 Indian seafarers held hostage by the Somalia pirates.
112. With regard to accidents, the Secretary, Shipping has deposed before the Committee that
New Port Entry Rules were notified, basically, to prevent old ships to call on our ports. Under
these rules, ships above 25 years are not allowed to come in unless they have a valid PNI
insurance and valid classification. This is working very well. Very old ships which are 30-35 years
old belonging to different companies were coming and causing accidents in the previous years. Last
year we had seen accident at Mumbai and every year major accidents are happening. As a result
of this initiative, there were not many major accidents this year. The Committee was also informed
that a very important Maritime Labour Convention which ensures appropriate labour conditions on
ships are made available to the workers. It is in an advanced stage of processing and we hope to
take it before the Cabinet very soon.
113. The Committee is concerned about the increasing cases of piracy and notes the
various initiatives taken for protecting the merchant ships from pirate attacks. The
Committee also shares the concerns of the Ministry of Shipping as regards deploying armed
guards in the vessels to deter the pirates on the high seas. The Committee feels that joint
efforts should be made with other coastal countries in strengthening security of our ships
passing through area of potential threat.

26
114. The Committee notes the steps taken to prevent abandoning of ships in the Indian

these should not be flowing into private hands. Therefore, the Committee recommends that

Ministry of Shipping should move a bill for making the necessary amendments to the Major

125. The Committee observes that Fifty-six per cent of the GBS goes to the shipping

fast. About 42 per cent of the fleet is over 20 years of age and another 11 per cent in the

nd in 2011 according to UNCTAD liner shipping

ores to bring it back to sustenance level. The Committee also directs to consider using port

OBSERV ATIONS/CONCLUSIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS — AT A GLANCE
The Committee appreciates 108% increase in Twelfth Plan allocation but takes a
serious note of the fact that during the Eleventh Plan period, of the total Gross Budgetary
Support of Rs. 3337.58 crore, the Ministry could incur actual expenditure of Rs. 2151.53
crore only. With such a foor spending during Eleventh Plan, 108% enhancement in the
allocations for the Twelfth Plan, throws a big challenge before the Ministry to optimally
utilize the enhanced amount during Twelfth Plan. The Committee recommends that the
Ministry may take necessary steps right from the beginning itself to ensure that the on-
going as well as proposed projects go as per the schedule. No expenditure should be incurred
hurriedly at the fag end of the year and it should be as per the guidelines in this regard.
Moreover, delay should also be avoided as it ultimately results into cost and time overruns.
There should not be any compromise on the quality of works. (Para 6)
ANALYSIS OF ANNUAL PLAN 2012-13
The Committee notes with concern that the Ministry was not able to utilize its funds
mainly due to ship-building and dredging subsidy schemes. It could have been avoided with
proper assessment and foresight as these schemes are not new. Underutilization, in fact,
defeats the purpose of having a planned budget and allocations itself. The Ministry has
claimed that except IWAI, the Shipping and Port sectors have expended the allocations
satisfactorily. Whereas, compared to the BE, the expenditure incurred in the Port Sector is
only 54.77% and 33.56% by the other organizations like DCI, ALHW, SCL, etc., altogether
in the Shipping sector the expenditure is about 71.77%. (Para 10)
The Committee further observes that the B.E. allocations had been reduced in many
sectors and there are under-utilizations as well. Major reductions have taken place in Ports,
Ship Building and Inland Water Transport. Only exception was Light Houses, allocation for
which was marginally increased. The Committee once again recommends that, the Ministry
should project a realistic demand, prepare right estimate and also execute its plans properly.
(Para 11)
ANNUAL PLAN 2013-14
The Committee observes that the GBS of 2012-13 at the BE stage was Rs. 817 crore
which was reduced to Rs. 502 crore in the RE. The actual spending was Rs. 494.83 crore.
The Committee feels that due to reduction/under-utilization of the allocations, the Planning
Commission had to peg the GBS during 2013-14 to Rs. 852 crore even though the projected
demand by the Ministry was Rs. 1329.42 crore. It can be seen that about 30% of the
projected demand has been cut by the Planning Commission. The Committee is of the view
that such a cut in allocation to the Ministry of Shipping could have been avoided if the
funds were expended optimally during 2012-13 as the Plan allocations have been decided on
the basis of actual expenditure made in the previous year. The Committee recommends that
the Ministry may make it sure that its proposed plan expenditure during 2013-14 may be
kept as per schedule so that the present allocation of Rs. 852 crore may not be reduced at
the RE stage as done in the previous years, leading to more cuts in the succeeding years.
(Para 16)

only 135 MMTPA. In this context, the Committee does not know on which grounds the
Maritime Agenda 2010-20 has been fixed with a target of 3130 Million Tonne port capacity
addition by the year 2020. The present day capacity of the Major Ports is only 696.53 MT
and the annual capacity addition ratio is mere 6.65%. The Committee is of the view that
even the Twelfth Five Year Plan target of 1229.24 MT by the year 2017 appears to be a
distant dream with the current pace of 6.65% capacity addition annually. (Para 30)
The Committee feels that major capacity addition has been done by the private ports
and the capacity addition by our Major Ports is not as much. Therefore, the Committee
recommends that Major Ports may be equipped with modern facilities so that the targets of
Maritime Agenda and that of the Twelfth Five Year Plan may be achieved in letter and
spirit. (Para 31)
The Committee feels concerned over the negative growth of traffic during 2011-12
in the major ports such as Mormugao (-40.46%), Visakhapatnam (-17.72%), Kolkata
(-15.23%), Chennai (-6.00%), Paradip (-2.48%) and JNPT (-1.76%). This is not a healthy
trend especially at a stage where ports are heading for capacity additions. As the Major
Ports are not able to find the required cargo as a result of ban on the mining activities,
the Committee recommends that the Ports may review the capacity addition targets keeping
in view the availability of cargo they may handle in future. The Committee recommends to
explore the possibility of alternate cargos for such ports, including cruise tourism for
Mormugao Port, so that negative growth in many of these Ports may be addressed.
(Para 32)
The Committee notes the port performance indices during the years 2011 and 2012.
Haldia and Mormugao have shown negative efficiency in comparison to the cargo handled
in other ports like Kandla, New Mangalore, JNPT, Mumbai etc. which are having the
average out puts at higher sides. The Committee recommends that the ports may try to
improve its efficiency as the private ports functioning at the vicinity may otherwise take
the advantages. (Para 33)
The Committee recommends that the proposed new Major Ports may be equipped
with container handling facilities as the future of the ports are now in the container sector
compared to other cargos. (Para 34)
Kolkata and Haldia Port System
The Committee welcomes the new initiatives taken for establishing two new Major
Ports in the country. The Committee also observes that the Kolkata Port has been running
in losses and the Haldia Port is earning much more and the Ministry is collecting money

31
from the Haldia Port and spending it on Kolkata Port. However, the Haldia Port is not being
developed, as is required. The Committee recommends that Haldia Port may be developed
to an independent port. (Para 40)
The Committee feels that like so many Ports abroad including the Shanghai Port,
which is the number one port in the world, the Kolkata Port has the potential to grow. But,
for this the port needs to be extended to deep sea. This will enable the port to pick up the
cargo from deep sea from mother ships and then to bring in through the barges into the
mainland. For this, the facilities/manpower with the CIWTC can also be meaningfully
utilized. (Para 41)
Road Connectivity to Ports
The Committee recommends that complete port connectivity is the urgent need of
the hour and remaining work should be completed without further delay. The Ministry of
Shipping may proactively engage itself with the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways
and the State Governments to finish the remaining work. The Committee also recommends
that wherever possible, inland water transport, railways and further sea connectivity may be
explored as a part of a compact and comprehensive modal mix and the Ports should not
depend exclusively on roads. The Committee desires that status report with regard to each
major port road connectivity project may be furnished. (Para 44)
Cabotage Law
The Committee feels that change in Cabotage Law is a welcome step and hopes that
Cabotage regulations at the ICTT would attract more vessels thereby increase the revenue
earning of the Cochin Port. (Para 47)
The Tariff Authority for Major Ports (TAMP)
The Committee recommends that the review of the TAMP should be done on priority
so that the Major Ports may be able to get a level playing field as compared to its counter
parts in the non major ports. (Para 49)
DREDGING CORPORATION OF INDIA (DCI)
The Committee observes that the DCI is presently having a total capacity of 914
lakhs cu.m. per annum. However, as per the data provided by the DCI, the dredging order
with them currently is 514 lakhs cu.m. only. The surplus capacity with them is calculated
to be 400 lakhs cu.m. That means 44% of the total dredging capacity with DCI will remain
unutilized during 2013-14. The Committee feels that the DCI can take up more work and
it, therefore, should try to get more orders. The Committee also notes the fleet strength
of the DCI is going to increase with the addition of new dredgers in the coming months.
(Para 56)
The Committee also notes that the projected dredging capacity during the terminal
year of Twelfth five year plan period for the Major ports would be 1229.24 MT which is
nearly 1.76 times of the existing capacity of the ports. The projected maintenance dredging
requirement of major and minor ports during Twelfth Plan is worked out to be 947.86 MCM.
The expected demand by the end of the Twelfth year plan in terms of cargo handling at
major Ports is 943.06 MT with an estimated annual growth of 10.98%. However, the
dredging orders of major ports awarded to DCI seem to be disappointing. The DCI is
incurring net loss of Rs. 57.15 crore during 2012-13 while the anticipated loss for 2013-14

32
is Rs. 41.45 crore. The Committee recommends that Major Ports should, apart from going
for open tenders for dredging, spare a certain portion of the dredging works to DCI so that
DCI could optimally use its capacity in the coming years. (Para 57)
As regards loss making trends of DCI in the recent years, the Committee also would
like to share its concerns over the observations given in the Audit Para No. 8 of 2012-13
regarding Dredging Corporation of India Limited which commented that:
“Management of Fuel - The Company did not focus on optimizations of expenditure on fuel
and lubricants. The company did not fix the norms for fuel consumptions rate on a
scientific assessment, followed inappropriate purchase procedure for sourcing the
requirement, did not determining competitive prices for procurement of fuel and lubricants
and had inadequate internal control procedures for procurement of fuel and lubricants.
There was no proper system and procedure to ensure regular reconciliation of fuel consumed
with the issues made, prompt raising of claims for fuel escalation as well as realizing the
amounts, linking the guaranteed performance and fuel supply rate agreed as per the
agreements for chartering dredgers. These deficiencies indicate a lack of professional
handling of fuel consumption issues.
As a result of the above deficiencies, the Company lost an opportunity to save Rs. 164.63
crore on fuel consumption during 2007-11. This amount is equal to 49 per cent of to profit
Before Tax (Rs. 335.19) reported by the Company during these years. This shows that a
professional approach in fuel management can bring in tremendous benefits to the Company
and improve its bottom line substantially.” (Para 58)
The Committee understands that audit objection is being separately addressed. It
would like to see its replies about it. The Committee, taking note of the situation,
recommends that the DCI may formulate a revised method for procurement and judicious/
economical use of fuels so that wastages may be minimized to make the company sustain
on its own. (Para 59)
SHIPPING SECTOR
The Committee notes that only 10 per cent of India’s EXIM cargo is carried by the
Indian Flag vessels. Similarly, on the shipbuilding side, our share in the global shipping
market is less than one per cent. The Committee recommends that Ministry of Shipping
needs to attend the sector for improving the prevailing situation. (Para 63)
SHIPPING CORPORATION OF INDIA LTD. (SCI)
The Committee observes that SCI is handling 32.62% of the total Indian tonnage.
However, the Committee also notes that during the year 2011-12, the SCI incurred a net
loss of Rs.428.21 crore. The total earnings and the profit both are on a downward path all
these years. In view of this, the Committee desires that clear vision, appropriate strategy
and professionalism can only help this Navratna PSU to get back its financial health.
(Para 69)
The Committee also observes that the loan liability of SCI has increased from
Rs. 6322.93 crore in 2011-12 to Rs.7289.44 crore. The total liability of SCI has increased
from Rs.7297.18 crore in 2011-12 to Rs.8725.95 crore in the year 2012-13 - an increase of
Rs.1428.77 crore. Compared to the previous year, this increase is about 20%. The
Committee observes that taking the compound interest factor also into consideration; the
total liabilities may overtake the assets of the company within a short span of time. The

33
Committee fears that SCI may go Air India way in the case of financial (mis)management.
The Committee feels that SCI may need to have a re-look at its fleet acquisition orders
already placed with a view to save it from falling into deep troubles. (Para 70)
The Committee notes the submission of SCI that “future acquisitions will be
considered based on need to acquire vessels and subject to availability of resources”. The
Committee feels that the decision on 62 vessel acquisition was taken not according to the
need to acquire vessels but the resources available for such a huge procurement. The
Committee therefore recommends that the remaining orders may not be further processed
unless and until the SCI becomes capable of bearing the liability on its own. (Para 71)
As the freight rates across all segments in the dry bulk sector were stifled by a
subdued commodity demand in the wake of frail global sentiments, the Committee feels
that the fleet acquisition plan of the SCI should be reviewed at appropriate levels and
remedial measures should be taken at the earliest. (Para 72)
COCHIN SHIPYARD LIMITED (CSL)
The Committee hopes that implementation of the above schemes will help the yard
to achieve higher growth and emerge as an internationally competitive shipyard to construct
world class ships and to become market leader in ship repair. (Para 74)
Indian Maritime University (IMU)
The Committee is happy to note that our well trained human resources have earned
name and fame across the world and the various courses offered by the IMU has enabled
us to meet the manpower requirement in the maritime sector. Since many posts in the
shipping sector under the Ministry itself are lying vacant, the Committee hopes the pass out
students will be able to find better employability in future. (Para 79)
The Committee has observed that the spending pattern of the IMU is satisfactory as
they have fully utilized the allocations during the years 2011-12 and 2012-13. The
Committee does not agree with the reduction of BE allocation at the RE stage during 2012-
13. This cut has been made at a time the university was carrying out significant
infrastructure development activities at its various campuses. However, the reduced
allocations has compelled the IMU to slowdown the constructions and thereby denying the
opportunity for admissions to many eligible students. The Committee feels concerned about
this and recommends that enough allocation may be made to the IMU in completing its
expansion projects so that eligible students may get admissions. (Para 80)
DIRECTORATE GENERAL OF LIGHTHOUSES AND LIGHTSHIPS
The Committee observes that the spending pattern of DGLL is far from satisfactory.
The allocations at RE during Eleventh Plan was Rs.243.00 crore of which the actual spending
was Rs.147.82 crore only. This is 60.83% of the GBS. The Committee also notes that many
of the projects proposed in the year 2003 are pending for environmental clearances even
though more than 10 years have passed. The Committee is doubtful about the fate of these
projects and recommends for a well organized way of planning and execution at the
administrative levels so that the planned projects may be completed as per schedule and the
amount spent is not wasted. (Para 86)
The Committee observes that as per the outcome budget, several schemes are
proposed to be completed within the financial year 2013-14 with a total expenditure of

34
Rs.95.15 crore. The Committee hopes that the works will be completed within the time limit
as fixed by DGLL. The Committee recommends that the new schemes also may be
implemented as per the schedule so that the funds allocated may be utilized optimally.
(Para 87)
The Committee notes the initiatives taken by the Ministry in promoting tourism-
through lighthouses and recommends that the techno - economic feasibility report may be
examined expeditiously. The Committee recommends that all lighthouses which are
historically important should be identified and placed in the map of light house tourism.
(Para 89)
INLAND WATERWAY AUTHORITY OF INDIA (IWAI)
97. The Committee is not satisfied with the pace at which the allocations are utilized
during the year 2012-13. The Committee also observes that waterways nos. 4 and 5, declared
in 2008 are still lying in papers only and have not become operational due to paucity of
funds. At the same time, IWAI has failed to expend its funds fully as they have managed
to utilise only Rs.65 crore till December, 2012 which became Rs. 146 crore till March, 2013.
This shows that bulk of the grants was expended within a period of 3 months. The
Committee observes that IWAI was in a spending spree during the closing months of 2012-13.
The Committee does not approve of this strategy of last-minute rush for spending by IWAI
which does not augur well for the health of an organization. (Para 97 )
The Committee observes that the total investment made for the development of IWT
in the last 25 years is just Rs.1100 crore. This is very meager in view of inland waterways
potential that we have. In view of our large number of major rivers and the role played by
inland water transport in the past, the Committee strongly recommends for strengthening
of the IWT sector in a big way which is a very cost effective and an environment friendly
mode of transport. The Committee is happy to see that Rs. 1500 crore has been given for
IWAI which is much more than total allocation to this sector so far. It hopes that the
Authority will be able to fruitfully utilize the funds during 2013-14. (Para 98)
99. The Committee feels that in view of vast potential for IWT sector, country has to
work aggressively in coming years for strengthening of IWAI by way of providing extra
manpower, technical know how, basic infrastructure, modern navigational facilities, berths
Jetties, etc., IWAI has to execute its projects and effectively utilize its capacity and funds
at hand. The Committee reiterates its recommendation that, experienced hands idling at
CIWTC and its infrastructure,  equipments, etc., may be engaged in the activities of IWAI.
In addition to this, IWAI may assess the manpower requirement in the coming days so as
to meet the requirement of manpower in its development projects. (Para 99)
The Committee has observed the growth of cargo transport during the period 2004-
05 to 2011-12 in two stretches, i.e. , Goa-Maharashtra and Kolkata-Bangladesh. The
Committee is, however, not satisfied on the prospects of other areas which are having ample
potential for cargo transportation. The Committee recommends that linking of waterways to
ports will enable an increased traffic movement in the IWT mode in the potential areas
especially those stretches which are still unutilized. In this regard Committee also
reiterates its Recommendations contained in its 189
th Report “Development of National
Waterways- Potential and Challenges which inter-alia  States:
“the Committee recommends that linking of ports in Karnataka, Gujarat and Tamil
Nadu also should be worked out as these states are having in-bound and out-bound
bulk cargo potential. The Committee recommends for developing the West coast –

35
Kandla, Mumbai, Murmogao, Kochi – and East coast – Kolkata, Paradip,
Vishakhapatnam, Chennai – coastal freight corridors. Investing in these corridors
will augment scale and improve the economics for coastal shipping, making it an
attractive alternative to other modes. Also, it will improve last mile road and rail
connectivity to and from ports.”
(Para 102)
The Committee, however is not satisfied with the pace of development of the NWs
4&5 which were declared way back in 2008. The Committee therefore recommends that the
Government should make the waterways fully functional which is the need of the hour. The
Committee hopes that more funds will be earmarked for the NWs 4&5 at the RE stage.
(Para 104)
CENTRAL INLAND WATER TRANSPORT CORPORATION LTD. (CIWTC)
The Committee reiterates its earlier recommendation that the employees of the
CIWTC are now surplus with them, who are experienced in the various fields of waterway
transportation. The Committee further recommends that Government may actively consider
the absorption of the experienced manpower of the CIWTC with the IWAI. In addition to
this, the request of CIWTC may be considered favorably by the Ministry for additional
funds of Rs.239.36 crore for meeting various expenses. (Para 107)
PIRACY, SAFETY AND SECURITY
The Committee is concerned about the increasing cases of piracy and notes the
various initiatives taken for protecting the merchant ships from pirate attacks. The
Committee also shares the concerns of the Ministry of Shipping as regards deploying armed
guards in the vessels to deter the pirates on the high seas. The Committee feels that joint
efforts should be made with other coastal countries in strengthening security of our ships
passing through area of potential threat. (Para 113)
The Committee notes the steps taken to prevent abandoning of ships in the Indian
waters. The Committee also draws the attention towards an abandoned ship causing damage
to the Pamban Bridge of Rameshwaram. The Committee recommends that the Ministry of
Shipping may take the immediate steps to move away the ship from the site to a safe area
as a first step. The Committee also recommends for taking stringent action against the ship
owner and the Committee may be informed about the follow up action in this matter.
(Para 114)
NORTH EAST REGION
The Committee recommends that Ministry of Shipping should work out the viable
plans for the North East separately keeping the requirement of each state so that the
alocations may be utilized for the development of the entire region. (Para 117)
The Committee also notes that lot of time and energy is wasted in transporting
equipment to the North-East. The only way, through which we can save this, is water
protocol with Bangladesh. If it is linked up to Chittagong, cargo from there can go straight
into the North-East. The Committee observes that if Dhubri, the lifeline for that entire
area, is developed and use Chittagong, the whole of North-East will get benefit out of it.
Therefore, the Committee recommends that this should be done expeditiously. (Para 118)
The Committee also notes that in addition to this, the curise tourism through the
wild life safaris, the villages, tea gardens, etc., also will be a boosting factor for the tourism

36
activities in the Region. The Committee recommends that the 10% allocation of the GBS
need to be properly utilized in the IWT sector and of the cruise tourism in the NE Region.
(Para 119)
OTHER ISSUES
The Committee fails to understand the motive behind handing over of a profitable
entity to the private hands. The Committee also recalls the recent incidents that happened
at the Haldia Dock Complex where the two terminals were abruptly closed by the private
operator causing irreparable loss to the Government. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that Government should review any such decision, if taken, as privatization of
profitable work at the Visakhapatnam Port. (Para 121)
The Committee observes that public money goes into the building, development and
upkeep of our Public sector ports. When the matters of generating revenue out of it come,
these should not be flowing into private hands. Therefore, the Committee recommends that
this reported pilferage at Haldia Port should be checked at once and a status report should
be furnished to the Committee in this regard. The Committee also recommends that the
Ministry of Shipping should move a bill for making the necessary amendments to the Major
Port Trust Act. (Para 124)
GENERAL OBSERV ATIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS
The Committee observes that Fifty-six per cent of the GBS goes to the shipping
sector but there is consistent decline in the share of Indian ships in the overseas trade
from 31.5 per cent in 2000 to 13.7 per cent in 2005 and further to 7.95 per cent in 2011.
Moreover, Indian vessels are older than the international average. These are ageing very
fast. About 42 per cent of the fleet is over 20 years of age and another 11 per cent in the
age group of 16 to 20 years. In terms of container ship operation, India’s world share is
1.74 per cent. Our country’s share is only 0.7 per cent in terms of compensated gross
tonnage in the world. India is ranked 22
nd in 2011 according to UNCTAD liner shipping
industry index, one step down from 21 st position in 2004. (Para 125)
During 2012-13, major and non-major ports in India registered an increase of only
1.8 per cent in cargo throughput over 2011-12. This is mainly attributable to a decline of
3.3 per cent in the cargo handled at major ports. That is, major ports have been in the
negative and minor are growing very fast. In contrast, non-major ports’ growth increased
to 10.3 per cent in the first half of 2012-13 compared to 8.2 per cent in the corresponding
period of 2011-12. (Para 126)
The Committee observes that earlier, the SCI had decided to invest in the Vizhinjam
Port Project and no development took place in this regard later on. The natural advantages
for a 16M draft without any major dredging works are available at Vizhinjam. However, the
Ministry of Shipping has not taken any interest in materializing the project to a reality. The
proposed port is able to handle the modern mother ships and that it may be able to grab
even the business of the nearest international ports. The Committee recommends that the
Ministry of Shipping may take necessary step with the State Government to develop this
port without delay. (Para 127)
The Committee observes that major ports in the country were functioning more like
landlords than mercantile business hubs so far as use of port assets are concerned. Some
of the major ports are also acting like moneylenders because they have a lot of money
parked in their kitty. The Committee feels bad that the ports cannot decide as to how to

37
spend the amount on their modernization and expansion. The Committee recommends that
these are serious issues which need to be addressed immediately. (Para 128)
Similarly, the Committee is highly concerned about the present condition of
Murmugao Port and recommends, going into handling diversified cargo other than mineral
ores to bring it back to sustenance level. The Committee also directs to consider using port
facilities for cruise tourism activities in Goa which has lot of potential to generate revenue.
(Para 129)

REPORT
The Ministry of Tourism is the nodal agency for the formulation of national policies and
programmes for the development and promotion of tourism in the country. In the process, the
Ministry consults and collaborates with other stakeholders in the sector including various Central
Ministries/agencies, the State Governments/Union Territory Administrations and the representatives
of the private sector.
2. The administrative head of the Ministry is the Secretary (Tourism). The Secretary also acts
as the Director General (DG) Tourism. Directorate General of Tourism has a field formation of 20
offices within the country and 14 offices abroad and one sub-ordinate office/project i.e. Indian
Institute of Skiing and Mountaineering (IISM)/Gulmarg Winter Sports Project. The overseas offices
are primarily responsible for tourism promotion and marketing in their respective areas and the field
offices in India are responsible for providing information service to tourists and to monitor the
progress of field projects.
3. Tourism is promoted within India primarily by the Ministry of Tourism with the help of 5
Regional Offices and 15 Sub-Offices under them, with the involvement of the State Governments
and with the help of modern and conventional tools of promotion.
4. India Tourism Development Corporation (ITDC) is the only public sector undertaking under
the Ministry of Tourism.
5. The Ministry also has the following autonomous institutions:
(i) Indian Institutes of Tourism and Travel Management (IITTM).
(ii) National Council for Hotel Management and Catering Technology (NCHMCT), and the
21 Institutes of Hotel Management (IHMs).
6. Major Programmes/Schemes of the Ministry of Tourism are:-
1. Product/Infrastructure Development for Destinations and Circuits
2. Overseas Promotion and Publicity including Market Development Assistance
3. Assistance to IHMs/FCIs/IITTM/NIWS/NCHMCT etc.
4. Domestic Promotion and Publicity including Hospitality
5. Incentives to Accommodation Infrastructure
6. Capacity Building for Service Providers
7. Computerization and Information Technology
8. Assistance for Large Revenue Generating Projects
9. Externally Aided Projects including Buddhist Centres
10. Market Research Professional Services including 20 years Perspective Plans
11. Creation of Land Bank for Hotels
12. Assistance to Central Agencies for Tourism Infrastructure Development
13. Construction of Building for IISM at Gulmarg, Kashmir

10. The Committee notes that during Eleventh Plan period, the Ministry of Tourism
could spend Rs.4896 crore out of the Rs.4953 crore allocated at RE, which is almost 98%
of the total allocations. The Committee also notes that the Ministry of Tourism has
sanctioned 1226 tourism projects for an amount of Rs.4090 crore during the Eleventh Five
Year Plan. But the Committee was not informed about the completion of these projects or
the current status of these projects. It hopes that after sanctioning the projects and
releasing the money, the Ministry of Tourism is monitoring its implementation by the State

4
Governments. It is learnt that the State Governments are diverting these funds according
to their own priority. The Committee recommends that the Ministry should actively pursue
each of these projects sanctioned to ensure that the sanctioned amount is utilized in the
prescribed manner for the approved project only.
11. The Committee observes that under these schemes, Union territories appear to have
been neglected as the data shows that very few projects were sanctioned to them. For
example, Lakshadweep–1, Daman and Diu–1, Dadra and Nagarhaveli–3, and nothing for
Andaman and Nicobar islands. The exceptions were Puducherry-20 and Chandigarh-11. If
non-receipt of the proposal has been the reason, the Committee recommends that the
Ministry of Tourism should guide and encourage these union territories to submit viable
projects so that they may also get the fund allocations under these very important schemes.
These areas have ample potential for tourism development.
12. The Committee also appreciates the NE-States on their eagerness in implementing
tourism projects during the Eleventh Plan period. All the NE States have got good amount
of allocations and that Committee hopes that all these projects are being implemented
earnestly and timely. This will increase the tourist visits in this region which will improve
their over all economic condition in the coming years.
13. The Committee also observes that bigger States having immense potential for
tourism development, particularly pilgrimage, wild life and niche tourism, have not had
commensurate projects/funds under these schemes. The Committee recommends that more
attention should be given during Twelfth Plan to those States which were yet to exploit their
potential for tourism development.

15. The Ministry of Tourism has informed that against Rs.1773.79 crore sought as Plan
allocation for the year 2013-14, Planning Commission allocated only Rs.1282.00 crore. The
Working Group on Tourism recommended various strategies to be taken for development and
promotion of tourism during Twelfth Plan period. Hence, substantial increases for major plan/
schemes were proposed by the Ministry of Tourism to achieve the desired targets. In view of the
reduced budget outlay it will be difficult to achieve the desired targets under all major schemes
such as product/infrastructure Development for Destination and Circuits, overseas promotion and
publicity, Assistance to IHMs/FCIs, domestic promotion and publicity etc.
16. During the course of evidence the Committee asked for the reasons behind the reduced
allocations at RE stage and the under-utilization of funds which was a deviation from the normal
practice of the Ministry of Tourism during the last many years. Secretary, Tourism explained that
due to a change in the interpretation in the norms for fund disbursement, the Ministry could not
spend last year Rs.360 crores.

6
17. The Secretary continued that due to a change in the interpretation of the rules regarding
utilization certificates by the Ministry of Finance, funds could not be allocated to various schemes
implemented by the Ministry. For instance, the Product Infrastructure Development for destination
and Circuits (PIDDC) were given Rs.575 crores but this year it has been reduced to 400 crores.
It is a drop of almost 40 per cent because the Ministry knows that with the new interpretation
of the rules they may not able to spend the allocation. The Secretary explained that during the year
2012-13, the Ministry of Finance insisted that utilization certificates of all the money allocated up
to the year 2010-11 should be obtained before releasing any money to the States. Even if, a single
scheme is lagging behind and the utilization certificates are not submitted by the concerned States,
the entire fund allocation to all the schemes of that particular State should be stopped.
18. Earlier the Ministry of Tourism was releasing 80 per cent of the allocation as first installment
and the utilization certificates were insisted only after a period of 18 months. The utilization
certificates were delayed due to delay in planning, acquisition of land, tendering, getting the DPR
done, allotment of work, etc. These preliminary things may take 14 to 15 months and during this
entire period they could not spend much of the allocation as the project will take off only after
completing all the above preliminary works. Therefore, all those schemes for which funds were
allocated were lagging behind and they could not submit the utilization certificate in time.
19. Since the Finance Ministry has insisted for the utilization certificates, the Ministry of
Tourism has changed the pattern of allocation and now the Ministry is allocating 20 per cent as
the first installment which is essential for completing all the preliminary works. Thereafter, they are
allocating 60 per cent for executing the work and finally 20 per cent as the last installment. In
fact, the Ministry of Tourism has pleaded with the Finance Ministry to permit them to adjust the
unspent balance with that particular State from one project to another, but that was also not agreed
to. Earlier the practice was that whatever the fund was available with the particular State was
readjusted against the active schemes within that State.
20. This Committee has always been arguing the case of Ministry of Tourism for
enhanced allocations every year during the examination of its Demands for Grants. The
Planning Commission, however, appears to have been reluctant to do so for reasons best
known to it. Normally, it does not give any reasons for this to a Ministry. During current
year also, only Rs.1282.00 crore has been allocated to the Ministry against a projected
demand of Rs.1773.79 crore. The Committee, keeping in view the various targets fixed for
development and promotion of tourism infrastructure, creating skilled and trained
manpower, exploring new tourism projects etc., reiterates its recommendation for providing
additional funds to the Ministry of Tourism so that the ideal of linking tourism with
employment generation and poverty alleviation could be achieved in reality.
21. The Committee notes that during the Eleventh Plan period, right from the opening
years, the spending had remained more than 98%. However, in the opening year (2012-13)
of the Twelfth Plan, the spending pattern had not been so. The BE 2012-13 stood at Rs.1210
crores which was reduced at the RE to Rs.950 crore. But only Rs.724.34 crore could be spent
upto February, 2013. If this spending is analyzed on the basis of the BE allocation of
Rs.1210 crore during the period, it forms only 60% of it. The Committee feels that there
are failures on the part of the Ministry in dealing with plan schemes whatever be the
adverse policy changes. The Ministry should have taken up the matter at the appropriate
Governmental levels, rather than blaming the system. The Committee recommends that
Ministry of Tourism needs to be more proactive and work as facilitator for implementation
of its schemes.
22. The Committee notes that the Ministry has not projected their achievement in
measurable terms by providing required information in quantified and comparable format to

7
the Committee. That would have helped the Committee to understand and appreciate the
real problems before the Ministry and concretize its opinion accordingly. Next time the
Committee would like to have information in user friendly format for its purpose.
23. The Committee also notes that some of the schemes such as incentives to
accommodation, assistance to large revenue generating projects, creation of land banks, etc.
are languishing for many years. The Committee recommends that these schemes may be
reviewed so that it may accomplish its targets.
24. The Committee observes that the strict guidelines on adherence to the utilization
certificate of each projects and further allocation of funds strictly thereafter has been able
to bring some accountability and discipline in the spending pattern of the Ministry. However,
the Committee is of the opinion that such measures should be based on practical
consideration as the infrastructure projects are required to get various sanctions/clearances
from so many agencies under different Ministries. Usually, the projects, involving land
acquisition and environment clearance are the most time consuming. Therefore, keeping all
these matters in mind, if the interpretation of rules/guidelines on fund disbursement
scheme has posed any problem to the ministries, it should be taken up at appropriate levels
and resolved as soon as possible.
25. The Committee notes that the Twelfth Plan has given emphasis to rural tourism and
projected tourism as a tool to reduce poverty. The Committee, however, finds no special
schemes or efforts to promote the rural tourism or spread the idea of tourism as a mass
activity. The Committee notes in the Budget 2013-14, just routine programmes which are
going on for the last so many years.
26. The Committee is also of the view that the plans and programmes of the Ministry
of Tourism should be aimed at positioning tourism as a major contributor of economic
growth and harness its direct and multiplier effects for employment and poverty eradication
in an environmentally sustainable manner. The schemes taken up by the Ministry should
be aimed at enhancing employment in the activities relating to tourism sector as well as at
fostering economic integration through developing linkages with other sectors.
27. The Committee further recommends that with the aim to achieve socio-economic
development in rural areas which have core competence in arts, crafts, heritage etc., the
Ministry of Tourism should provide assistance for development of tourism infrastructure and
capacity building of rural inhabitants in the States. The Ministry need to pursue with the
State Governments for completion of rural tourism projects sanctioned in a particular
financial year within a fixed time-frame.
PRODUCT/INFRASTRUCTURE DEVELOPMENT FOR DESTINATIONS AND CIRCUITS
28. The Plan Allocation during 2013-14 is Rs.400.00 crore under Product/Infrastructure
Development for Destinations and Circuits (PIDDC). The allocation for 2012-13 was Rs.575.00
crore in BE which was reduced to Rs.480.00 crore in RE. The expenditure upto February, 2013
is given to be Rs.343.71 crore. The actual expenditure under PIDDC during 2011-12 was
Rs.599.20 crore.
29. Ministry of Tourism has informed that under the Centrally Sponsored Scheme of Product/
Infrastructure Development for Destinations and Circuits, they extend Central Financial Assistance
to the State Governments/Union territory Administrations for tourism projects, identified in
consultation with them, for the improvement of existing tourism products and also for developing
new ones. 100% Central Assistance is given under the scheme for development of destinations/
circuits including mega projects, and also for rural tourism infrastructure development.

8
30. The Ministry of Tourism provides financial assistance upto Rs.5.00 crore for the
development of destinations and Rs.8.00 crore for circuits. The upper limits of financial assistance
for development of mega destinations and circuits are Rs.25 crore and Rs.50 crore respectively.
For rural tourism infrastructure development, the thrust is on development of tourism infrastructure
at the identified rural tourism sites so that socio-economic benefits of tourism reach to the rural
community. A maximum of Rs.50.00 lakh is sanctioned for each project.
31. The Ministry has launched a scheme for development of nationally and internationally
important destinations and circuits through Mega Projects. So far, 54 mega projects have been
identified, out of which 40 projects have already been sanctioned. The mega projects are a
judicious mix of culture, heritage, spiritual and eco-tourism and aim to give tourists a holistic
perspective.
32. To achieve a higher level of coordination between various Ministries on issues of tourism
development, an Inter-Ministerial Coordination Committee for Tourism Sector (IMCCTS) was set
up in 2011-12 under the Chairmanship of Principal Secretary to the Prime Minister.
33. The scheme of Rural Tourism was started by the Ministry in 2002-03 with the objective
of showcasing rural life, art, culture and heritage at rural locations and in villages, which have core
competence in art & craft, handloom, and textiles as also an asset base in the natural environment.
It aimed to benefit the local community economically and socially, as well as to enable interaction
between tourists and local population for a mutually enriching experience.
34. Under this Scheme, the development/strengthening of physical infrastructure at the identified
rural site is supplemented by the capacity building of the local population to develop the identified
site as a rural tourism product. Rural tourism projects at 186 villages in 29 States/Union territories
have been sanctioned by the Ministry of Tourism since the inception of the scheme. 56 of these
sites are located in the North–Eastern region. A total amount of Rs 55.40 crores was sanctioned
for Rural Tourism projects during the Eleventh Five Year Plan. Projects at 90 sites have been
completed by December, 2012.
35. During the Twelfth Five Year Plan, the present scheme of Rural Tourism is being replaced
with the scheme of Rural Tourism Cluster. The modified scheme aims at developing a cluster of
villages a tourism product.
36. The Secretary, Tourism during the meeting informed about change in the funding pattern
for the tourism projects from the earlier pattern of 80% and the 20% to 20%-60%-20% for which
18 months time has been allowed for making expenditure at each phase.
37. The Committee notes that allocations for PIDDC scheme are getting reduced as
compared to allocations made during 2011-12 and 2012-13. The Committee also notes that
current year allocation stands further reduced at Rs.400 crore. The Committee thus finds
a regular reduction in allocation from the 2011-12 onwards. A re-interpretation of the
guidelines for funds disbursal in this regard was given as the reason. The Ministry of
Finance regulations provides that spending pattern of the first quarter is criteria for getting
eligible for subsequent allocations on various schemes of the States. The Committee
observes that these guidelines may have adverse impact on other projects also and in such
a case no scheme could be properly implemented by the States. The Committee recommends
that the utilization certificates may be obtained scheme/project-wise. If a particular scheme/
project is lagging behind in its execution, it should not be a reason to deny fund to the
other schemes/projects of the State. The Committee recommends that the guidelines on the
utilization certificates may be reviewed by the Ministry of Finance so that the proposed
projects may not be affected by the bottlenecks in the fund allocation norms.

9
38. The Committee observes that eventhough the rural tourism scheme was started in
the year 2002-03, the scheme has not made much progress so far. Only 186 projects have
been sanctioned since the inception of the scheme. The completion status is less than 50%
as only 90 projects out of 186 have been completed during a decade, i.e., 2002-2012. Now
the scheme has been replaced with Rural Tourism Cluster scheme. The Committee observes
that undue delay in implementing the scheme is not acceptable. The Committee
recommends that the Ministry of Tourism may set the guidelines in such a way that the
scheme may yield results at the earliest.
39. The Committee recommends that Ministry of Tourism should ensure convergence of
resources and expertise through coordinated efforts with State/UT Governments and
stakeholders for an integrated and intensive development of tourism infrastructure in the
country through careful planning and execution while giving importance for improvement in
accessibility, environmental and other aspects.
40. The Committee notes that some projects identified in the years 2008-09, 2009-10 or
2010-11 are yet to take off like Aurangabad destinations of Maharashtra, Eco and Adventure
circuit, Arunachal Pradesh, Mubarak Mandi Heritage, Jammu and Kashmir etc. as no fund
allocations have been made for these so far. The Committee recommends that the
concerned State Governments may be encouraged to take the follow-up actions in these
regards and the funds may be granted in each case at the earliest.
DOMESTIC CAMPAIGN
41. The Secretary, Tourism submitted that as far as domestic campaign to promote tourism is
concerned, it is the social awareness campaign that the Ministry undertakes, and does not promote
individual destinations, with the exception of the North-East and Jammu and Kashmir. Ministry of
Tourism just had a very successful International Tourism Mart for the North-East, at Guwahati.
Such a Mart is organized only for the North-East and not for any other Indian State.
42. Ministry of Tourism also provides financial assistance to tourism service providers approved
by the Ministry of Tourism, Government of India or by the State Tourism Department in the case
of North Eastern States and Jammu and Kashmir for participation in travel marts, annual
conventions of Indian Association of Tour Operators/Travel Agents Association of India/Association
of Domestic Tour Operators of India/Adventure Tour Operators Association/Federation of Hotels
and Restaurants Association of India/Hotels Association of India or any other National level Travel/
Tour Association approved/sponsored/recognized by MOT.
43. The various domestic campaign initiatives undertaken by the Ministry of Tourism during the
year 2012-13 included the following:
✜ Social Awareness Campaigns were released on Doordarshan in July, 2012 and in
September–October, 2012. Campaigns on Social Awareness with the themes of
Atithidevo Bhava, Campaign Clean India and Hunar Se Rozgar were released on Radio
Channels in July, 2012.
✜ The Ministry released campaigns on Doordarshan to promote tourism in the North East
Region and the State of Jammu and Kashmir in September–October, 2012.
✜ An outdoor campaign was undertaken in the T3 Terminal of the Delhi Airport and in
the arrival hall of Mumbai International Airport to showcase the tourism destinations
and products of the country.

10
✜ Campaign as part of Campaign Clean India was undertaken on FM Radio Stations
across the country as well as on Railway Tickets to promote awareness about the need
for Cleanliness and Hygiene.
✜ A Social Awareness Campaign is also being undertaken on Digital Cinema Screens
across the country.
44. The total expenditure up to February, 2013 under the head Domestic Promotion and
Publicity including Hospitality (DPPH) out of the RE amount of Rs.65.00 crore during 2012-13 was
Rs.55.62 crore. During the year 2013-14 the amount sanctioned is Rs.120.00 crore.
45. The Committee was informed by the Ministry that the Domestic Television Campaigns on
Social Awareness, North-East and Jammu and Kashmir on private television channels could not be
undertaken due to rate revision and changes in the guidelines of Directorate of Advertising and
Visual Publicity (DAVP) which resulted in reduced expenditure.
46. The Ministry proposes following activities under the head Domestic Promotion and Publicity
including Hospitality (DPPH) during 2013-14:
• Social Awareness Campaigns in the print and electronic (television and radio) media

• Advertising Campaigns in the print and electronic (television and radio) to promote

• Luxury Tax: The State Governments/UTs have the power to levy luxury tax on hotel

of luxury tax is on printed tariff as against the actual tariff paid by the visitor. The
actual tax rates shoot of up to 30% as the tariff charged can be substantially less than

• Taxes on Food and Beverages : V AT on food items ranges from 5% to 16.84% in
various states. Similarly, V AT on liquor varies from 13% to 58%. In addition, from

Tourist Transport Association (ITTA), for a 3 day package between Delhi, Agra and
Jaipur, the total rate and passenger tax paid is 23% of the package cost.

compared to the competing destinations. This has not only deterred the domestic travel
but also made the packages for international tourists costly.
94. The Committee observes that the luxury tax on the hotel tariff ranges from 4% to
20% which may shoot up to 30% in the off season. Also the V AT on food items ranges from
5% to 16.84%. Tourist used to get discounts on the printed rates of room rent etc during
the off season but the tax should be paid on the original rate. The Committee recommends
that the tax concern of the tourism industry may favourably be considered.

multiplicity of taxes at inter-state borders. This is acting as an impediment to seamless

ENVIRONMENT AND TOURISM
96. The Ministry of Tourism has given that as per the Supreme Court directions, the Ministry
of Environment and Forests has issued guidelines for tourism activities in tiger reserves in the
country. As per this guideline, no tourism activity is permitted in the core areas of Tiger reserves.
The Ministry of Tourism is in favour of regulated tourism in protected areas of the country. The
Ministry of Tourism does not favour a total ban in protected Areas including Tiger Reserves.
International Practices/best National practices should be taken into consideration by the Ministry of
Environment and Forests in finalizing eco-tourism guidelines for Protected Areas. Regulated and
controlled tourism in protected Areas is found to be generally helpful globally in conservation
efforts for wildlife in different countries.
97. As per these guidelines, hotels at the project stage itself are required to incorporate
various eco-friendly measures like sewage treatment plant (STP), rain water harvesting system,
waste management system etc. Once the hotel is operational, it can apply for classification under
a Star category to the Hotel and Restaurant Approval Classification Committee (HRACC) of the
Ministry. During the physical inspection of the hotel by the HRACC Committee, it is ensured that
in addition to the aforementioned measures, other measures like pollution control, introduction of
non-CFC equipment for refrigeration and air conditioning, measures for energy and water
conservation are also undertaken by the hotel. Under the guidelines for project level and
classification/re-classification of operational hotels it has been prescribed that the architecture of
the hotel buildings in hilly and ecologically fragile areas should keep in mind sustainability and
energy efficiency and as far as possible be in conformity with the local ethos and use local
materials.
98. The guidelines for tourism in and around Tiger reserves titled ‘National Tiger Conservation
Authority (Normative Standards for Tourism activities and Project Tiger) Guidelines, 2012' would
promote regulated tourism benefiting wildlife conservation and local communities.
99. As per these guidelines, all the States/UT Administrations have been asked to notify the
State-level eco-tourism strategy within a year from the date of notification of these guidelines. The
guidelines have recommended identification and monitoring of ecologically sensitive areas
surrounding the tiger reserves to ensure ecological integrity of corridor/buffer areas which will
prevent encroachment.
100. The Committee recommends that tourism activities should be based on scientific
carrying capacity and sustainability principles. As such, the normal peaceful living of the
wild life should not be disturbed by the tourism activities. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that the ‘National Tiger Conservation Authority (Normative Standards for
Tourism activities and Project Tiger) Guidelines, 2012' should strictly be adhered to, for an
eco-friendly tourism development in the country.
101. The hotel projects also need to follow the guidelines as regards conservation of
natural resources, increased use of recycled products, solar energy, water conservation like
rain water harvesting etc. The Committee recommends that Ministry of Tourism should
strictly monitor other measures like pollution control, introduction of non-CFC equipment

21
for refrigeration and airconditioning, measures for energy and water conservation which are
to be undertaken by the hotels.
102. The Committee recommends that tourism activities at the protected areas should be
regulated as per the environment protection guidelines. No development is sustainable if it
is acted against the existence of nature. The Committee recommends that there should be
sincere efforts in environment protection while enhancing tourism facilities.

minimum 8th class pass, under “Hunar Se Rozgar” scheme. ITDC is also paying a scholarship of
Rs. 1400 as Ashok Fellowship to each trainee through its own resources. ITDC has launched a
community based development programme ‘Ashok Prayas’ and is helping in running centres for
skill development for marginalized and deprived children and women. On successful completion of
the training, it also assists the students in finding suitable placements.
107. The Committee was given to understand that occupancy in ITDC hotels has remained
40-50 percent even in the peak seasons. The Committee feels this is on low side and does
not know the reasons for this. ITDC has to function and compete with the professionally-
managed hotels in private sector. Therefore, it has to be competitive as regards services
offered by them.

22
108. The Committee noticed that the websites of the Ministry of Tourism or the Incredible
India has no advertisement of ITDC hotels. The Committee feels that proper links and
advertisements about ITDC Hotels may be given in all the websites under the Ministry of
Tourism. The Committee feels that ITDC hotels should also be marketed as part of the
overseas campaign.
109. The Committee notes that the financial performance of ITDC has improved during
the last two years. The Committee is hopeful that ITDC would keep its recovery path intact
in the coming years. The Committee appreciates ITDC on performing its social commitment
by extending its help organizing training of youth and contributing to the Clean India
Campaign.
110. The Committee recommends that light and sound shows have to be introduced in
other tourist spots of the country so that the famous tourist places may be made more
attractive to the visitors. Simulator based light and sound shows as available in the
Chardham Temple, Gangtok can be experimented in other parts of the country with
different themes. ITDC may take the initiative in this regard.
VISA ON ARRIV AL
111. As a facilitative measure to attract more foreign tourists to India, the Government launched
a scheme of Tourist Visa on Arrival (TVOA) for the nationals of five countries namely Finland,
Japan, Luxembourg, New Zealand and Singapore with effect from 1.1.2010 as a pilot project for
one year. The scheme was found to be useful by foreign nationals. The Government of India
extended the TVOA scheme for the nationals of the above mentioned five countries. Further, the
TVOA scheme was extended to the nationals of Cambodia, Laos, Philippines and Vietnam with
effect from 1.1.2011 and the nationals of Indonesia and Myanmar with effect from 28.1.2011.
Presently the scheme is available to the nationals of eleven countries. TVOA facility is presently
available at the international airports of Delhi, Mumbai, and Chennai and Kolkata.
112. An independent study conducted by the Indian Institute of Tourism and Travel Management
(IITTM) has noted that TVOA scheme has a significant and positive impact on the decision to
travel to India. This scheme needs to be expanded to cover more countries and more ports of
entry. The Ministry of Tourism had proposed extension of TVOA to the following markets:
(i) Germany, France, Spain, Poland, Sweden and Norway to cover the European and
Scandinavian countries which are key inbound markets
(ii) Russia, Ukraine, Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan to cover the emerging markets from the
CIS countries
(iii) Brazil and South Africa to cover foster IBSA Cooperation and Trinidad and Tobago to
foster our historical links
(iv) Thailand, Malaysia and Brunei to cover all the ASEAN countries which will be
consistent with our look east policy
113. The Ministry of Tourism had also proposed extension of TVOA to more airports namely
Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Kochi, Goa, Bodhgaya and Thiruvananthapuram.
114. The Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) has recently informed that a decision has been taken
not to extend the TVOA facility to any other country for the present. However, they agreed to the

23
TVOA scheme being extended to International Airports like Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Kochi, Goa and
Thiruvananthapuram once the proper infrastructure is in place.
115. Keeping in view the recent travel trends, the Ministry of Tourism now also proposes TVOA
scheme for South Korea, which is a very important tourist generating market.
116. As proposed by Ministry of Tourism, the Ministry of External Affairs, has decided to grant
‘Long Term Tourist Visas’ of five (05) years duration with multiple entry facilities carrying a
stipulation of 90 days of each visit on a pilot basis to the nationals of the following 18 selected
countries:–
(1) France (2) Germany (3) Luxembourg (4) Netherlands (5) Belgium (6) Finland (7) Spain
(8) Switzerland (9) Norway (10) Iceland (11) New Zealand (12) Japan (13) South Korea
(14) Argentina (15) Brazil (16) Chile (17) Mexico (18) Vietnam.
117. The Secretary Tourism during the course of evidence stated that tourist visa on arrival has
improved in the last two years. Still, there are two-three major stumblingblocks in this regard. For
example, Japanese and German tourists have language problem as tourists cannot read/write
English. Therefore, unscrupulous elements are exploiting potential tourists in Japan, Germany and
Korea because they interpret the visa form and charge hefty sums for this. Regarding North-East,
he said, there is one problem – the inner line permit can be got by a tourist one but, unfortunately,
they don’t get the permit while leaving the country. They have to reach India before the permit
is issued, still not certain whether they will go to that part of the North-East or not. This is very
disconcerting for the foreigners’.
118. The Committee notes the recent development in the visa-on Arrival Policy. The
Committee is surprised to hear that because of non-availability of foreign language experts
of Japanese, German etc. the Ministry is seeking help from locals for the visa related
issues in the foreign countries.
119. The Committee recommends that our visa forms should be bilingual incorporating
the local language of the country. This will facilitate the tourists and increase their
confidence in visiting our country. The Tourism promotion offices should play a major role
in this regard. The Committee has reason to believe that many of our Tourism promotion
offices are filled up with deputationists who have no idea about tourism of India or the local
languages of the countries they are posted.
120. The Committee recommends that there should be clarity in issuance of inner-line
permits for the North-East. The Ministry of Tourism should take up the issue with the
Ministry of Home Affairs to clear all confusions in this regard. The Committee recommends
for immediate corrective measures in this regard.
NICHE TOURISM PRODUCTS
121. The Ministry of Tourism has taken the initiative of identifying, diversifying, developing and
promoting niche products of the tourism industry. This is done in order to overcome the aspect
of ‘seasonality’, and to promote India as a 365 days destination, attract tourists with specific
interests, and to ensure repeat visits for the unique products in which India has comparative
advantage. Accordingly, Cruise Tourism and Adventure Tourism have been identified by the Ministry
of Tourism for development and Promotion:

24
Cruise Tourism
122. Central financial assistance for Cruise Tourism projects was sanctioned for Development of
Tourism Infrastructure in Willington Island, Cochin Port, during the year 2008-09 for an amount

Trust for development of Cruise Passenger facilitation centre at Cochin Port.
123. The Committee recommends for more cruise tourism projects at the viable states on
the lines of the initiative taken in Cochin Port. All the Major Ports, especially the
Mormugao Port has immense potential of cruise tourism which needs to be explored by the
Ministry of Tourism for development.
Adventure Tourism
124. Central Financial Assistance is being extended to State Governments/Union Territory
Administrations for development of tourism Infrastructure in destinations including adventure

sports, winter/water related sports, trekker huts, wildlife viewing facilities, etc. Financial assistance
to State Governments is also provided for purchase of water sports equipment consisting of
kayaks, canoes, paddle boats, fibre glass boats, hovercrafts, water scooters, etc.
125. The Committee notes the various measures taken in the Adventure tourism. The
Committee also recommends that adequate trained people should be deputed in all the
adventure spots to monitor the participants and for rescue operations if required.
126. The Committee was informed that the Ministry of Tourism has identified many niche
tourism products such as Medical, Wellness, Golf, Polo, Meetings, Incentives Conferences and
Exhibitions (MICE), Eco-tourism and Film Tourism.
127. The Committee feels that there is lot of potential in all these new tourism products.
The Ministry of Tourism should work on a detailed guide map on all these areas.
SAFETY AND SECURITY
128. The Ministry of Tourism has informed the Committee that they are concerned about the
safety and security of tourists at various destinations and hence, has taken the following measures:
(i) For the safety and security of tourists, the Ministry of Tourism has advised State
Governments/Union Territory Administrations to deploy tourist police. Some of the
State Governments have, in fact, deployed tourist police in one form or the other.
(ii) Further, the guidelines for formation of Tourist Security Organization(s) comprising
Ex-servicemen, formulated by the Ministry of Tourism, Government of India in

for necessary action.
(iii) In addition, the Union Ministry of Tourism along with stakeholders has also adopted
the ‘Code of Conduct for Safe and Honourable Tourism’ which is a set of guidelines
to encourage tourism activities to be undertaken with respect for basic rights like
dignity, safety and freedom from exploitation of both tourists and local residents in
particular women and children.

25
(a) The Pilot Scheme of Tourist Facilitation and Security Organization (TFSO)
comprising of Ex-servicemen of India for the safety and security of tourists in
the States and Union Territories with the assistance of Ministry of Defence
(Exservicemen Welfare Fund) has been operationalized (in the States of Uttar
Pradesh, Rajasthan and Andhra Pradesh), on cost sharing basis between the
partnering States with the Government of India.
129. Regarding the new initiatives taken for the security and safety of tourists the Secretary
tourism stated that Ministry is setting up an Infoline round the clock manned by proficient people,
preferably by ladies in nine languages, out of it, six languages are of UN, Hindi, Japanese and
German. This infoline will cater to all the needs/help including police help to the tourists.
130. The Committee observes that safety and security is equally important, if not more,
for the growth of tourism sector. The Committee is concerned about the recent incidents
of attacks on tourists at different parts of the country. In addition to this, the Committee
noticed that even though safety guidelines are in place, these are less enforced and the
authorities are negligent towards these aspects until there are some incidents. All the State
Governments therefore may be persuaded/helped to set up tourism Police and prevent touts
and goons from various tourist destinations, airports, railway stations, etc. The Committee,
therefore, recommends that the safety measures should be strictly implemented and
monitored at the different levels. The 24x7 infoline in foreign languages is a welcome step
up to attract the tourists. However, the Ministry should ensure that the people who are
manning it are capable and the service is available at ease. It should assist the tourists,
whenever they want.
GENERAL OBSERV ATIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS
131. The Committee observes that the Tourism Ministry is mainly a funddisbursing
agency. More than 90 per cent of its Plan allocation every year goes to four schemes
relating to infrastructure development, training assistance to institutes and publicity -
overseas and domestic. Once these funds are released, it seems it is left with the State
Governments and Union territories to utilise them. Nowhere is it reflected how the Ministry
is monitoring the utilisation of these funds and how they get feedback on whether the
States and Union territories are actually utilising these funds for the purpose for these
funds have been allocated. The Committee desires to know whether there is any robust
mechanism at different levels to coordinate these various aspects.
132. The Committee observes that sky rocketing of airfares and lack of government
control over it has recently affected the domestic tourist movement in the country. The
Committee also observes that higher user fee and ATF surcharges have eventually made the
air traffic journey un-affordable to many. The DGCA has taken some steps in this regard.
The Committee however, recommends that a more regular and strict watch on predatory
airfares being resorted by the airlines needs to done to prevent unreasonable airfares
especially during the peak seasons.
133. The Committee also observes that the rail travellers are facing problems due to
shabby coaches which are usually unclean with rodents roaming freely. The toilets are very
dirty and are seldom cleansed during the journey. Beggar menace and under quality food
served are other areas to be immediately attended. All these problems have made the train
journey a nightmare for most of the travellers and the tourists in particular. The
Committee recommends that Ministry of Tourism may take up the matter with Railway

26
Board so that the train journey may be made more attractive and comfortable to the
tourists.
134. The Committee observes that we are not utilizing the full potential of tourism in
India. We always feel very sad about the fact that, probably, there is no country like ours
that has snow, hills to seas and beaches, adventure tourism, wildlife tourism, medical
tourism, etc., within the country. India has such a wide variety and destination. In spite of
that, the confidence does not seem to come that we are able to actually reach anyway close
to using our potential.
