Peripheral Expressways
33. The Committee was informed that currently the Western Peripheral Expressway (WPE) and
Eastern Peripheral Expressway (EPE) are being constructed. The Western Peripheral Expressway,
on the western side of Delhi, passes through Haryana. The total cost of the project is Rs.1367
crores and the project will be implemented by Haryana State Industrial Development Corporation
(HSIDC).
34. It was further informed that due to inordinate delay, the cost of land acquisition and other
activities has increased from Rs.844 crores to Rs.2550 crores and both these projects are running
years behind original target date of completion.
35. The Eastern Peripheral Expressway on the eastern side of Delhi, passes through Haryana
and UP with the project cost of Rs.2290 crores. The project will be implemented by National
Highways Authority of India (NHAI). The total cost of land acquisition for these two expressways
is about Rs.1307 crores. On completion of Western Peripheral Expressway and Eastern Peripheral
Expressway, Delhi is expected to get relief from those inter-state vehicles which are passing
through Delhi at present although not destined for Delhi. The total length of the WPE is 135.65
km and in EPE the total length is 135 km.
National Urban Transport Authority of India
36. The Committee was informed that at present, there is no unified law in the country
governing urban transport/urban mobility. In the absence of any unified law on the subject, all
agencies under Central/State/Urban local governments work in isolation. As such it is proposed to
set up a National Urban Transport Authority of India with the following proposed functions under
a separate Act:

7
(i) Set standards including safety standards and specifications for all urban transport
modes;
(ii) Setting and monitoring standard service level benchmarks for urban transport in
general and different modes in particular;
(iii) Setting standards and overseeing the implementation of standards/parameters for
National Mission for Sustainable Habitat;
(iv) Standardization and indigenization;
(v) Develop alternative financial models for UT projects;
(vi) Preparation of model documents, model concession agreements for P&P, national
database for urban transport, guidelines to regulate and manage urban freight
transport;
(vii) Setting and monitoring standards for urban road safety including urban road safety
audit;
(viii) Setting standards and overseeing implementation of National Public Transport Helpline
and National Common Mobility Card ‘More’;
(ix) Manage dedicated Urban Transport Fund at Central Government level;
(x) To develop capacity building across different levels of Government to achieve above
objectives;
(xi) To promote research and innovation in the field of urban transport;
(xii) Overseeing the implementation of NUTP across India;
(xiii) Advise centre, states and ULB on various aspects relating to Urban Transport as may
be referred to it.
37. In this context, a Working Group for drafting law on urban transport/urban mobility/NUTAI
has been constituted.
Legislative/Rules framework
38. The Government of National Capital Territory of Delhi informed the Committee that its
Transport Department carries out various functions relating to policy formulation in Delhi. These
functions include statute related work and also physical policies as enumerated earlier. Normally,
the responsibility for managing the urban transport rests with the State Governments but as far as
NCT of Delhi is concerned, there are several key agencies like DDA, MCD, NDMC, Traffic Police
and Transport Department that play important role in urban transport planning and implementation.
Further, several Acts and Rules, which have important implication in dealing with urban transport
issues, are administered by the Central Government.
Constitution of Delhi Urban Mass Transit Authority (DUMTA)
39. The Committee was informed by the Delhi Government that the international experience
suggests that in all major cities transport functions are integrated and are handled by one agency
which performs different functions through its subsidiaries or instrumentalities. ‘Transport of
London’ is not only responsible for city transport in London but also handles the road networking
and traffic regulation, is responsible and has the freedom to plan, set-up, operate and manage such
networking through various subsidiaries. It has set-up separate wings for technical analysis and

8
input including demand assessment, fair fixing, route and frequency planning to provide sustainable
public transport network. Similar is the situation in major cities of US. Mass Transit Authority of
Boston and of New York handle all transport issues for the respective cities. In fact, in US, all
the major cities have set up such Transit Authorities to handle city transport matters including
traffic policing, the Committee was informed.
40. Delhi being a metropolitan city and growing at a faster pace, there is a need to look into
the quality of transport infrastructure it has and the level of infrastructure it needs to meet the
requirement of a world class city. It was in this context as also in order to tackle the problem
of multiplicity of agencies dealing with transport, the Government of NCT of Delhi has decided
to constitute an integrated unified authority for handling all transport related functions. Accordingly
in April 2010, the Council of Ministers of the Government of NCT of Delhi cleared a draft bill for
setting of ‘Delhi Urban Mass Transit Authority’ (DUMTA) for comprehensive planning,
development, operation, management and regulation of mass transit facilities under unified structure
in the NCT of Delhi for accessible, economic, efficient, reliable, safe and sustainable public
transport in NCT of Delhi. An attempt thus was made by Delhi Government to combine planning,
provisioning and regulatory functions including land use planning of areas meant for public transit
facility under one agency. It would be an Authority on the lines of Land Transport Authority of
Singapore City, Transport for London for City of London and Mass Transit Authority for City of
New York, the Committee was informed.
41. The Authority is proposed to be an empowered and apex multi member representative body
consisting of Chief Minister as its Chairperson with several members from various organizations
including the one from Delhi Traffic Police. For better operation, efficiency and co-ordination,
PWD and Traffic Police is to be managed by the proposed Authority. In April 2010, the said draft
Bill, as required, was sent to the Union Ministry of Home Affairs for prior approval of the Central
Government before its introduction in the Legislative Assembly of Delhi.
42. When the Committee enquired about the status of the Delhi Urban Mass Transit Authority
(DUMTA) Bill, 2010, the Ministry of Home Affairs informed that it is still under consideration of
the Ministry. They further informed that the Union Ministry of Urban Development was working
on a draft Unified Metropolitan Transport Authority (UMTA) Bill, 2012 meant to be created in
million plus cities and was still to be finalized. Like UMTA, the DUMTA Bill, 2010 will also require
wider consultations with various stakeholders in order to avoid possible overlapping, encroachment
etc. upon the powers of Central Government agencies/Acts, etc.
Setting up a Unified Metropolitan Transport Authority (UMTA)
43. When asked about DUMTA as well as UMTA Bills, the Ministry of Urban Development
informed the Committee that setting up a single authority in the form of a Unified Metropolitan
Transport Authority (UMTA) for planning, coordination, management and monitoring was on the
anvil for the entire public transport system for Delhi and NCR. To start with, it may be set up
for Delhi. It is extremely important that one single body is established under legislation to be
chaired at the highest level, to coordinate all planning and operations of the transport system in the
city. The city must have one single agency that develops the Transport Plan and there cannot be
separate plans developed by agencies such as DMRC, DTC, etc. without proper coordination
between them. Such a body must include all the major stakeholders including the Traffic Police,
so that it ensures effective coordination and strongly discourages planning in isolation. This could
be on the lines of similar organizations for Transport working for major cities like London,
Singapore, Vancouver, etc. All of them have strong legislative backing.
44. This proposed agency i.e. UMTA, it was argued, could function at two levels, one level
undertakes strategic planning and fund allocation from dedicated urban transport fund, and the

9
second level could be responsible for the overall coordination between the different components of
the overall transport system, monitoring and enforcement of plans formulated by UMTA. One such
unified authority, the Committee was informed, has been constituted for Hyderabad Metropolitan
Region by an Act of the Andhra Pradesh Legislature (G.O. MS. No.624) deals with issues related
to traffic and transportation in the Hyderabad Metropolitan Region. Some of its functions are to
oversee the implementation of various traffic and transportation measures undertaken by various
agencies in the region, to ensure that effective public transport systems are in place for the
metropolitan region, and to integrate various routes of public transport and issues including
combined ticketing and feeder services.
45. The Committee was further informed that the Master Plan of Delhi-2021 also talks of
setting up a single authority for planning/development, implementation and enforcement of the
policies which may be framed in transport sector. A Committee under the Chairmanship of
Secretary, Union Ministry of Urban Development, Government of India had made recommendations
about UMTA for Delhi in February, 2006 to Government of Delhi. However, the same is yet to be
implemented.
46. The Committee was informed that a Unified Traffic and Transportation Infrastructure
(Planning and Engineering) Centre (UTTIPEC) had already been set up in 2008 in DDA under the
Chairmanship of Lt. Governor, Delhi, under Section 57 of the Delhi Development Act. The primary
aim of UTTIPEC is to ensure that various engineering solutions being implemented by various
agencies are well coordinated and not mutually exclusive. While setting it up, it was intended that
it would ultimately become a part of the UMTA for Delhi as and when it is set up.
47. The Ministry of Urban Development argued before the Committee for having better
institutional machinery like UMTA for public transport system in NCR, all the operators should be
brought under its fold. This would, inter-alia , include:
(a) A robust mechanism to develop a comprehensive long range mobility plan for Delhi and
NCR;
(b) A common fare collection system;
(c) A common passenger information system i.e, a public transport help line;
(d) Multi-modal integration at the level of infrastructure, fares, operations and information;
(e) A data collection and analysis centre;
(f) An IT and communications backbone;
(g) A mobility agency to function as a centralized command and control centre;
(h) A common control centre for automated and computerized management of auto
rickshaws and taxis;
(i) Implementing and operationalizing Reciprocal Common Transport Agreement in NCR;
(j) Developing legislative cover that supersedes the existing enactments and allows the
UMTA to take over the complete planning, coordination and management functions.
UTTIPEC can become the technical arm of UMTA.
48. The Ministry of Urban Development informed the Committee that till such time UMTA is
set up, it is proposed that a Task Force under Secretary, Ministry of Urban Development can
function as the policy making body for Delhi and NCR considering its special nature wherein
different States, agencies and host of other Central and State agencies were involved. As regards
States, their Chief Secretaries may be invited to the meetings of the said Task Force. UTTIPEC

10
can become the technical arm of UMTA, as and when set up, and be responsible for overall
coordination, management and enforcement issues.
49. The Ministry of Urban Development further informed the Committee that even after
extensive network of metro rail as well as buses by DTC, the availability of safe, affordable, quick,
comfortable and accessible public transport in the National capital Region is far lesser as compared
to the demand. Presently, the focus is more on supply side. For providing more space to
personalized vehicles, pedestrian paths and cycle paths are being encroached upon through parking
and widening of roads for motor vehicles which is making accessing public transport cumbersome
and unsafe as each public transport user is essentially a pedestrian first. There is also a need to
curtailing the use of private transport for example, by congestion charging, restrictions on parking
and high parking fee, etc.
NCT Government and Traffic enforcement in Delhi
50. Regarding the implementation and enforcement of the Motor Vehicle Act (hereinafter
referred as MV Act) and the Rules made thereunder, the representative of the Government of NCT
of Delhi submitted before the Committee that Section 213 of the MV Act, 1988 gives powers to
State Governments to establish a Motor Vehicles Department for carrying into effect the provisions
of the MV Act. Government of NCT of Delhi has already delegated powers to the officers of the
rank of Assistant Commissioners of Police and above of Delhi Police to suspend the permits of
transport vehicles for violating the various provisions of the MV Act. Delhi Police has also been
vested with powers under the MV Act to prosecute the drivers and owners of the motor vehicles
for offences relating to license, registration, permit, limits of speed, driving regulation and
adherence to traffic signs and signals. In addition, Delhi Police has also powers under the Delhi
Police Act to regulate and control the motor-vehicles. On the specific request of Delhi Police and
Directions of Court of Law, Government of NCT of Delhi has also delegated its powers to Delhi
Police under relevant Section of the MV Act for compounding of offences, removal of unauthorized
hoardings and to get particulars of drivers or conductors of motor-vehicles committing any
offence.
51. It may also be noted that currently, Delhi Traffic Police is regulating the traffic and
checking violations of various provisions of the MV Act and Rules framed thereunder. Delhi
Transport Department also has an ‘Enforcement Wing’ to deal with enforcement issues arising from
time to time in focused manner. Of the staff strength of 193 personnel, 150 are deployed in about
30 teams of 5 officials each. These teams are deployed in the field with specific instructions to
focus on particular type of vehicles or offences, as following:–
● Focused enforcement on offences – most of which cannot be delegated by the State
Government or can be enforced only by these officers of the Motor V ehicles
Department or are not delegated to the Police: such as over loading of goods vehicles
etc.
● Conduct special drives from time to time in which the limited manpower concentrates
its attention on specific offences/categories of vehicles.
● Traffic investigation of specific complaints and necessary action thereon.
Delhi Government and Delhi Traffic Police
52. Government of NCT of Delhi also submitted that although Traffic Police is the main agency
for enforcement of the Motor Vehicle Act and Rules, there is hardly any information flow in a
structured manner to the Transport Department. It is a very strange situation where the Traffic
Police is enforcing the provisions of Motor Vehicles Act on behalf of Transport Department in view

11
of certain powers delegated to it, but it reports to the Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of
India. Hence, the Rules are made by the one set of officials while these are enforced by another
set of officials, both of whom report to different authorities. Government of NCT of Delhi realizes
that the responsibility of the Transport Department does not go away with the delegation of power
but it cannot be exercised in vacuum of information. Comprehensive guidelines are being finalized
for proper feed-back from Traffic Police being enforcement agency with respect of various powers
delegated by the Government regarding transport sector.
53. While the Government of NCT of Delhi has decided to strengthen its Enforcement Branch
with additional manpower, vehicles and technological support, even then the primary responsibility
of enforcing the rules, permit conditions etc. is going to rest with the Traffic Police due to their
size of the manpower, powers delegated by the Transport Department and specific power given
under the Motor Vehicle Act and Rules.
54. According to the Government of NCT of Delhi, it is unable to seek full cooperation from
the Delhi Police in managing the ever increasing traffic problems in Delhi. It was suggested that
the Police Department should be reorganized into Traffic, Law and Order (General Security) and
VIP security. It was suggested that while the security may be looked after by the Central
Government directly, ‘General Security’ and ‘Traffic Wing’ may be placed under the Government
of NCT of Delhi. Thus, the Government of NCT of Delhi tried to make out a strong case for
transferring the Delhi Traffic Police to its control. The Committee was informed that the proposal
for transferring the control of Delhi Traffic Police to Government of NCT of Delhi was taken up
with the Union Ministry of Home Affairs which controls Delhi Police and their comments were still
awaited.
55. When asked, the Union Ministry of Home Affairs informed the Committee that the proposal
was being examined in detail. The Ministry of Home Affairs argued that the Traffic Police was an
intrinsic part of the Delhi Police and Section 3 of the Delhi Police Act provides that “There shall
be one police, force for the whole of Delhi and all officers and subordinate ranks of the police
force shall be liable for posting to any branch of the force including the Delhi Armed Police”.
Under Article 239 AA, of the Constitution of India (Special provisions with respect to Delhi),
entries 1 and 2 of the State List i.e. “Public Order” and “Police” are the subjects outside the
purview of the Legislative Assembly of Delhi and function under the control of an Administrator
appointed under Article 239 of the Constitution i.e., Lt. Governor. The functioning of the Traffic
Unit, Police district, Security, Police Control Room, etc. are complementary to each other and
function in tandem, particularly during VVIP movements, rallies/processions and demonstrations,
sports events, events of national importance such as Republic Day, Independence Day, police
bandobust for the occasions like Trade Fair, Ramlilas, Religious festivals, etc. This aside, there are
administrative and disciplinary issues, which warrant the existence of one single police force in the
capital. Therefore, a standalone traffic unit is not feasible. The Committee was informed that in
view of the position explained above, it is not considered feasible to accept the request to bring
the control of Delhi Police under the Government of NCT of Delhi.
56. Regarding enforcement of MV Act and Rules made thereunder, the Ministry of Urban
Development submitted before the Committee that the enforcement mechanism needs considerable
improvement. It would be appropriate if all the functions of enforcement including the traffic police
are brought under the jurisdiction of the UMTA and all enforcement responsibilities should rest with
the proposed UMTA.
Observations/Recommendations of the Committee
57. The Committee, after examining the papers/documents submitted to it and hearing
the arguments of various stakeholders on the subject learnt that there are around 27 odd

12
authorities/agencies for managing the public transport in the National Capital Region and
the existing arrangement needs a total revamp. In fact, the creation of NCR posed newer
challenges for promoting a seamless, accessible, safe, affordable and comfortable transport
in the region. A large number of non-destined vehicles, commercial and private, pass
through Delhi everyday to reach other States. Five National Highways are converging in
NCT Delhi adding to insurmountable pressure on the Delhi Roads.
58. The Committee feels that pressure of ever increasing population, unprecedented
proliferation of private vehicles, lack of adequate space for roads, parking etc., existence of
multiple authorities/agencies responsible for different aspects of transport management
leads to the existing chaos on the roads in the NCR. Even the Metro connectivity has also
reached its saturation point. The Committee finds that these authorities and agencies
responsible for planning, development, operation, management, etc. of transport facilities/
services available in NCR being independent of one another work in isolation. Hence, the
existing confusion and chaos on the roads.
59. Another major challenge is the absence of a unified law for governing urban
transport in the country. As a result, the enforcement of different Rules/Regulations by
different State Governments and other agencies within the NCR is done in isolation. Thus,
the existing enforcement arrangement for concerned rules/regulations, in fact, is highly
fragmented and diffused. As such, there is an absence of an effective and integrated
enforcement formal mechanism having a shared mandate/authority from all the concerned
- NCT Government, State Governments, Union Ministries of Urban Development and Home
Affairs and various agencies such NDMC, MCD, DDA, DMRC, DTC, Delhi Police etc.
60. The Committee finds that as far as Delhi is concerned, while planning is with the
Union Ministry of Urban Development, management of traffic is with the Delhi Police, which
is under the Union Ministry of Home Affairs, NCT Transport Department is responsible for
issuing licenses and registering vehicles under the Motor Vehicle Acts and Rules. From
planning to enforcement each Ministry/Department perform its duties exclusively without
having any formal coordination between them.
61. The Committee finds that an interim solution for the problems in public transport
system in National Capital Region is the proper and planned traffic management, stricter
licensing system, integration of bus services with metro and effective utilization of ring
railways in the entire region. The long term solution will be introduction of Unified
Metropolitan Transport Authority (UMTA) having a jurisdiction over National Capital Region
at the earliest. Such a unified authority would be empowered to deal with important aspects
relating to planning, operationalizing, management, regulation, enforcement, etc. of an
effective transport system which has the consent/approval from all the State Governments
including NCT Government and Union Ministries of Road Transport and Highways, MOUD
and MHA.
62. The Committee noted a perceptible resistance on the part of various authorities
and agencies like Delhi Government, State Governments, Ministries of Urban Development
and Home Affairs, Delhi Police, Delhi Development Authority, DMRC, etc. to effect any
change in the existing control over different aspects of public transport system. They
appeared to be unwilling to forego their authority, even while each authority is working
at cross purposes. There is a lack of clear vision and coordination regarding how the
transport network should be designed, developed and implemented. Individual agencies
such as the NCT Government, Union Ministry of Urban Development, Ministry of Home
Affairs/Delhi Police, Delhi Metro Rail Corporation (DMRC), the Delhi Transport
Corporation (DTC), the Indian Railways appear to be making their plans in isolation. As

13
a result, services of different modes do not complement each other. Coupled with this,
policies with regard to other inter-linked issues such as creation of parking facilities,
transit-oriented development, road-widening activities, are not aligned with those of
others.
63. The Committee is aware that some amount of multiplicity of authorities is in-built
into our system which is unavoidable. Many activities that are involved fall in the domain
of authorities at different levels supported by constitutional and statutory provisions. The
only option in this situation could be having a unified authority which could be delegated
necessary powers in respect of everything required for managing/providing a seamless,
efficient, affordable, safe and sustainable transport in NCR.
64. The Committee feels that this unified authority could coordinate between various
authorities in Transport Sector which is extremely essential to ensure world class transport
facility with adequate safety and security for the citizens of Delhi particularly for the
women using these faculties. Technology can play a crucial role in effective co-ordination
also.
65. The Committee finds that currently there are many authorities for enforcement of
traffic related Rules and Regulations, traffic police and the motor vehicle inspectorate being
two of them. This causes undue rivalry and ‘empire building’. This is further compounded
by the fact that the Police does not function under the Government of Delhi but under the
Union Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA).
66. Besides, Union Ministry of Road Transport and Highways (MORTH) which is
responsible for administering six Acts/Rules/Regulations in this regard. Motor Vehicles
Rules and Carriage by Roads, Road Transport Corporation being few of these. Delhi Police
that enforces important Rules for traffic control comes under the MHA. Delhi Government,
now being an elected one having an elected Assembly cannot be expected to remain outside
of the loop because people hold it responsible for problems of traffic in Delhi. This
helplessness is reflected in its several attempts (by NCT Government) to get control of
Traffic Police and have DUMTA for this purpose.
67. DUMTA Bill prepared by NCT Government is pending with MHA and the Ministry of
Urban Development (MOUD). But the MOUD has come up with an idea of UMTA for Delhi
for which it will be the controlling authority . Whether this pr oposal had been discussed with
NCT Government and the Governments of Uttar Pradesh, Haryana and Rajasthan as well as
the Ministry of Home Affairs is not known. Now, we have a situation where we have a
proposal for DUMTA under NCT Government, UMTA by Union Ministry of Urban
Development. More recently, NCRPB has also taken some steps to set up National Urban
Transport Authority of India (NUTAI), a separate agency to ensure smooth transportation in
the region. The Committee learnt that State Governments have some reservations about
certain important issues involved. The Committee appreciates this effort of NCRPB but has
serious reservations about its smooth functioning. It should not be allowed to turn out to
be yet another agency adding to existing confusion.
68. The Committee wishes to point out that the Ministry of Road Transport and
Highways (MORTH) had brought a National Road Safety and Traffic Management Board Bill
in 2010 which was considered by this Committee and returned to the Ministry with certain
suggestions/recommendations as 160
th Report in July, 2010. This Bill sought to set up a
Board for, among other things, ensuring an effective road safety and traffic management
system and practices. When asked, the MORTH informed that the Bill is in the process of
finalization and will be introduced in Parliament after it is ready.

14
69. The MORTH argues that there should be a single Act to control the movement of
motor vehicles over the entire country for better efficiency and results. It is also of the
view that the existing system of control/implementation gets diluted due to involvement of
other Ministries/Departments who propose to bring their own Act for regulation of various
aspects resulting in conflict/duplicity in Regulations. These also sometimes do not reflect
the point of view of all the stakeholders. Therefore, the various issues relating to road
transport should remain under the umbrella of one Act and one Ministry to optimize the
responsibility and administration with respect to these regulations. It suggests to utilize the
existing Transport Development Council under this Ministry to integrate all these aspects.
70. In view of several such proposals to set up different Authorities separately, the
Committee feels that there is a need for constitution of a Task Force or GOM to consider/
examine all the issues in consultation with the concerned Governments/Ministries to work
out the most workable mechanism for this purpose. It may consider the considering
proposals of MOUD for UMTA that of NCT Government for DUMTA, National Road Safety
and Transport Management Board of MORTH and NUTAI by NCRPB. The existing system
should be revamped at the earliest which is acceptable to all and has consent/mandate of
all.
71. The Committee feels that there is a need for reviewing the role and performance of
National Capital Region Planning Board in addressing the transportation issues of NCR.
Whether the NCRPB set up way back in 1985 has been able to fulfill its mandate during
these more than three decades of its existence? The Committee notes that the Western
Peripheral Expressway (KMP Expressway) and the Eastern Peripheral Expressway can bring
a lot of relief to the transport in Delhi Region. However, the Committee also notes that the
construction of the Expressways are moving in a snail’s pace which need to be completed
at the earliest. The Committee also notes the problems faced in funding of these projects
and hopes that the Union Government will sort out the issues with the respective
stakeholders of these projects to complete them without further delay.
72. The Committee finds that another impediment in management of public transport
system in NCR is the implementation of Central Motor Vehicle Acts/Rules by the respective
States individually. The Committee feels that to address this issue, Central Motor Vehicle
Acts/Rules may be implemented uniformly for the entire NCR in consultation with the State
Governments.
73. The Committee feels that the focus for public transport in NCR should be a multi-
modal, efficient and integrated (rail, road and pedestrian). In absence of this, personalized
transport will continue to increase and public transport will remain fragmented and scanty.
The Committee hopes that the Union Government in consultation with the State
Governments of Delhi, Haryana, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh will address the issues
concerning public transport system in NCR on priority.

ANNEXURE-IV
(vide Para 28)
Measures to improve the public transport system in Delhi
Technological upgradation
(i) GPS Based Bus Tracking and Monitoring System:  With a view to improve reliability of bus
operations, GPSs have been installed in about 3000 DTC and all 430 cluster buses. Now on line
real time monitoring of the bus operations is being carried out from the ‘‘Command and Control
Centre” established at ISBT, Kashmere Gate with a cost of Rs. 30 crores. The system has helped
in better regulation for safety and reliability of the bus operations by monitoring of relevant data
with regard to routes, deviations, over-speeding, unauthorized stoppages etc. for buses.
(ii)  Operations Control Centre (OCC): There has been a quantum leap in terms of the
Information and Communications Technology (ICT) based transportation projects. Each being
interlinked with the other, a need was felt to develop a Command and Control Centre to integrate,
manage and monitor the transportation system and intervene in case of a crisis. Transport
Department has developed a state of the art Operations Control Centre at ISBT, Kashmere Gate.
The OCC shall operate and control the following systems:-
o Intelligent Signaling System (ISS)
o Bus Rapid Transit (BRT) Corridor
o Automatic Vehicle Location System (A VL)
o Automatic fare collection Systems (AFCS)
o Private Stage carriage buses in 17 Clusters
OCC is equipped with servers that are linked to the ISS, A VL and AFCS components in the field,
in real time through GPRS and Optical Fiber Cable (OFC). The activities will be monitored on
Barco screens installed in the OCC and LCD panel in addition to the work stations of the respective
staff. The Command Centre is manned 24 hours for real time monitoring of all activities. For the
ISS the OCC work towards facilitating a smooth flow of traffic. It will be capable of:
o Live traffic monitoring on BARCO Screen
o on-line fault detection system
o Advanced traffic information and management system
o CCTV recording system
o Management and Operation of entire signaling system.
(iii) Passenger Information System (PIS):  It is a part of the GPS based Bus Tracking System.
The GPS gives the location of the bus and a backend application uses this information to calculate
the Expected Arrival Time of the bus. This information is then transmitted to the PIS boards that
are installed at the bus stops. The PIS has been installed by DIMTS in 90 BQS on the BRT
corridor and 125 BQS in the NDMC area. It is in the process of coordinating the roll out of PIS

22
in 375 additional BQS in Delhi. The project is expected to be completed within the next six months.
With full roll out of PIS, the commuter would also be able to plan his/her journey by sending the
bus arrival query through SMS.
(iv) Electronic Ticketing Systems:  Electronic Ticketing System is functioning successfully in
cluster buses for last one year. It is planned to extend this System in DTC buses. It has been
decided to have a Common Mobility Card for Metro and Public Transport Buses. Modalities in this
regard are being worked out for the extension of Metro card on cluster and DTC buses.
(v) Automated Vehicle Inspection System:  With a view to improve road worthiness for safe
transportation, the transport department of national capital territory of Delhi is modernizing its road-
worthiness inspection facilities for commercial vehicles provided at the Vehicles Inspection Unit,
Burari. Five automated Inspection and checking lanes have been made operational and
e-commissioning of another six lanes is in progress. As of now, all buses, trucks, tourist taxis,
school cabs and three-wheeled goods carriages vehicles tests are conducted on automated I and
C test lanes before grant/renewal of certificate of fitness.
(vi) Interlinking of Zonal offices and Inspection Unit: All zonal transport offices, Vehicles
Inspection Unit and Auto rickshaw Unit at Burari have been interlinked. The interlinking of data
base of driving licenses in real time has made it possible for the issuance of driving license to the
citizens of Delhi from any zonal transport office in Delhi.
(vii) Networking of Pollution checking facilities: About 600 Pollution Checking Centers have
been authorized to facilitate checking of pollution levels and issue of Pollution under Control
Certificates (PUCCs) to the motorists. All the Centers have been connected in a web-based
network. Now the pollution levels of vehicles checked at these centers are uploaded on real time
basis. This helps in creation of comprehensive database on emission characteristics of vehicles in
different categories and age groups and issuance of automatic notices etc. It has been made
mandatory for these Centers to affix a hologram having security features on the Certificates being
issued by them with a view to curb the issue of fake Certificates.

Committee desired to know the policy of Government in promoting public transport system in the
country and the interface of Central and State Governments in this regard. Issues of poor
monitoring of transport system, violation of licensing terms and conditions by the private carriers

system in Delhi, were also raised by the Committee.

the country. The Secretary stated that Government had initiated a multi-pronged strategy to address
the issue of road safety in the country and the role of drivers’ training institutes in imparting

1
REPORT
The Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Government on the
observations/recommendations as contained in its One Hundred and Eighty Ninth Report on the
“Development of National Waterways – Potentials and Challenges” which was presented to the
Hon’ble Chairman, Rajya Sabha on the 6
th February, 2013 and presented to both the Houses of
Parliament on the 27 th February, 2013.
2. The Action Taken Replies have been received from the Ministry of Shipping vide their O.M.
dated the 29 th July, 2013 in respect of all the observations/recommendations contained in the
Report.
3. The Committee desires that final replies in respect of those observations/
recommendations which have been categorized as interim replies by the Committee should
be furnished to it at the earliest.
4. On scrutiny of the Action Taken Replies, the Committee has made observations on each
item of Action taken/proposed to be taken by the Ministry of Shipping. The recommendations of
the Committee contained in the One Hundred and Eighty Ninth Report, action taken thereon by the
Ministry and further recommendations/observations of the Committee on each item of action taken
has been given in the succeeding paragraph.
5. The Committee notes that Inland Water Transport (IWT) is a fuel efficient and environment
friendly mode of transportation. India is richly endowed with navigable waterways, comprising
rivers, canals, backwaters, creeks, etc. that can be developed as alternate mode of transportation
in the coming years.
(Para 71 of the 189
th Report)
Reply of the Government
6. Government is in agreement with the Committee’s observations and is taking necessary
measures to make the National Waterways navigable and a viable alternate mode of transport.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
7.  The Committee notes that the Government is in agreement with the Committee’s
recommendation.
8. This Committee has always stood for developing water transport in a big way, which also
has immense potential. It has been emphasizing this through its recommendations given in various
reports, latest being its 177
th Report on Demands for Grants, 2012-13 of the Ministry of Shipping.
This inter alia  states that water transport has various advantages compared to road transport.
Water transport is cheaper, can handle huge volumes of cargo and has less impact on environment.
The Committee had felt that a strong inland water transport system would be able to handle an
efficient, cheaper and environment-friendly cargo transport system. The Committee had strongly
recommended to make available adequate resources in order to have a well-connected water
transport facilities throughout the country.
 (Para No. 72)
Reply of the Government
9. Government provides grants to Inland Waterways Authority of India (IWAI) for development

2
of National Waterways in the country. Government also provides 100% funding to the North
Eastern States under Central Sector Scheme for the development of Waterways. By and large, there
is no financial crunch to develop IWT infrastructure on the National Waterways. An amount of
Rs.1500 crore has been earmarked for this sector during Twelfth Plan period. Government is also
exploring the possibility of assistance from World Bank as well as private sector in the development
of our National Waterways especially NW-4 and 5.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
10. The Committee is happy to note that the Ministry of Shipping has received funds up
to the tune of Rs. 1500 crore to be expended during the Twelfth Five Year Plan and the
Ministry also observes that the said amount is adequate for the development of Inland
Water Transport. In view of this the Committee hopes that now the work will be expedited
in all the National Waterways declared till date.
NATIONAL POLICY
11. India has inland waterways with a navigable length of 14,500 km., but the Committee is
constrained to state that even though National IWT Policy document prepared in the Ninth Plan
prescribed for making efforts for pooling the resources through captive users and PSUs, with
liberal investments in IWT sector, the Government have failed to implement the vision of the policy
document in actual terms over these years. On the contrary, water transport has shrunk even in
those areas with great potential. The Committee also notes that lack of adequate policy support for
the sector was also compounding the problems, leading to IWT losing its competitive edge over
other modes of transport. The other modes of transport received policy support and huge
investment in developing its infrastructure, whereas the water transport seems to have been
neglected or has not received the required attention of the policy makers and the Government. The
Committee, therefore, recommends that Government of India should take necessary follow up
actions on the Inland Water Transport Policy Document of 2001 for the optimum utilization of our
potential in the water transport sector.
 (Para No.73)
Reply of the Government
12. The expenditure on IWT sector from Rs. 385 crore in the Tenth Plan has increased to
Rs. 560.48 crore in the Eleventh Plan. During the Twelfth Plan Inland Water Transport is one of
the thrust areas. A total allocation of Rs. 1500 has been made for the Twelfth Plan for the IWT
Sector. Action has already been taken on all the major policy items enumerated in IWT policy of
2001. Some of the important items on which action has been taken are as under:–
(a) The IWAI Act was amended to enable authority to enter into Joint Ventures. IWAI had
formed three Joint Ventures with two private sector companies.
(b) Depreciation rate for Inland Vessels was made at par with sea going vessels.
(c) Investors in Inland Waterways infrastructures are provided income tax rebate similar
to National Highways.
(d) Customs duty for certain equipments related to Inland Water Transport sector has been
reduced.
(e) IWAI Act has been amended to enable it to raise fund from the market through issue
of bonds etc.

3
Due to increase in the level of infrastructure available on NW-1, 2 and 3 under the above
mentioned policy, confidence of private sector has increased in the IWT sector. This is reflected
in the conclusion of Haldia-Farakka coal transportation project in which a private sector company
has invested about Rs.650 crore in creating IWT infrastructure. Under this project transportation
of 3 million tonnes of coal every year would be made from Haldia to the NTPC Power station at
Farakka. However, since the IWT sector has remained dormant for a long time, it is expected that
only gradually the IWT activity in the National Waterway would increase across the country.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
13. The Committee takes note of all the encouraging developments taking place at IWT
Sector as detailed by the Ministry.
14. Having emphasized this, the Committee is of the view that IWT as a mode of transportation
cannot be considered in isolation. It needs to be integrated with other modes of transportation to
achieve maximum benefits. Centre-level coordination would be required for this. The Committee
also recommends that IWT operators should be given a level-playing field vis-à-vis those in other
modes-road and rail transports.
(Para No.74)
Reply of the Government
15. For an integrated approach to the development of IWT sector with other modes of
transport, a study was entrusted to M/s RITES on 4.2.2013. The report has been recently
submitted by RITES and is under examination in IWAI. Based on the outcome of the study,
necessary steps would be initiated for integrating the waterways with Rail and Road. In order to
provide level playing field to Inland Water Transport sector vis-a-vis Rail and Road, transportation
subsidy as available to road and rail for North Eastern Region (NER) has been made available to
IWT sector also. IWT has also recently been included in the scheme for subsidy for transportation
of fertilizers at par with road and railway.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
16. The Committee would like to know about the details of recommendations made by
M/s RITES as submitted to the Ministry of Shipping. The Ministry may also inform this
Committee about the implementation status of the same.
17. The Committee notes that national highways are contributing about 40% of the road
accidents and trucks being the major contributor in this. The water transportation being the safest
mode can reduce the road accidents and resulting casualties significantly. It also reduces treatment
and rehabilitation costs to a great extent. Moreover, the land acquisition for the Highways/Roads
have been a major problem which is not only sensitive issue but also it is highly time taking and
costly exercise. There is shortage of free land for road construction. Switching to water mode,
therefore, would become the most viable option to reduce the dependency on roads, particularly
for bulk cargo transport. It has lot of tourist potential especially for pilgrimage, which is mainly
located on river sides.
 (Para No.75)
Reply of the Government
18. Ministry is in agreement with the recommendation of Committee. Ministry of Shipping has
already initiated steps for modal Shift of cargo from Rail and Road to Inland Waterways and
coastal shipping.

4
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
19. The Committee notes that the Ministry has agreed to its recommendation.
FUND ALLOCATIONS
20. Even in the operational waterways, the Committee notes, lack of maintenance and sufficient
funds are the main reasons for insignificant use of National Waterways. We have five national
waterways so far, of which only three are operational and rest of two are to be started since last
three years. The Committee recommends that adequate funds need to be allocated separately for
maintenance and development of the national waterway which are presently in use. The Committee
notes with dismay and express its unhappiness for not being able to operationalize NW-4 and 5 so
far. It is believed that these national waterways will be operationalized on PPP mode as has been
decided by the Planning Commission. This Committee does not know why this has been kept
languishing. The Committee feels that Planning Commission is not much interested in the
development of waterways in the country as their reluctance to allocate adequate budget has
resulted the two national waterways NW-4 and 5 remain on mere papers. To avoid further delay,
the Committee recommends to allocate adequate financial support soon for operationalizing these
waterways.
(Para No.76)
Reply of the Government
21. The IWAI is developing the first three National Waterways (NW-1, 2 and 3) for shipping
and navigation by providing a navigational channel with targeted depth and width for most part of
the year, aids for day and night navigation, and fixed/floating terminals at selected locations for
berthing and loading/unloading of vessels and inter-modal connectivity at a few selected locations.
Central Plan funds are being provided separately for maintenance and development of the first three
National Waterways to IWAI in their Annual budget. The commercially viable stretches of NW 4
and 5 are proposed to be developed under PPP mode with Viability Gap Funding (VGF). The report
of M/s Grant Thorton, which was appointed by Department of Economic Affairs (DEA), has been
received. The report is under examination in IWAI. Further, the Ministry of Shipping is also
considering availing technical and financial assistance from World Bank for the development of
National Waterways.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
22. The Ministry has informed the Committee that commercially viable stretches of the
NW 4 and 5 are proposed to be developed under PPP mode. The Committee fails to
understand why only the commercially lucrative and viable stretches should go into private
hands through PPP. Does it mean that the non profitable and riskier sections would be left
to the Government (Inland Water Transport Authority of India). The Committee does not
agree with the idea of handing over only the profitable stretches of the  NW 4 and 5 to
private partners.  The Committee would also like to know about the observations made in
the report of M/s Grant Thorton, which was appointed by Department of Economic Affairs
(DEA), had been received by the Ministry of Shipping.
23. The Committee notes that severe dearth of infrastructure and lack of modernization are
the major factors bedeviling the Inland Water Transport sector in the country. The Committee
notes that Infrastructure creation requires continued efforts, better planning and larger quantum
of funds.
 (Para No. 77)

5
Reply of the Government
24. Investment in IWT sector has a long gestation and returns are over a period of time. To
ensure better planning and to adopt latest technology, Ministry of Shipping would take further steps
to strengthen IWAI especially its technical manpower. This would help in better conceptualization
and execution of projects on NWs. It is reiterated that sufficient allocation of plan funds for the
development of IWT sector has been made during Twelfth Plan.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
25. The Committee notes the reply.
26. The Committee also notes that not only the allocations made for IWT has been inadequate
but also till the end of Eleventh Plan expenditure of an amount of Rs. 1168 crore approximately
has been incurred. Further only an amount of Rs. 1500 crore has been allocated by the Planning
Commission, whereas, the working group has projected requirement of funds to the tune of
Rs. 10,500 crore for the Twelfth Five Year Plan. This trend can be observed in the previous Plan
periods like Eigth, Ninth and Tenth also. All the above periods, the Budget Estimates and the actual
expenditure incurred left huge gaps. It is a matter of concern for the Committee that even the
inadequate funds are also not being optimally utilized. Besides, there is no specific planning and
roadmap for mobilizing required investment for the creation of infrastructure and modernization of
the existing waterways and also operationalizing new ones that are pending. The Committee
recommends that government should come out with comprehensive projects for development of
IWT in the country in a time bound manner and sanctions for the same should be made accordingly.
(Para No.78)
Reply of the Government
27. The funds allocated to IWAI in its initial years were very meager. However, allocation of
funds improved from Ninth Plan onwards. Since its inception in 1986, till 2012-13, an amount of
Rs. 1794 crore has been allocated to IWAI. The expenditure pattern of IWAI has been increased
from the level of Rs. 35 crore in Eigth Plan to Rs. 151 crore in Ninth Plan to Rs. 385 crore in
Tenth Plan and Rs. 560 crore in Eleventh Plan period. During the Twelfth Five Year Plan an
allocation of Rs. 1500 crore has been made for IWT sector. During 2012-13, IWAI was able to
spend Rs. 146.02 crore. A Plan outlay of Rs. 200 crore has been provided for the current financial
year. IWAI has been advised to finalise suitable action plan to utilise the funds provided to them
during the Twelfth Plan.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
28. The Committee notes that the Ministry has advised  the IWAI to finalise suitable
action-plan to utilise the funds provided to them during the Twelfth Plan. The Committee
further observes that the Ministry may also ensure compliance thereof.
29. In this connection, the Committee would like to reiterates its recommendation contained in its
130
th Report on the “National Waterway (Lakhipur- Bhanga stretch of the Barak River) Bill, 2007”.
The Committee had expressed its concern about the discontinuance of the centrally sponsored scheme
for IWT development in the country by the Planning Commission, the Committee was of the view
that the decision of the Planning Commission to convert the Centrally Sponsored Scheme (CSS) for
IWT development into central sector scheme would adversely affect the pace of development of
Inland Water Transport in the country. The Committee had recommended for the revival of the
centrally sponsored scheme for overall development of the IWT sector.
(Para No. 79)

6
Reply of the Government
30. The Planning Commission is being requested to reconsider its decision and reintroduce the
Centrally Sponsored Scheme especially in view of the fact that IWT is one of the thrust areas of
the Government during Twelfth Plan period.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
31. The Committee would like to reiterate its recommendation made earlier for the
revival of the centrally sponsored scheme for overall development of the IWT sector. The
Committee notes that in pursuant to its recommendation the Ministry has approached the
Planning Commission  to reconsider its decision and reintroduce the centrally sponsored
scheme. The Committee desires that matter may be followed-up persistently till the final
decision is taken and also keep the Committee informed about the progress in the matter.
32. The Committee would like to reiterate its recommendation made on its 130
th Report, which
was about the proposed NW-6. The Committee was of the view that the proposed NW-6 would
boost the rural economy and provide IWT connectivity for movement of commodities between the
port of Haldia/Kolkata through Indo-Bangladesh protocol route for transit and trade in hinterland
and Bangladesh. Besides decongestion of roads and fuel saving, it would provide port hinterland
connectivity, better environment corridor and generate employment among weaker sections and
increase tourism activities in the region. The Committee had recommend that the existing protocol
routes connecting NW-1 and NW-6 and NW-2 and NW-6 may be taken up with the Bangladesh
on an expeditious way to convert these waterways into international waterways for effective
transportation of inter-country movement of goods between hinterland cities and Bangladesh. But
in the process the security concern should not be compromised in any way.
(Para No. 80)
Reply of the Government
33. The National Waterway (Lakhipur-Bhanga stretch of River Barak) Bill 2013 has been
introduced in Rajya Sabha on 22.3.2013. The development of Lakhipur-Bhanga stretch of river
Barak (NW-6) would provide an alternate connectivity to the North Eastern States of Manipur,
Mizoram, Nagaland and Tripura. These States are dependent on only road/rail connectivity passing
through the narrow “chicken neck” at Siliguri. The proposed NW-6 shall provide port connectivity
with Kolkata and Haldia through the existing Indo-Bangladesh Protocol Route. For maintenance of
the stretches of the Indo-Protocol route, which is important for transit of cargo, the Government
of India pays 10 Crore Takas every year to Bangladesh. Government of India has already taken
up with the Bangladesh Government to develop the Protocol routes with adequate width and LAD
to enable at least 330 days in a year. A Joint Standing Monitoring Mechanism (JSMM) has already
been formed. The purpose of the JSMM is to identify the stretches where dredging and other river
conservancy work would be required to enable smooth transportation and transit of goods through
the Bangladesh side of the protocol route to destination in North Eastern part of the Country.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
34. The Committee notes the reply.
DREDGING CHANNELS, TERMINALS AND NAVIGATION
35. The Committee notes that waterways do not have the required depth, width and vertical
(overboard) clearance which would allow vessels to pass through easily. It should be noted that
even if any stretch of waterway to be used is not navigable, the entire stretch becomes useless.

7
Moreover, the waterways should have all-weather operations. The Committee also notes that the
width of the canals varies from 9m to 20m. It makes movement of the barges (having width of
around 9 meters) very difficult in the narrow stretches. Also the presence of low-lying bridges
across the canals acts as hindrance for the movement of vessels with cargo. The Committee,
therefore, recommends that IWAI should make a policy standard for all the navigable canals in
order to ensure required depth and width in all the waterways.
(Para No. 81)
Reply of the Government
36. The IWAI has already classified all five NWs as per IWAI (classification of inland
waterways in India) Regulation; 2006.The developmental works are being carried out keeping in
view of the stipulations made under the above classification. Any cross structure coming up on
NWs has to follow prescribed horizontal and vertical clearance guidelines as per this notification.
It is the endeavour of the Government to ensure unhindered navigation and development of the
waterways to the standard as specified for NWs in IWAI (classification of Inland Waterways in
India) Regulation, 2006. The recommendation of the Committee to ensure required depth and width
in NWs has been noted for further necessary action.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
37. The Ministry has given assurance to ensure required depth and width in National
Waterways. However, the Committee considers that it is an interim reply, pending the final
reply to come from the Ministry.
38. The Committee also recommends that periodical dredging of the waterway wherever
essential needs to be carried out by the IWAI/Major Ports to ensure that bulk cargoes can be
handled safety and without delay.
(Para No. 82)
Reply of the Government
39. Due to the alluvial nature of NW-1 and 2 with meandering and braided channels in the
upstream portion of the waterway as well simultaneous shoal formations, it is difficult to maintain
a permanent navigational channel. IWAI has, however, been carrying out maintenance dredging in
the NW-1 and 2 using its own dredgers. With maintenance dredging and bandalling it is providing
targeted LAD, in NW-1 and NW-2 for about 330 days in a year. On NW-3, which is not an alluvial
river, IWAI is undertaking capital dredging, after which depth can be maintained, all through the
year with nominal maintenance dredging.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
40. The Committee notes the reply. Recommendations made at para 37 above may be
seen.
41. The Committee notes that the modern day navigation aids have been developed and
implemented by most of the major ports in the country. Therefore, the IWAI could seek the
expertise of the same from the major Ports like Mumbai Port Trust, Jawaharlal Nehru Port Trust,
etc., for making the navigation along the waterways hassle free. Also the GPRS used by many
agencies also can be applied in the NWs to monitor the vessels. The IWAI may take the expertise
from the agencies which are working under the Ministry of Shipping in this field. The Committee
also recommends that initiatives need to be taken to facilitate night navigation in order to meet the
quantity requirements of the industries along the waterways.
(Para No. 83)

8
Reply of the Government
42. The IWAI has already provided night navigation facilities in Diamond Harbour-Ballia stretch
(1030 km.) of NW-1, Dhubri- Silghat stretch (442 km.) of NW-2 and entire stretch of NW-3
(205 km.). Besides, IWAI has already setup DGPS stations at three locations in NW-1 and at two
locations on NW-2. One more station on NW-1 and 2 more stations on NW-2 will be commissioned
shortly. With this, the entire stretch of NW-1 and 2 will have the coverage of DGPS signals. The
entire stretch of NW-3 has the coverage of DGPS signals received from the DGPS stations
established by Director General of Lighthouses and Lightships (DGLL). This project has been
implemented in consultation with DGLL. However, as recommended by the committee, IWAI would
seek advice of the Major Ports in case required for installing and operating modern navigational aids.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
43. The Committee is happy to note the progress made with regard to night navigation
facilities in NWs 1, 2 and 3 and hopes that steps would be taken up with regard to other
NWs and the same pace of work would be maintained in future also.
44. The Committee recommends that the road/rail bridges constructed over the canals/
waterways should not become hindrances in passing of a loaded barge. As the Committee has been
informed that a bridge at Kovilthottam around half a kilometer away from Chavara towards Cochin
side, which posed problems for the free movement on waterway for Indian Rare Earths Limited
(IREL). The Committee recommends that wherever possible, existing bridges should be redeveloped
for providing the required vertical clearance.
(Para No. 84)
Reply of the Government
45. As per section 14 (1) (e) of IWAI Act (82 of 1985) IWAI is empowered to remove or alter
any obstructions or impediment in the National Waterways which may impede the safe navigation
after making compensation to person(s) suffering damage by such removal or alteration. IWAI has
already taken action for reconstruction of the Kovilthottam foot over bridge and work has recently
been entrusted by IWAI to CPWD.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
46. The Committee appreciates that the IWAI has already taken action for
reconstruction of the Kovilthottam foot over bridge and the work has been already

action-plan to utilise the funds provided to them during the Twelfth Plan. The Committee
further observes that the Ministry may also ensure compliance thereof. (Para:28)

revival of the centrally sponsored scheme for overall development of the IWT sector. The
Committee notes that in pursuant to its recommendation the Ministry has approached the
Planning Commission  to reconsider its decision and reintroduce the centrally sponsored
scheme. The Committee desires that matter may be followed-up persistently till the final

decision is taken and also keep the Committee informed about the progress in the
matter. (Para:31)

Waterways. However, the Committee considers that it is an interim reply, pending the final
reply to come from the Ministry. (Para:37)

seen.                                                                               (Para:40)
The Committee is happy to note the progress made with regard to night navigation
facilities in NWs 1, 2 and 3 and hopes that steps would be taken up with regard to other
NWs and the same pace of work would be maintained in future also. (Para:43)

reconstruction of the Kovilthottam foot over bridge and the work has been already
entrusted by IWAI to CPWD. Committee hopes that it would be completed expeditiously.

The Committee notes that the Ministry has directed the IWAI to arrange for field
visits in order to sensitise the fishermen. The Committee would like to see the compliance
of IWAI in the matter. The Committee would also like to mention here that during its last
study visit to Kerala it was observed  that the same problem of blockage of navigational
channels due to laying of fishing nets is still continuing. In view of that, the Committee

fully navigable. (Para:64)

Section 18 of the Air Corporations Act, 1953 confers monopoly right of operation of

their associates) while there is an impression that the Open Sky Policy announced by 
Government in April, 1990 permits under strict operation of Air services by Air Taxi 
Operators. · 
The Air Corporations Act, 1953 Section 18(1) provides as under:-
" ..... It shall not be lawful for any person othe r.. than the Corporation or "their 
Associates to operate any scheduled air transport service from, to, in or across . 
India ...... " 
Sub-section 2 of the said Section also provi~es::_ 
"Any person who operates a scheduled air transport service in contravention of the 
provisions of this Section shall be liable in..{espect of each offence tQ. a fine which 
may extend to One Thousand Rupees or to imprisonment which may extend to three 
months or to both." 
1.2 Under the said Act, Corporations means ''Indian Airlir.es" and "Air India Inter­
national" established under Section 3 of the Act and Corporation means either of the

be abolished. - -·-· . . 
4. Air . Taxi servicecan b~ operated both as a charter or on a non-charter basis. The 
schedule of operations not necessary to take approval for each flight separately from the

than those of Indian Airlines and Vayudoot on a pro-rated basis. This restriction will be

CHAPTER II 
VIEWS OF MINISTRY OF CIVIL AVIATION 
The Secretary, Department of Civil Aviation, while deposing before the Committee on 
9.6.1993 admitted that the present ongoing liberalisation of economic policy started from the 
aviation. He submitted that still there is no clarity 'about this Policy. After announcement of 
the Policy in April, 1990 it was felt that it required amendment in the Air Corporations Act, 
1953. Views were expressed that the policy should 9e modified und made conforming to the 
existing law. However the Government decided to go ah'ead with the policy announced in 
April, 1990 and a Bill to repeal the Air Corporations Act. 1953 was introduced in the · 
Parliament in May, 1992. He referred to the questions raised in and outside the Parliament 
about the legality of policy on Air Taxis Operation. The Secretary admited that the existing 
Law and the Policy announced are at vuriance unU Government propose to amend the 
. existing law. Secretary, Ministry of Civil Aviation also admitted before the Committee that 
generally after introduction of a Bill in the Parliamem it goes through the process to become 
Act. But in the instant case it has not happened so far. The Bill has been pending 
consideration for more than a year after its introduction in may, 1992. The main reason for 
non consideration of the amendment is that there is lack of clarity in the Government Policy 
regarding operation of Air Taxis. The intention of the Government is to amend the existing 
Air Corporations Act, 1953 so as to be consistent with the Government Policy on Air Taxi 
Operation. Till amendment is made in the existing law, the policy is to keep the operation of 
air taxis limited within the law. Under the existing law, any scheduled flights can only be 
operated by the Air Corporations mentioned under Act. Air Corporations means Air India 
or lnidian Airlines or their Associates. The Act further defines the "Scheduled air transport 
_ service" as an air transport service undertaken between the same two or more place and 
according to a published time table or with flights so regular or frequent that they constitute 
a recognisably systematic series, each flight being open to use by members of the public. 
• "The law does not prohibit operation of non scheduled flights. When asked to comment on 
the fact whether the Air Taxis Operation are at present not operating any scheduled flights 
· and whether such flights are legal under the law, the Secretary, Ministry of Civil Aviation, 
· informed. 
"That is the law according to our understunding and we have consulted the Law 
Ministry. I would like to tell the Committee that considerable amount of examination 
has taken place and what 1 am submitting before the Committee is the result of our 
interaction with legal experts. What is scheduled air transport service is already 
defined in the Act. It is very clear and it is a very tightly drafted law. Section 2 of 
the Act clearly defines what is scheduled air transport service." 
"I must submit again for the purpose of clarity that the pe~mits given by the DGCA 
for air-taxi operation are issued under the guidelines, making it abundantly clear that 
the permit is given for non-scheduled operation. DGCA cannot give permission _ for 
scheduled operation. Sir, I am confident that' I will clarify the position to your full 
satisfaction. The permit is issued only for non-scheduled operation. _Now the point 
that the hon. Chairman mentioned is that after all they are not free to operate from 
anywhere and at any time they like .. and in reality whether somebody is actually 
authorising air taxis to operate scheduled air transport service attracting the 
limitations imposed by the Act."

CHAPTER V 
CONCLUSIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS 
Prior to 1953, nine air corporations were functioning namely Air India Ltd., the 
Air Services of India Ltd., The Airways (India) Ltd .. the Bharat Airways Ltd., the 
Deccan Airways Ltd., the Himalayan Aviation Ltd., The Indian National Airways 
Ltd., the Kalinga Airlines and the Air India International Ltd. The Air Corporations 
Act, 1953 came into force with effect from 25th May, 1953 to provide for establish­
ment of Air Corporations, to facilitate acquisition of the · undertaking belonging to 
erstwhile air companies by the newly formed Air Corporations and gerterally to make 
further and better provisions for the operation of air transport services. The Act 
conferred a monopoly right of operation of scheduled air transport services on the Air 
Corporations namely Air India and Indian Airlines and their associates. 
, 5.2 (i) The major change in Government' policy came in January 1987 when 
Indian and Foreign carriers were given freedom to operate cargo flights in 
and outside the country. In ·a- way Government had 'Open Sky Policy' 
only limited to cargo flights thereafter. 
(ii) On April 11, 1990 Government went one step further. The then Civil 
Aviation Minister made a suo-moto statement in the Parliament liberalising 
the policies regarding Cargo Flights, Air Charter and Air Taxis. 
(iii) Though . the Government never admitted it but this suo-moto statement 
was taken by the people as 'Open Sky Policy' for passengers flights also. 
And as a result a number of · air taxi operators came forward and started 
their operations. Though in legal terms-:- these air taxi operators were 
operating non-scheduled flights, for all practical purposes, they were 
operating as regular private airlines. · 
(iv) It seems that when Government realised these anomalies, the then Civil 
Aviation Minister introduced a Bill in Parliament to re{>eal the Air Cor­
porations Act, 1953 on the 4th May, 1992 which is still pending. For 
strange reasons the Government is neither pressing the Bill nor withdraw­
ing it. 
(v) Due to this indecisiveness of the Government, presently there is a con­
fused policy regarding entire Aviation Industry. Neither Indian Airlines is 
allowed to retain its monopoly status nor it is thrown open to competi­
tion. And the private taxi operators are neither allowed to grow freely 
nor are asked to shut immediately. Indian Airlines is not sure about · its 
role in future Aviation Policy. Private Taxi Operators also have apprehen­
sions in their mind about their own status also. M9reover, they are con­
stantly complaining about stepmotherly treatment right from not allowing 
the time tables to be published. space problems and daily overdos~ of 
guidelines. . " --~ 
5.3 The Committee feels that such a confused and indecisive policy of Aviation 
·· , . will prove to be disasterous for the entire Aviation · Industry and, 'therefore, ·recom­
- mends that the Air Corporations Act, 1953 should be repealed in the Monsoon of 
Parliament. ' - · · : ... 
5.4 The Committee also recommends the Government to chalk out a clear cut 
Aviation Policy without further delay, defining the role and status of Govern .ment and 
D.G.C.A., national and · private air carrieJ:S and enact a new. law, if necessary.

PROJECT FINANCE MODEL 
(i) Under this model, an Indian Company with upto 100% equity of Non-Resident Indians shall 
be set up. Repatriation of dividends will be admissible on the same principle as is followed in 
respect of Non-Resident Indians while setting up industries under 74% schemes. 
(ii) Such a company may acquire aircraft by raising foreign currency loans. However. payment of 
these loans shall not be guaranteed by the Government of India or by any Indian Institutions 
(Bank or Financial Institution). The lenders may be permitted to have a charge on security of 
the aircraft. They may also obtain a guarantee of any overseas promoter or overseas 
institution. • 
(iii) Repayment of principal of foreign currency loans or interest thereon shall be permitted from 
the net foreign exchange earnings of the company . The formula for calculations of net foreign 
exchange earnings shall be worked out by the Department of Civil Aviation on the lines of the 
Reserve Bank of India formula in the case of Air India and India Airlines. 
(iv) Dividend, if any. may be allowed to be repatriated <mly after generating surplus net foreign 
exchange earnings over and above the requirements of repayment of principal and interest. 
(v) Repatriation of equity capital shall not be allowed for the firest five years of operation of the 
Air Taxi Scheme. Thereafter, it may be repatriated in the same manner, the Non-Resident 
Indians arc permitted while setting up manufacturing industries under 74% Schemes subject to 
the condition that repatriation will be only out of the accumulated net foreign exchange 
earnings that may have remained after regular payment of principal. interest and dividend, if 
any. 
~. LEASE FINANCE MODEL

be set up. Repatriation of dividends would be admissible on the principal which is followed in 
respect of Non-Resident Indians while setting up industries under 74% schemes. 
(ii) Such a company may take aircraft on lease for running Air Taxi Service. The lease rental in 
foreign exchange may be paid only from the net foreign exchange earnings of the company to 
be calculated in the manner indicated in the Project Finance Model above. 
(iii) The dividend and repatriation formula shall be as indicated in the Project Finance Model.

2. At the outset, the Chairman informed the Members of the Committee that he had 
suggested to the Secretariat that the matter regarding Government policy on Air-Taxi 
operation, its impact on Indian Airlines and the matter connected therewith should from the 
agenda of the next meeting of the Committee and Relevant papers/materials be collected 
and obtained from the Ministry. 
3. The Chairman gave the background of the subject chosen for the discussion. ·He 
informed that the Air Corporations Act of 1953 had not been ameqded. Still private airlines 
have been allowed to operate which is in consistent with the existing provisions of the Act. 
53 

The said Act permits only the domestic Indian Airlines, although the Air Corporations 
(Transfer of Undertaking & Repeal) Bill had been introduced and was pending for 
ccnsideration. Members unanimously approved the subject selected for consideration of the 
Committee. 
4. During the general discussion, some Members pointed out. that private airlines were not 
observing safety rules. These air taxis were supposed to pperate on remote routes although 
they were found to be operating on regular routes. Seating capacity had also been exceeded. 
Some MembeJs were of the view that there should be healthy competition between the 
domestic airlines and the private air taxis for the benefit of the country and for that purpose 
certain guidelines were required to be formulated to improve the performance of the · air 
taxis and the domestic airlines. Some Members reffered to the induction of _the staff in the 
private air taxis from abroad. They suggested that there should be no compromise so far the 
question of national security was concerned. They wanted Government to take all 
precautions to ensure that the security of the country was not jeopardised. Some Members 
also referred to the inherent defects in the whole set up entrusted to deal with the operation 
of Indian Airlines. They were of the view that the staff were more concerned about their 
pay and allowances rather than their output. They opined that because of the failure of 
Indian Airlines, Private air taxis had been introduced for which the Indian Airlines itself had 
to share the responsibility. 
5. The Committee thereafter decided to hear Secretary, Department of Civil Aviation 
on the above matter at its next meeting to be held on Wednesday, the 9th June, 1993 . . 
6. The Committee then adjourned at 5.45 p.m. to meet again at 10.00 a.m. the next

INTRODUCTION
I, the Chairman, Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport,
Tourism and Culture, do hereby present on its behalf this Two Hundredth Report  on ‘Development
of Tourism, National Highways and Water Transport in Kerala and Cochin Shipyard Limited’.
2. Kerala, with its uniqueness has become one of the major popular tourist destinations of the
world. The tourism industry’s contribution to the state’s economy is also commendable. However,
a need was evident to channalise Kerala’s tourism potential into a customized revenue harnessing
source without disturbing natural environment and by enhancing the cultural integrity of local
people. The Committee, in continuation to its special focus on promotion of Tourism in various
regions of India, took up the study visit to a few of tourist destinations in Kerala i.e., Kochi,
Munnar and Thekkady, between 24
th to 31 st May, 2013. The Committee made similar studies
previously on North-East region and Jammu and Kashmir.
3. The Committee examined various issues such as Cruise, Wellness, Medical, Wildlife, Tea
and Eco tourism of Kerala, Spice route and Muziris heritage projects, Rationalization of Inter-State
tourist permits, Heavy taxation, Comprehensive waste management, National Highways issues, River
tourism and linking of ports on NW3, IWT connectivity to ICTT. The Committee noted the
difficulties in achieving these objectives viz., Non-availability of Visa-on arrival, Promoting of
tourist destinations of Kerala nationally and internationally, Limited air connectivity, Maintenance and
construction of national highways, Rail-road-waterway linkages, Maintenance dredging, etc.
4. The Committee also took up the study of Cochin Shipyard Limited and examined the
challenges it is facing in Shipbuilding and Ship repair sectors.
5. The Committee expresses its gratitude to the officers of the Ministry of Tourism, Ministry
of Road Transport and Highways, Ministry of Shipping, National Highways Authority of India,
Inland Waterway Authority of India, Cochin Shipyard and Officers of State Government of Kerala,
Tour-Travel and Hotelier Associations of the State and others for their cooperation in furnishing the
required feedback and information in connection with the examination of the subject and also for
making valuable suggestions for improving the tourism scenario in these States.
6. The Committee considered and adopted the Report in its meeting held on the 23
rd August, 2013.
